12	\section{Hypotheses, scope, and concessions}
13	\label{sec:eval-hypotheses}
14	
15	This chapter reports the iteration-count, runtime, and accuracy measurements that characterise the build against \texttt{SolverLN} and LQNS. It is organised around seven falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H7) derived from the spine claim, and three explicitly conceded limits on the evidence.
16	
17	The corpus is the 61-fixture evaluation suite specified in \texttt{report/evaluation-suite-spec.md}. Partition A (36 fixtures) is the core-coverage set: single-class chains at three depths and three populations (A1, 9), multi-class shared-callee topologies under three asymmetry patterns (A2, 12), multi-server processors across three capacities and three load regimes (A3, 9), and a mixed-topology subpartition for realistic LQN configurations (A4, 6). Partition B (10 fixtures) is the F24 scale axis: task counts \{5, 10, 20, 40, 60\} in both chain and fan-out shapes at population N=30. Partition C (15 fixtures) is the boundary set: fan-out caller topologies of widths 2/3/4 at two caller capacities (C1, 6), INF-scheduled callee tasks (C2, 3), multi-class × multi-entry interaction (C3, 3), and explicit boundary cases at low load, near saturation, and the structural-predicate threshold (C4, 3). The 61-fixture evaluation suite reported here is parallel to, not a re-use of, the 63-fixture organic test corpus the contribution chapter describes; the organic suite drove the build's design history, while this suite is the systematic measurement instrument constructed against the evaluation goals.
18	
19	The spine claim the chapter characterises, in its post-ablation calibrated form, is that the difference between \texttt{SolverLN} and \texttt{SolverLNSimple} on closed LQN models is measurable on two surfaces. On iteration count, approximately three-quarters is attributable to \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{iter\_min} convergence floor (within F20), with the remaining quarter reflecting genuine algorithmic difference. On runtime, two machineries the construction omits impose per-iteration cost without iteration-count or accuracy effect: the interlock correction (F17), whose cost grows with fan-out breadth across the corpus, and the unconditional task-caller traversal computed but not consumed (F24), whose cost is detectable only on the two deepest Partition B chain fixtures and is at the noise floor elsewhere. The simple solver's omission of F20's moving-average machinery has a small accuracy cost --- loss of tight-LN-match on a minority of fixtures, which retain match within tolerance of LQNS V5 --- which we quantify. The corpus measurements support a 75.5\% / 24.5\% split rather than an exact three-quarters / one-quarter; the spine claim's "approximately" qualifier is calibrated to that figure rather than to the round fraction.
20	
21	The chapter's argumentative spine is seven falsifiable hypotheses.
22	
23	\textbf{H1 — Correctness on the core partition.} On Partition A (single-class chains, multi-class shared-callee, multi-server PS, mixed topology), \texttt{SolverLNSimple} matches \texttt{SolverLN} to within \texttt{atol = 1e-3, rtol = 5e-2} on every metric on every fixture. \textit{Confirmed by:} 36/36 Partition A fixtures classified as \texttt{match-ln} in the baseline dataset. \textit{Falsified by:} any Partition A fixture in \texttt{match-neither} or \texttt{match-lqns-only}. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-correctness}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-partition-a-reldiff}.
24	
25	\textbf{H2 — Iteration-count reduction on the core partition.} On Partition A, \texttt{SolverLNSimple} converges in strictly fewer outer iterations than \texttt{SolverLN} on every fixture. \textit{Confirmed by:} every Partition A fixture has \texttt{sim\_iters < ln\_iters}. \textit{Falsified by:} any Partition A fixture where \texttt{sim\_iters >= ln\_iters}. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-iteration-comparison}, Tables E4.1 and E4.2.
26	
27	\textbf{H3 — F24 has zero effect on iteration count.} Disabling F24 (the \texttt{ptaskcallers} random walk in \texttt{updateMetricsDefault}) changes no fixture's iteration count. \textit{Confirmed by:} every fixture's \texttt{f24off.ln\_iters == baseline.ln\_iters}. \textit{Falsified by:} any fixture where \texttt{f24off.ln\_iters != baseline.ln\_iters}. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-f24-per-partition} and Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter}.
28	
29	\textbf{H4 — F24's per-iteration cost is detectable only at deep chain depths on Partition B.} Per-iteration time decreases by 1.17$\times$ at \texttt{tasks40\_chain} and 1.45$\times$ at \texttt{tasks60\_chain} when F24 is disabled, with the chain-depth-monotone shape (1.01$\times$ at \texttt{tasks5\_chain} growing to 1.45$\times$ at \texttt{tasks60\_chain}) consistent with \texttt{ptaskcallers}'s matrix-power cost scaling with call-graph depth; all other B fixtures and every non-B partition mean sit within $\pm$6\% of unity under medianed measurement. \textit{Confirmed by:} per-iteration time \texttt{base\_ms\_per\_iter / f24\_ms\_per\_iter} above 1.15 only on the two deepest chain fixtures, with monotone growth across chain depth from \texttt{tasks5} to \texttt{tasks60}. \textit{Falsified by:} no chain-depth trend on B, or detectable F24 effect on fan-outs at any breadth (the medianed replay shows the original single-capture 1.57$\times$--1.74$\times$ flat fan-out band was JIT-noise). \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter} and Figure~\ref{fig:eval-interlock-speedup}.
30	
31	\textbf{H5 — F20 dominates the iteration-count difference.} Disabling F20 (iter\_min plus moving-average plus hard-reset) reduces total corpus iterations by at least 60\%. \textit{Confirmed by:} \texttt{f20off.ln\_iters\_total < 0.40 × baseline.ln\_iters\_total}. \textit{Falsified by:} a total iter-count reduction below 60\% — which would indicate that the moving-average or hard-reset arms were the dominant cost. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-iter-counts} (baseline total 3,801, f20off total 1,248, a 3.05x reduction).
32	
33	\textbf{H6 — F20-off carries an accuracy cost on a minority of fixtures.} Disabling F20 moves some fixtures out of the \texttt{match-ln} tolerance bar. \textit{Confirmed by:} any net loss of \texttt{match-ln} fixtures between baseline and f20off, with the size of the loss quantified per partition. \textit{Falsified by:} no change in the match-ln distribution, or a uniform accuracy degradation across the whole corpus rather than a concentrated one. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses} (baseline 50/61 match-ln, f20off 44/61, the six lost fixtures concentrated in A1/A2/C3/C4).
34	
35	\textbf{H7 — A residual algorithmic difference remains after F20+F24-off.} Even with both machineries disabled, \texttt{SolverLN} still uses more iterations than \texttt{SolverLNSimple}. \textit{Confirmed by:} \texttt{alloff.ln\_iters\_total > sim\_iters\_total}. \textit{Falsified by:} \texttt{alloff.ln\_iters\_total <= sim\_iters\_total}. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-residual}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-gap-closure} (alloff total 1,248, sim total 418, so the ablation closes (3,801 − 1,248) / (3,801 − 418) = 75.5\% of the iteration-count difference).
36	
37	Two further hypotheses were added after the Pass-2 captures (Section~\ref{sec:eval-apparatus}) extended the decomposition; they sit alongside H1--H7 rather than replacing them, and the chapter reports their evidence in Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} and Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} respectively.
38	
39	\textbf{H8 — F17 is a runtime-surface contributor whose per-iteration cost grows with fan-out breadth.} Disabling F17 (the interlock correction) changes no fixture's iteration count and no fixture's accuracy classification, but cuts per-iteration runtime by a factor that is approximately flat on chain topologies (~1.10x regardless of task count) and grows monotonically with fan-out width (1.18x at tasks=5 to 3.81x at tasks=60). \textit{Confirmed by:} every fixture's \texttt{f17off.ln\_iters == baseline.ln\_iters}; match-status distribution identical; per-iteration ratio splitting cleanly by topology shape on Partition B. \textit{Falsified by:} any iter-count or match-status change, or no monotone growth with fan-out width. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter}.
40	
41	\textbf{H9 — F15 is the load-bearing accuracy machinery for multi-entry / multi-class fixtures.} Disabling F15 (the per-iteration class-switching routing-probability update) leaves iteration counts and most-of-corpus accuracy classifications unchanged, but moves a concentrated set of multi-entry / multi-class fixtures from \texttt{match-ln} to \texttt{match-lqns-only}. \textit{Confirmed by:} \texttt{f15off.ln\_iters} bit-identical to baseline across all 61 fixtures; exactly 13 fixtures move classification, all in multi-entry / multi-class subpartitions (5 A2, 4 A4, 1 C2, 3 C3); A1, A3, B, C1, C4 unaffected. \textit{Falsified by:} a diffuse accuracy effect across the corpus, no fixture moving classification, or affected fixtures outside the multi-entry / multi-class subpartitions. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary}, F15 paragraph.
42	
43	\textbf{Limits to the evidence.} Three limits constrain how strongly the chapter can argue from the corpus measurements, and we name them upfront. First, aggregate wall-clock numbers from single captures sit inside a JIT/cache run-to-run noise band: a separately captured medianed N=3 replay of F24-off against a medianed N=4 baseline collapses F24's apparent 1.68x single-capture aggregate speedup to 1.02x, an independent measurement that the original single-capture F24 aggregate sat inside the noise band. We therefore use per-iteration B-partition timings as the load-bearing F24 evidence rather than the corpus aggregate, with the medianed replay showing F24's per-iteration effect is detectable only on the two deepest chain fixtures (\texttt{tasks40\_chain} 1.17$\times$, \texttt{tasks60\_chain} 1.45$\times$); all other B fixtures and every non-B partition mean sit within $\pm$6\% of unity (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} Finding 2). Second, the F20 condition bundles three arms (the \texttt{iter\_min} floor, the window-weighted moving-average convergence test, and the hard-reset verification pass), and the chapter decomposes them via a separate Arm A condition (the floor in isolation): the floor accounts for $\approx$92\% of F20's iter-count effect and preserves accuracy on all 61 fixtures, while the residual moving-average + hard-reset machinery is the accuracy-preserving part whose omission costs six fixtures' \texttt{match-ln} classification (Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Arm A subsection). Third, the \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} fixture passes its match-LN assertion by means of the helper's match-either-LN-or-LQNS semantics: the two references disagree on this fixture, with \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falling within tolerance of LQNS V5 (\texttt{sim\_vs\_lqns} 3.10e-02) while \texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} 4.76e-02 sits just below the \texttt{rtol} bar, and the simple solver hits its 100-iteration cap on this fixture; we carry the row with a \texttt{‡} marker and characterise it explicitly in Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} rather than absorbing it silently.
44	
45	The remainder of the chapter works through these hypotheses in order, beginning with the measurement apparatus the rest of the analysis depends on.

64	\label{sec:eval-iteration-counters}

66	Before reporting comparison numbers, this section further explains the instrumentation touched upon in the Contributions chapter that powers the testing and characterisation.
67	
68	\subsection{Test corpus}
69	\label{sec:eval-corpus}
70	
71	The 61-fixture \texttt{LayeredNetwork} evaluation suite is constructed top-down from the five measurement goals stated at the start of this chapter, separate from the collected corpus accumulated through the build history, which served as a regression net in development. The separation is desired as the corpus that drove construction cannot independently grade it, becoming victim to survivorship bias (fixtures kept only because the artefact already handles them). The evaluation corpus is therefore partitioned by the model classes the spine claim names, not by the failing fixtures the build's features responded to.
72	
73	Partition A (36 fixtures) is the positive-evidence set spanning the spine's claimed scope, containing single-class chains at three depths \{3,5,8\} $\times$ three populations \{20,50,100\} (A1, 9), multi-class shared-callee under three asymmetry patterns $\times$ two populations $\times$ two demand or think-time ratios (A2, 12), multi-server processors at three capacities \{2,4,8\} $\times$ three load regimes (A3, 9), and six mixed-topology configurations approximating realistic multi-tier systems including a three-tier web/app/DB shape, a multi-class multi-server combo, a multi-class multi-entry combo, and a four-tier deep chain (A4, 6). Fixtures in A are designed to be well-behaved. 
74	% Think times are tuned so that per-server utilisations fall in a moderate range, demand is spread across tiers rather than concentrated at the leaf where AMVA's approximation widens.
75	
76	Partition B (10 fixtures) targets F24 execution time scaling. It consists of task counts \{5, 10, 20, 40, 60\} $\times$ two shape classes (linear chain and fan-out tree). Population is held at N=30 across the partition so that runtime differences across fixtures are attributable to graph size, not to N. The spec's original N=50 was reduced to N=30 after the \texttt{tasks40\_fanout} and \texttt{tasks60\_fanout} fixtures failed to complete within practical \texttt{SolverLN} timeouts. 
77	
78	Partition C (15 fixtures) is the boundary set, deliberately constructed near regimes where the spine claim's approximations are expected to fail rather than to confirm them. Three fan-out widths \{2,3,4\} $\times$ two constrained caller capacities \{c=1, c=2\} (C1, 6) target the topologies most likely to exhibit inter-layer oscillation in the coupling iteration, three INF-scheduled callee configurations (C2, 3) exercise the bare-demand heuristic, three multi-class $\times$ multi-entry configurations (C3, 3) probe the interaction surface the multi-class/multi-entry fix addresses, and three explicit boundary cases at near-saturation (target $u \approx 0.95$), the structural-predicate threshold ($N \approx c$), and near-trivial load (C4, 3) characterise where the simple solver's approximations transition.
79	
80	The corpus was designed around the model classes the spine claim names --- single-class chains across depth and population, multi-class shared callees, multi-server PS, and mixed realistic-topology LQN configurations --- and exercises every feature the contribution chapter introduces except activity-graph awareness. It does not exercise the activity-graph machinery (Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step6}): every fixture has the canonical one-bound-activity entry shape that replies at the bound activity, with no precedence relations between activities. As a consequence the per-activity visit weights, the AND-fork $E[\max]$ correction, and the reply phase-1 / phase-2 split all sit dormant on the corpus, and the iteration-count and runtime numbers reported in this chapter therefore characterise the rest of the build. The activity-graph machinery's correctness is demonstrated separately by the targeted DAG fixtures in \texttt{SolverLNSimpleDagTest} and the phase-walker unit tests in \texttt{LqnGraphPhase1Test}; this chapter does not extend that demonstration into a quantitative per-fixture comparison against \texttt{SolverLN} or LQNS V5, and a corpus-scale evaluation of the activity-graph features remains future work.

82	\subsection{Iteration counters}
83	
84	Each solver's iteration count is recorded by a counter. \texttt{SolverLNSimple} exposes its count via \texttt{iters[0]++} in the \texttt{Runnable} passed into \texttt{iterateCoupledMva}. \texttt{SolverLN} uses \texttt{SolverLN.maxitererr.size()}, the per-iteration maximum-error array's size at termination, to get its count. \texttt{SolverLQNS} looks at \texttt{SolverLQNS.result.iter}, the LQNS binary's \texttt{result-general.iterations} attribute.
85	
86	Whilst the three counters provide a good insight into the iteration behaviour, they are not strictly comparable. \texttt{SolverLN}'s reported count includes zero-padding prepended to \texttt{maxitererr}, plus a hard-reset verification pass after the main convergence loop terminates. The reported count is therefore \texttt{actual\_iters + 2} at minimum, biasing the comparison slightly away from \texttt{SolverLN}.
87	
88	A second non-comparability is structural. One outer iteration of \texttt{SolverLNSimple} runs a bounce sweep $(0, 1, \ldots, N{-}1, N{-}2, \ldots, 1)$ over all $N$ layers ($2N{-}1$ per-layer MVA solves in a single bidirectional pass), whereas one outer iteration of \texttt{SolverLN} or LQNS runs the layer sweep in a single direction, alternating top-down/bottom-up by iteration parity ($N$ per-layer MVA solves per iteration). The $2N{-}1$-versus-$N$ asymmetry invites a per-iteration-work correction, however simply deflating \texttt{SolverLNSimple}'s iteration advantage by a factor of two is unsound: configuring \texttt{SolverLNSimple} to run with the reference solvers' single-direction elevator sweep \emph{raises} both its iteration count and its overall runtime, because per-iteration fixed costs absorb most of the $2N{-}1$-versus-$N$ asymmetry. The bounce's higher per-iteration cost is outweighed by its iteration-count saving, so the $\times 2$ correction is not a good fit. The full sweep-order study this follows from --- comparing the bounce against forward, reverse, double-forward, and the reference solvers' true-elevator order --- is reported in Section~\ref{sec:DRAFT-perf-optimisation}.
89	
90	\subsection{The match protocol}
91	\label{sec:eval-match-protocol}
92	
93	The \texttt{util.assertResultsMatch} helper runs all three solvers on each fixture, collecting each solver's output table and computing the worst-case raw relative difference across every value using \texttt{|sim − ref| / max(|ref|, 1e-6)}. NaN-vs-NaN (seen in Util and ResidT of entries) are treated as an agreement. As we designed our solver to compare with \texttt{SolverLN}, the LQNS result table has two differences that we use helpers to patch. Where LQNS reports NaN for \texttt{ResidT} on task rows, the helper synthesises this as \texttt{Q/X} from the same row's QLen and Tput. Where LQNS reports NaN for activity \texttt{Util}, the helper synthesises a per-server $X{\cdot}D/c$ from the activity's host-demand mean and the row's Tput. LQNS's $\Sigma_r X_r{\cdot}D_r$ \texttt{Util} convention is also normalised to LN's per-server convention by dividing by the host's server count $c$ on finite multi-server PS processors. The fixture pass/fail decision uses the minimum table comparison slack, passing whenever \texttt{SolverLNSimple} matches either reference.
94	
95	Each fixture is classified as \texttt{match-ln} (within \texttt{atol = 1e-3, rtol = 5e-2} of \texttt{SolverLN}), \texttt{match-lqns-only} (not within LN tolerance but within \texttt{atol = 1e-3, rtol = 1e-1} of LQNS), or \texttt{match-neither} (within tolerance of neither). This is because we use \texttt{SolverLN} as our main comparator, using a looser fallback for LQNS when the two disagree. Our evaluation corpus records 50 \texttt{match-ln} / 11 \texttt{match-lqns-only} / 0 \texttt{match-neither}. The eleven \texttt{match-lqns-only} fixtures come from similar families, all containing a fanout pattern, providing evidence of design-divergent regimes between the two reference solvers. The chapter does not adjudicate which reference is correct when they diverge, instead read as coverage against the two-reference sets.
96	
97	\subsection{Capture pipeline}
98	\label{sec:eval-capture-pipeline}
99	
100	Each fixture is solved once per solver per condition, with timings taken via \texttt{System.currentTimeMillis()} immediately bracketing the \texttt{solver.iterate*()} and \texttt{new SolverLQNS(...)} calls inside the helper. A \texttt{@BeforeAll} warmup runs a test fixture three times, with data capture suspended, sufficient to JIT-compile the core MVA kernels and solver loops. JIT-warmed timings are reproducible to within a few milliseconds at sub-100 ms scale and a few hundred milliseconds at larger scale, well below the ablation's expected effect sizes. 
101	
102	Aggregate-corpus timings from single captures, however, are sensitive to run-to-run JIT/cache state. A separately captured medianed N=3 replay of the F17/F24 ablations (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}) demonstrates this directly: F24-off's apparent 1.68x single-capture aggregate speedup collapses to 1.02x under medianing against a medianed N=4 baseline --- no algorithm-level change of that size exists --- and the joint F17+F24-off aggregate (originally 2.04x, anomalously lower than F17-off-alone's 2.67x) re-orders to 2.68x, correctly exceeding F17-off-alone's medianed 2.45x. We therefore avoid single-capture corpus-level aggregate runtime claims and use per-iteration evidence (when iteration counts match) and medianed values (where available) as the load-bearing comparison.

\chapter{Evaluation}
\label{ch:eval}








%TODO:entire intro
\section{Hypotheses, scope, and concessions}
\label{sec:eval-hypotheses}

This chapter reports the iteration-count, runtime, and accuracy measurements that characterise the build against \texttt{SolverLN} and LQNS. It is organised around seven falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H7) derived from the spine claim, and three explicitly conceded limits on the evidence.

The corpus is the 61-fixture evaluation suite specified in \texttt{report/evaluation-suite-spec.md}. Partition A (36 fixtures) is the core-coverage set: single-class chains at three depths and three populations (A1, 9), multi-class shared-callee topologies under three asymmetry patterns (A2, 12), multi-server processors across three capacities and three load regimes (A3, 9), and a mixed-topology subpartition for realistic LQN configurations (A4, 6). Partition B (10 fixtures) is the F24 scale axis: task counts \{5, 10, 20, 40, 60\} in both chain and fan-out shapes at population N=30. Partition C (15 fixtures) is the boundary set: fan-out caller topologies of widths 2/3/4 at two caller capacities (C1, 6), INF-scheduled callee tasks (C2, 3), multi-class × multi-entry interaction (C3, 3), and explicit boundary cases at low load, near saturation, and the structural-predicate threshold (C4, 3). The 61-fixture evaluation suite reported here is parallel to, not a re-use of, the 63-fixture organic test corpus the contribution chapter describes; the organic suite drove the build's design history, while this suite is the systematic measurement instrument constructed against the evaluation goals.

The spine claim the chapter characterises, in its post-ablation calibrated form, is that the difference between \texttt{SolverLN} and \texttt{SolverLNSimple} on closed LQN models is measurable on two surfaces. On iteration count, approximately three-quarters is attributable to \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{iter\_min} convergence floor (within F20), with the remaining quarter reflecting genuine algorithmic difference. On runtime, two machineries the construction omits impose per-iteration cost without iteration-count or accuracy effect: the interlock correction (F17), whose cost grows with fan-out breadth across the corpus, and the unconditional task-caller traversal computed but not consumed (F24), whose cost is detectable only on the two deepest Partition B chain fixtures and is at the noise floor elsewhere. The simple solver's omission of F20's moving-average machinery has a small accuracy cost --- loss of tight-LN-match on a minority of fixtures, which retain match within tolerance of LQNS V5 --- which we quantify. The corpus measurements support a 75.5\% / 24.5\% split rather than an exact three-quarters / one-quarter; the spine claim's "approximately" qualifier is calibrated to that figure rather than to the round fraction.

The chapter's argumentative spine is seven falsifiable hypotheses.

\textbf{H1 — Correctness on the core partition.} On Partition A (single-class chains, multi-class shared-callee, multi-server PS, mixed topology), \texttt{SolverLNSimple} matches \texttt{SolverLN} to within \texttt{atol = 1e-3, rtol = 5e-2} on every metric on every fixture. \textit{Confirmed by:} 36/36 Partition A fixtures classified as \texttt{match-ln} in the baseline dataset. \textit{Falsified by:} any Partition A fixture in \texttt{match-neither} or \texttt{match-lqns-only}. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-correctness}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-partition-a-reldiff}.

\textbf{H2 — Iteration-count reduction on the core partition.} On Partition A, \texttt{SolverLNSimple} converges in strictly fewer outer iterations than \texttt{SolverLN} on every fixture. \textit{Confirmed by:} every Partition A fixture has \texttt{sim\_iters < ln\_iters}. \textit{Falsified by:} any Partition A fixture where \texttt{sim\_iters >= ln\_iters}. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-iteration-comparison}, Tables E4.1 and E4.2.

\textbf{H3 — F24 has zero effect on iteration count.} Disabling F24 (the \texttt{ptaskcallers} random walk in \texttt{updateMetricsDefault}) changes no fixture's iteration count. \textit{Confirmed by:} every fixture's \texttt{f24off.ln\_iters == baseline.ln\_iters}. \textit{Falsified by:} any fixture where \texttt{f24off.ln\_iters != baseline.ln\_iters}. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-f24-per-partition} and Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter}.

\textbf{H4 — F24's per-iteration cost is detectable only at deep chain depths on Partition B.} Per-iteration time decreases by 1.17$\times$ at \texttt{tasks40\_chain} and 1.45$\times$ at \texttt{tasks60\_chain} when F24 is disabled, with the chain-depth-monotone shape (1.01$\times$ at \texttt{tasks5\_chain} growing to 1.45$\times$ at \texttt{tasks60\_chain}) consistent with \texttt{ptaskcallers}'s matrix-power cost scaling with call-graph depth; all other B fixtures and every non-B partition mean sit within $\pm$6\% of unity under medianed measurement. \textit{Confirmed by:} per-iteration time \texttt{base\_ms\_per\_iter / f24\_ms\_per\_iter} above 1.15 only on the two deepest chain fixtures, with monotone growth across chain depth from \texttt{tasks5} to \texttt{tasks60}. \textit{Falsified by:} no chain-depth trend on B, or detectable F24 effect on fan-outs at any breadth (the medianed replay shows the original single-capture 1.57$\times$--1.74$\times$ flat fan-out band was JIT-noise). \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter} and Figure~\ref{fig:eval-interlock-speedup}.

\textbf{H5 — F20 dominates the iteration-count difference.} Disabling F20 (iter\_min plus moving-average plus hard-reset) reduces total corpus iterations by at least 60\%. \textit{Confirmed by:} \texttt{f20off.ln\_iters\_total < 0.40 × baseline.ln\_iters\_total}. \textit{Falsified by:} a total iter-count reduction below 60\% — which would indicate that the moving-average or hard-reset arms were the dominant cost. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-iter-counts} (baseline total 3,801, f20off total 1,248, a 3.05x reduction).

\textbf{H6 — F20-off carries an accuracy cost on a minority of fixtures.} Disabling F20 moves some fixtures out of the \texttt{match-ln} tolerance bar. \textit{Confirmed by:} any net loss of \texttt{match-ln} fixtures between baseline and f20off, with the size of the loss quantified per partition. \textit{Falsified by:} no change in the match-ln distribution, or a uniform accuracy degradation across the whole corpus rather than a concentrated one. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses} (baseline 50/61 match-ln, f20off 44/61, the six lost fixtures concentrated in A1/A2/C3/C4).

\textbf{H7 — A residual algorithmic difference remains after F20+F24-off.} Even with both machineries disabled, \texttt{SolverLN} still uses more iterations than \texttt{SolverLNSimple}. \textit{Confirmed by:} \texttt{alloff.ln\_iters\_total > sim\_iters\_total}. \textit{Falsified by:} \texttt{alloff.ln\_iters\_total <= sim\_iters\_total}. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-residual}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-gap-closure} (alloff total 1,248, sim total 418, so the ablation closes (3,801 − 1,248) / (3,801 − 418) = 75.5\% of the iteration-count difference).

Two further hypotheses were added after the Pass-2 captures (Section~\ref{sec:eval-apparatus}) extended the decomposition; they sit alongside H1--H7 rather than replacing them, and the chapter reports their evidence in Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} and Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} respectively.

\textbf{H8 — F17 is a runtime-surface contributor whose per-iteration cost grows with fan-out breadth.} Disabling F17 (the interlock correction) changes no fixture's iteration count and no fixture's accuracy classification, but cuts per-iteration runtime by a factor that is approximately flat on chain topologies (~1.10x regardless of task count) and grows monotonically with fan-out width (1.18x at tasks=5 to 3.81x at tasks=60). \textit{Confirmed by:} every fixture's \texttt{f17off.ln\_iters == baseline.ln\_iters}; match-status distribution identical; per-iteration ratio splitting cleanly by topology shape on Partition B. \textit{Falsified by:} any iter-count or match-status change, or no monotone growth with fan-out width. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}, Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter}.

\textbf{H9 — F15 is the load-bearing accuracy machinery for multi-entry / multi-class fixtures.} Disabling F15 (the per-iteration class-switching routing-probability update) leaves iteration counts and most-of-corpus accuracy classifications unchanged, but moves a concentrated set of multi-entry / multi-class fixtures from \texttt{match-ln} to \texttt{match-lqns-only}. \textit{Confirmed by:} \texttt{f15off.ln\_iters} bit-identical to baseline across all 61 fixtures; exactly 13 fixtures move classification, all in multi-entry / multi-class subpartitions (5 A2, 4 A4, 1 C2, 3 C3); A1, A3, B, C1, C4 unaffected. \textit{Falsified by:} a diffuse accuracy effect across the corpus, no fixture moving classification, or affected fixtures outside the multi-entry / multi-class subpartitions. \textit{Evidence:} Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary}, F15 paragraph.

\textbf{Limits to the evidence.} Three limits constrain how strongly the chapter can argue from the corpus measurements, and we name them upfront. First, aggregate wall-clock numbers from single captures sit inside a JIT/cache run-to-run noise band: a separately captured medianed N=3 replay of F24-off against a medianed N=4 baseline collapses F24's apparent 1.68x single-capture aggregate speedup to 1.02x, an independent measurement that the original single-capture F24 aggregate sat inside the noise band. We therefore use per-iteration B-partition timings as the load-bearing F24 evidence rather than the corpus aggregate, with the medianed replay showing F24's per-iteration effect is detectable only on the two deepest chain fixtures (\texttt{tasks40\_chain} 1.17$\times$, \texttt{tasks60\_chain} 1.45$\times$); all other B fixtures and every non-B partition mean sit within $\pm$6\% of unity (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} Finding 2). Second, the F20 condition bundles three arms (the \texttt{iter\_min} floor, the window-weighted moving-average convergence test, and the hard-reset verification pass), and the chapter decomposes them via a separate Arm A condition (the floor in isolation): the floor accounts for $\approx$92\% of F20's iter-count effect and preserves accuracy on all 61 fixtures, while the residual moving-average + hard-reset machinery is the accuracy-preserving part whose omission costs six fixtures' \texttt{match-ln} classification (Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Arm A subsection). Third, the \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} fixture passes its match-LN assertion by means of the helper's match-either-LN-or-LQNS semantics: the two references disagree on this fixture, with \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falling within tolerance of LQNS V5 (\texttt{sim\_vs\_lqns} 3.10e-02) while \texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} 4.76e-02 sits just below the \texttt{rtol} bar, and the simple solver hits its 100-iteration cap on this fixture; we carry the row with a \texttt{‡} marker and characterise it explicitly in Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} rather than absorbing it silently.

The remainder of the chapter works through these hypotheses in order, beginning with the measurement apparatus the rest of the analysis depends on.
















\section{Measurement apparatus}
\label{sec:eval-apparatus}
\label{sec:eval-iteration-counters}

Before reporting comparison numbers, this section further explains the instrumentation touched upon in the Contributions chapter that powers the testing and characterisation.

\subsection{Test corpus}
\label{sec:eval-corpus}

The 61-fixture \texttt{LayeredNetwork} evaluation suite is constructed top-down from the five measurement goals stated at the start of this chapter, separate from the collected corpus accumulated through the build history, which served as a regression net in development. The separation is desired as the corpus that drove construction cannot independently grade it, becoming victim to survivorship bias (fixtures kept only because the artefact already handles them). The evaluation corpus is therefore partitioned by the model classes the spine claim names, not by the failing fixtures the build's features responded to.

Partition A (36 fixtures) is the positive-evidence set spanning the spine's claimed scope, containing single-class chains at three depths \{3,5,8\} $\times$ three populations \{20,50,100\} (A1, 9), multi-class shared-callee under three asymmetry patterns $\times$ two populations $\times$ two demand or think-time ratios (A2, 12), multi-server processors at three capacities \{2,4,8\} $\times$ three load regimes (A3, 9), and six mixed-topology configurations approximating realistic multi-tier systems including a three-tier web/app/DB shape, a multi-class multi-server combo, a multi-class multi-entry combo, and a four-tier deep chain (A4, 6). Fixtures in A are designed to be well-behaved. 
% Think times are tuned so that per-server utilisations fall in a moderate range, demand is spread across tiers rather than concentrated at the leaf where AMVA's approximation widens.

Partition B (10 fixtures) targets F24 execution time scaling. It consists of task counts \{5, 10, 20, 40, 60\} $\times$ two shape classes (linear chain and fan-out tree). Population is held at N=30 across the partition so that runtime differences across fixtures are attributable to graph size, not to N. The spec's original N=50 was reduced to N=30 after the \texttt{tasks40\_fanout} and \texttt{tasks60\_fanout} fixtures failed to complete within practical \texttt{SolverLN} timeouts. 

Partition C (15 fixtures) is the boundary set, deliberately constructed near regimes where the spine claim's approximations are expected to fail rather than to confirm them. Three fan-out widths \{2,3,4\} $\times$ two constrained caller capacities \{c=1, c=2\} (C1, 6) target the topologies most likely to exhibit inter-layer oscillation in the coupling iteration, three INF-scheduled callee configurations (C2, 3) exercise the bare-demand heuristic, three multi-class $\times$ multi-entry configurations (C3, 3) probe the interaction surface the multi-class/multi-entry fix addresses, and three explicit boundary cases at near-saturation (target $u \approx 0.95$), the structural-predicate threshold ($N \approx c$), and near-trivial load (C4, 3) characterise where the simple solver's approximations transition.

The corpus was designed around the model classes the spine claim names --- single-class chains across depth and population, multi-class shared callees, multi-server PS, and mixed realistic-topology LQN configurations --- and exercises every feature the contribution chapter introduces except activity-graph awareness. It does not exercise the activity-graph machinery (Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step6}): every fixture has the canonical one-bound-activity entry shape that replies at the bound activity, with no precedence relations between activities. As a consequence the per-activity visit weights, the AND-fork $E[\max]$ correction, and the reply phase-1 / phase-2 split all sit dormant on the corpus, and the iteration-count and runtime numbers reported in this chapter therefore characterise the rest of the build. The activity-graph machinery's correctness is demonstrated separately by the targeted DAG fixtures in \texttt{SolverLNSimpleDagTest} and the phase-walker unit tests in \texttt{LqnGraphPhase1Test}; this chapter does not extend that demonstration into a quantitative per-fixture comparison against \texttt{SolverLN} or LQNS V5, and a corpus-scale evaluation of the activity-graph features remains future work.

\subsection{Iteration counters}

Each solver's iteration count is recorded by a counter. \texttt{SolverLNSimple} exposes its count via \texttt{iters[0]++} in the \texttt{Runnable} passed into \texttt{iterateCoupledMva}. \texttt{SolverLN} uses \texttt{SolverLN.maxitererr.size()}, the per-iteration maximum-error array's size at termination, to get its count. \texttt{SolverLQNS} looks at \texttt{SolverLQNS.result.iter}, the LQNS binary's \texttt{result-general.iterations} attribute.

Whilst the three counters provide a good insight into the iteration behaviour, they are not strictly comparable. \texttt{SolverLN}'s reported count includes zero-padding prepended to \texttt{maxitererr}, plus a hard-reset verification pass after the main convergence loop terminates. The reported count is therefore \texttt{actual\_iters + 2} at minimum, biasing the comparison slightly away from \texttt{SolverLN}.

A second non-comparability is structural. One outer iteration of \texttt{SolverLNSimple} runs a bounce sweep $(0, 1, \ldots, N{-}1, N{-}2, \ldots, 1)$ over all $N$ layers ($2N{-}1$ per-layer MVA solves in a single bidirectional pass), whereas one outer iteration of \texttt{SolverLN} or LQNS runs the layer sweep in a single direction, alternating top-down/bottom-up by iteration parity ($N$ per-layer MVA solves per iteration). The $2N{-}1$-versus-$N$ asymmetry invites a per-iteration-work correction, however simply deflating \texttt{SolverLNSimple}'s iteration advantage by a factor of two is unsound: configuring \texttt{SolverLNSimple} to run with the reference solvers' single-direction elevator sweep \emph{raises} both its iteration count and its overall runtime, because per-iteration fixed costs absorb most of the $2N{-}1$-versus-$N$ asymmetry. The bounce's higher per-iteration cost is outweighed by its iteration-count saving, so the $\times 2$ correction is not a good fit. The full sweep-order study this follows from --- comparing the bounce against forward, reverse, double-forward, and the reference solvers' true-elevator order --- is reported in Section~\ref{sec:DRAFT-perf-optimisation}.

\subsection{The match protocol}
\label{sec:eval-match-protocol}

The \texttt{util.assertResultsMatch} helper runs all three solvers on each fixture, collecting each solver's output table and computing the worst-case raw relative difference across every value using \texttt{|sim − ref| / max(|ref|, 1e-6)}. NaN-vs-NaN (seen in Util and ResidT of entries) are treated as an agreement. As we designed our solver to compare with \texttt{SolverLN}, the LQNS result table has two differences that we use helpers to patch. Where LQNS reports NaN for \texttt{ResidT} on task rows, the helper synthesises this as \texttt{Q/X} from the same row's QLen and Tput. Where LQNS reports NaN for activity \texttt{Util}, the helper synthesises a per-server $X{\cdot}D/c$ from the activity's host-demand mean and the row's Tput. LQNS's $\Sigma_r X_r{\cdot}D_r$ \texttt{Util} convention is also normalised to LN's per-server convention by dividing by the host's server count $c$ on finite multi-server PS processors. The fixture pass/fail decision uses the minimum table comparison slack, passing whenever \texttt{SolverLNSimple} matches either reference.

Each fixture is classified as \texttt{match-ln} (within \texttt{atol = 1e-3, rtol = 5e-2} of \texttt{SolverLN}), \texttt{match-lqns-only} (not within LN tolerance but within \texttt{atol = 1e-3, rtol = 1e-1} of LQNS), or \texttt{match-neither} (within tolerance of neither). This is because we use \texttt{SolverLN} as our main comparator, using a looser fallback for LQNS when the two disagree. Our evaluation corpus records 50 \texttt{match-ln} / 11 \texttt{match-lqns-only} / 0 \texttt{match-neither}. The eleven \texttt{match-lqns-only} fixtures come from similar families, all containing a fanout pattern, providing evidence of design-divergent regimes between the two reference solvers. The chapter does not adjudicate which reference is correct when they diverge, instead read as coverage against the two-reference sets.

\subsection{Capture pipeline}
\label{sec:eval-capture-pipeline}

Each fixture is solved once per solver per condition, with timings taken via \texttt{System.currentTimeMillis()} immediately bracketing the \texttt{solver.iterate*()} and \texttt{new SolverLQNS(...)} calls inside the helper. A \texttt{@BeforeAll} warmup runs a test fixture three times, with data capture suspended, sufficient to JIT-compile the core MVA kernels and solver loops. JIT-warmed timings are reproducible to within a few milliseconds at sub-100 ms scale and a few hundred milliseconds at larger scale, well below the ablation's expected effect sizes. 

Aggregate-corpus timings from single captures, however, are sensitive to run-to-run JIT/cache state. A separately captured medianed N=3 replay of the F17/F24 ablations (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}) demonstrates this directly: F24-off's apparent 1.68x single-capture aggregate speedup collapses to 1.02x under medianing against a medianed N=4 baseline --- no algorithm-level change of that size exists --- and the joint F17+F24-off aggregate (originally 2.04x, anomalously lower than F17-off-alone's 2.67x) re-orders to 2.68x, correctly exceeding F17-off-alone's medianed 2.45x. We therefore avoid single-capture corpus-level aggregate runtime claims and use per-iteration evidence (when iteration counts match) and medianed values (where available) as the load-bearing comparison.


\section{Correctness}
\label{sec:eval-correctness}

The simple solver's iteration-count and runtime claims rest on its outputs being numerically faithful where they claim to be. This section establishes that, on the 36 core-coverage fixtures (Partition A), \texttt{SolverLNSimple} matches \texttt{SolverLN} to within the project's standard tolerance (\texttt{atol = 1e-3}, \texttt{rtol = 5e-2}) on every metric on every fixture.


% \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} is a four-tier multi-class chain with two entries on the middle tier; it is the realistic-chain-with-multi-entry-middle fixture the contribution chapter's late multi-class/multi-entry fix was designed to address. The simple solver runs to its 100-iteration cap on this fixture without satisfying its inner \texttt{iter\_tol = 5e-3} convergence criterion, while still producing output within 4.76e-02 of \texttt{SolverLN} — just under the \texttt{rtol = 5e-2} bar. The helper's match-either semantics absorb the borderline case: the two references disagree on this fixture, with \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falling within tolerance of LQNS V5 (\texttt{sim\_vs\_lqns} 3.10e-02) while \texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} 4.76e-02 sits just below the \texttt{rtol} bar; we report this honestly with the ‡ marker and a paragraph in Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} rather than treating the assertion pass as a clean match. The remaining 35 of 36 Partition A fixtures match \texttt{SolverLN} to at least one order of magnitude below \texttt{rtol} and most to three or four orders below.

The fixture with the largest residual, 2.81e-02, is the lowest-load, lowest-capacity multi-server configuration in the corpus, where the AMVA approximation itself has its widest deviation from the exact solution. The simple solver and \texttt{SolverLN} both substitute AMVA's \texttt{R ≈ D} approximation at the host on this fixture, where the residual is the divergence within the AMVA approximation. On the high-load fixtures, where the queueing tail dominates, the agreement tightens to 4.70e-04 or better.

The simple solver's coupling formulas were derived against the same \texttt{SolverLN.buildLayers} decomposition that \texttt{SolverLN} itself uses, and the per-layer MVA solves delegate to the same logic. The simple solver's omissions are in the outer coupling loop's machinery, none of which alters the layered fixed point the iteration converges to. The 36/36 match on Partition A therefore shows that the simple solver reaches the same fixed point through a leaner outer loop, finding an almost equal solution.

With correctness established on the core partition, iteration count and runtime can be compared on like terms, as we have shown the simple solver's faster convergence is not gained by giving up accuracy on the topologies it claims to handle.

\section{Iteration-count comparison}
\label{sec:eval-iteration-comparison}

The chapter's headline claim is that \texttt{SolverLNSimple} converges in substantially fewer outer iterations than the two comparator solvers across the corpus. This section reports those counts, inspects them by model partition for clarity, and acknowledges the one comparison bias towards \texttt{SolverLNSimple}'s count (\texttt{SolverLN}'s +2 hard-reset offset). The bounce sweep's $2N{-}1$ layer-visits per iteration are not treated as a bias to be corrected, for the reasons established in Section~\ref{sec:eval-iteration-counters}, however they cannot be compared like-for-like.

\textbf{Finding 1: Total iteration counts.} Across 61 fixtures, \texttt{SolverLNSimple} uses 418 outer iterations in total, \texttt{SolverLN} uses 3,801, and LQNS uses 774. The simple solver runs in 9.1x fewer iterations than \texttt{SolverLN} and 1.9x fewer than LQNS on the corpus aggregate as measured. These are raw counts, reported as the algorithmic-effort metric without a per-iteration-work deflator (Section~\ref{sec:eval-iteration-counters}). Two adjustments,  removing the +2 hard-reset offset for \texttt{SolverLN} and expressing \texttt{SolverLNSimple}'s count in the references' single-direction elevator-sweep units by applying a 1.65x scaling factor, narrow the gap to 5.3x for \texttt{SolverLN} and 1.1x for LQNS. 

\textbf{Finding 2: Per-partition aggregates.} The per-partition picture reveals the source of the headline gap. On every subpartition of A and on every subpartition of C, \texttt{SolverLN}'s mean iteration count is exactly 53. Partition B varies on the chain and fan-out fixtures with a larger task count, where topology-driven convergence carries \texttt{SolverLN}'s count above the floor.

\label{sec:eval-runtime}

Iteration-count savings translate into wall-clock savings only if per-iteration costs are comparable. This section reports the per-fixture wall-clock comparison across all three solvers using the instrumentation described earlier. Firstly, the LQNS time includes the REST round-trip to the Docker container that hosts LQNS, contributing a measured median 18 ms per call. \subsection{LQNS net of REST round-trip overhead}

We instrument \texttt{SolverLQNS} to record per-call \texttt{rest\_call\_ms} (the HTTP block enclosing the remote solve) and \texttt{lqns\_elapsed\_ms} (the kernel solve, parsed from the LQXO), then run a test on every fixture and subtract the REST overhead \texttt{lqns\_rest\_call\_ms − lqns\_elapsed\_ms} from each result. We see that the LQNS corpus total drops from 20,887 ms to 19,238 ms, tightening \texttt{SolverLNSimple} ÷ LQNS from 1.08x to 1.00x. 314	\section{SolverLN Ablations}
315	\label{sec:eval-ablations}

319	
320	The runtime and iteration-count gaps reported above are attributed to specific \texttt{SolverLN} machineries by ablation: each subsection disables one machinery (or arm of one) and measures the change in iteration count, runtime, and accuracy classification against baseline. Three machineries carry the decomposition. The interlock subsystem (F17 and F24) is a runtime-surface contributor with no iteration-count or accuracy effect on this corpus; the convergence-control bundle (F20) is the dominant iteration-count contributor and carries a small, concentrated accuracy cost; and a residual algorithmic difference survives once both are disabled. The three subsections take them in that order.
321	
322	\subsection{Interlock machinery (F17, F24)}
323	
324	\texttt{SolverLN}'s LQNS-V5-style interlock subsystem comprises two main runtime-surface contributors. The first is the per-iteration metric-propagation block in \texttt{updateMetricsDefault} that builds a discrete time Markov chain random walk over the call graph, via matrix powers \texttt{P\textasciicircum{}step}, to compute the probability that each task is transitively called by another. Although its stated purpose is to feed the interlock pipeline, the matrix \texttt{ptaskcallers} has no consumer, causing wasted compute. The second is the rest of the interlock pipeline. This includes \texttt{initInterlock} static analysis at construction, the per-iteration \texttt{updatePopulations} and \texttt{refreshJobs} calls, the \texttt{ClosedClass.setPopulation} writeback in \texttt{updateLayers}, and the \texttt{computeInterlockProb} consumer that reads those F17 static tables. 
325	
326	Interlock correction only fires when two or more client tasks call into the same shared server task. The corpus's topologies do not exercise that behaviour. This causes the interlock consumer in \texttt{updatePopulations} to short-circuit before computing the adjustment, meaning the computed data structures are never read. If the interlock case did fire, it would modify residence and call-service times, changing both iteration count and converged values, however \textit{on this corpus} it cannot. The two machineries are therefore predicted to add per-iteration cost without affecting iteration count or accuracy. This section confirms both predictions while characterising the contrasting shapes of their per-iteration contributions.
327	
328	\textbf{Finding 1: The interlock machinery as zero iteration-count effect and zero accuracy effect.} Disabling the \texttt{ptaskcallers} calculation leaves every fixture's iteration count identical to baseline (corpus aggregate 3,801). Disabling the interlock pipeline does the same. The metric outputs produced from each fixture are also identical. This is the simplest hypothesis confirmation in the chapter. It is not a claim that the interlock correction is useless in general, but that on a corpus that never triggers it, the supporting machinery runs every iteration and pays its full per-iteration cost despite not altering a single output.
329	
330	\textbf{Finding 2: The interlock components have complementary per-iteration scaling shapes, with F24's effect concentrated on deep chains.} F24's \texttt{ptaskcallers} per-iteration cost is detectable only on the two deepest Partition B chain fixtures (\texttt{tasks40\_chain} 1.17$\times$ speedup, \texttt{tasks60\_chain} 1.45$\times$), with every other Partition B fixture and every non-B partition mean within $\pm$6\% of unity. The depth-monotone scaling on chains (1.01$\times$ at \texttt{tasks5\_chain} growing to 1.45$\times$ at \texttt{tasks60\_chain}) is consistent with the random walk's matrix powers being proportional to call-graph size; on fan-outs F24-off is indistinguishable from baseline at any breadth (0.98--1.00$\times$). The interlock pipeline (F17) exhibits topology-shape-dependent cost in the opposite direction, approximately flat on chain fixtures (1.04--1.09$\times$) whilst fan-out fixture speedups grow monotonically from 1.13$\times$ to 3.43$\times$ as task count grows --- the data-structure refresh, where each call out contributes to the overall cost, dominates on wide fan-outs. The Finding 2 values quoted here are from a separate medianed N=3 replay (one capture per condition per run, three runs back-to-back, computed against a medianed N=4 baseline); the original single-capture data had reported a tight 43--48\% F24 speedup across all nine partitions, which the medianed replay shows was substantially JIT-noise --- the per-partition mean F24-off speedup collapses to 0.89--1.06$\times$ across all nine partitions under medianing (Table~\ref{tab:eval-f24-per-partition}), with only the deep B chains showing detectable per-iteration F24 cost.

405	\textbf{Residual per-iteration gap to \texttt{SolverLNSimple}.} On the two widest fan-out fixtures the F17 cut alone closes essentially the whole per-iteration gap to \texttt{SolverLNSimple} (\texttt{tasks60\_fanout}: baseline LN/Sim 6.5$\times$ $\to$ 1.9$\times$; \texttt{tasks40\_fanout}: 7.4$\times$ $\to$ 3.0$\times$); on chains and narrower fan-outs the residual gap to the simple solver remains multiples wide after the cut.
406	
407	\textbf{Finding 3: F17-off + F24-off jointly --- the total cost of removing the interlock subsystem on this corpus.} The joint ablation disables both pieces of interlock work simultaneously: the \texttt{ptaskcallers} compute (F24) and the entire \texttt{options.config.interlocking}-gated pipeline (F17). The corpus iteration count and \texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} match distribution are invariant (Finding 1). Under medianed N=3 captures against a medianed N=4 baseline, the corpus wall-clock under \texttt{f17\_f24off} is 921,012 ms vs baseline's 2,464,596 ms (a 2.68$\times$ aggregate speedup), and the B-partition wall-clock drops from 2,402,680 ms to 868,039 ms (a 2.77$\times$ B-aggregate speedup over the same 1,098 iterations). Table~\ref{tab:eval-f17_f24-per-iter} reports the per-fixture B per-iter values against the F17 $\times$ F24 multiplicative prediction (the per-fixture product of the F17 and F24 speedups in Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter}); under medianing, the joint cut correctly exceeds F17-alone on every B fixture and multiplicativity holds cleanly (\texttt{meas $\div$ pred} = 1.01--1.07 across all ten B fixtures).
408	
409	The table's load-bearing signals remain on the two largest fan-out fixtures (where absolute baselines are multi-second and any residual run-to-run noise is a small relative perturbation): \texttt{tasks60\_fanout} drops from 8,317.1 ms/iter baseline to 2,393.2 ms/iter joint (3.48$\times$ joint speedup), and \texttt{tasks40\_fanout} from 2,476.2 to 992.4 ms/iter (2.50$\times$). On those two fixtures the joint cut closes the LN-Sim per-iteration gap to 1.9--3.0$\times$ from baseline ratios of 6.5--7.4$\times$ --- on the widest fan-out fixture, the per-iteration gap to \texttt{SolverLNSimple} is essentially eliminated.

448	\textbf{Mechanism: refuted candidate, hedged refinement.} F24's mechanism is straightforward and visible directly in \texttt{SolverLN.java}: \texttt{ptaskcallers}'s random walk loops over task-caller pairs, with cost approximately proportional to the call graph's size. F17's mechanism is less clean. The natural candidate --- that interlock probability is computed per pair of tasks calling a common server, giving O(k$^2$) growth in fan-out width $k$ --- is refuted by direct inspection of the source. The B fan-out fixtures have exactly one client task per server (the reference task T0 makes $k$ independent calls, but each callee is called by T0 alone), so the caller-pair loops inside \texttt{findInterlockForServer} short-circuit at the \texttt{clientEntryPairs.size() < 2} guard before doing real work. The caller-pair quadratic loops never execute on these fixtures, and \texttt{computeInterlockProb} is never invoked; the cost responsible for the observed scaling must lie elsewhere. A refined mechanism is consistent with the source but is \textit{not} provable from \texttt{SolverLN.java} alone: the fan-out caller's host layer (P0) carries one closed class per outgoing synchronous call, so P0's class count grows linearly with $k$; per-iteration interlock work calls \texttt{refreshJobs()} on every layer, which hard-rebuilds each layer's \texttt{NetworkStruct} through O(nclasses) inner loops, and the downstream per-layer MVA/NC solve may re-derive cached state after the refresh. The combination is consistent with the measured scaling --- extra cost rides on P0's growing class count, amplified by whatever downstream solver work the rebuild triggers --- but the amplification step is not visible in \texttt{SolverLN.java}; confirming it requires either profiling the network solver or auditing \texttt{SolverMVA} / \texttt{SolverNC}'s caching behaviour across hard refreshes. The chapter therefore states what the data shows (F17's per-iteration cost grows with fan-out breadth) without claiming the source explains it. The full source-level investigation, with the refutation and the refined mechanism developed in detail, is recorded in \texttt{report/data/f17-mechanism-findings.md}.

450	\subsubsection*{Targeted F17 accuracy probe on interlock-triggering models}
451	\label{sec:eval-interlock-accuracy-probe}
452	
453	Finding 1's accuracy claim is scoped to the 61-fixture corpus, which (by inspection of the \texttt{findInterlockForServer} branch-point test, in the interlock subsection's mechanism paragraph above) never exercises the interlock correction. That scoping leaves an open question: on models that \textit{do} trigger interlock, does the F17 correction make a measurable accuracy difference? This subsection answers it with a small targeted probe, kept separate from the main corpus so the interlock subsection's corpus-aggregate statistics remain calibrated against their original scope.
454	
455	\textbf{Methodology.} Four fixtures, all 3-tier (or 4-tier) diamonds where one upstream reference task \texttt{R0} fans out to two intermediates which call a shared single-server FCFS server \texttt{TS}: \texttt{P1\_directInterlock} at $n \in \{8, 16\}$, \texttt{P2\_transitiveInterlock} (extra intermediate layer between branch point and shared server), and \texttt{P4\_multiclassInterlock} (two parallel diamonds, two reference classes, shared bottleneck). The FCFS scheduling on \texttt{TS} is essential: \texttt{initInterlock} skips INF-scheduled task servers at line 4002 of \texttt{SolverLN.java}, so the corpus's INF-on-PS pattern (used throughout \texttt{sharedCalleeMC} and similar) cannot reach the correction even when topologically interlock-shaped. Each fixture is solved under three configurations: \texttt{lqsim} (LQNS discrete-event simulator, 100k samples, ground truth), \texttt{ln\_baseline} (\texttt{SolverLN} with \texttt{config.interlocking = true}), and \texttt{ln\_f17off} (\texttt{SolverLN} with \texttt{config.interlocking = false}). The F17 accuracy contribution is reported as the difference between the two LN configurations' worst-case relative difference vs \texttt{lqsim} across \{QLen, RespT, Tput\} on every matching node name. \texttt{Util} is excluded because LQNS reports total $\Sigma X{\cdot}D$ while \texttt{SolverLN} reports per-server $\Sigma X{\cdot}D / c$ on multi-server PS hosts --- the convention mismatch would dominate any rel-diff comparison. The fixtures and runner live at \texttt{jar/src/test/java/jline/solvers/ln\_simple/fixtures/InterlockProbeFixtures.java} and \texttt{SolverLNInterlockAccuracyTest.java} respectively; the captured CSV is \texttt{report/data/interlock-probe.csv}, the per-node tables (one row per model node, columns per solver) are at \texttt{report/data/interlock-probe-tables.md}. The reported \texttt{lqsim} rel-diff has a Monte Carlo standard error: re-running each fixture with a fresh \texttt{lqsim} sample (\texttt{InterlockProbeFullTableTest}) and recomputing the worst rel-diff from the resulting tables shifts each cell by $\leq 0.5$ percentage points relative to the captured CSV, well below the F17 contribution magnitude reported here.
456	
457	\textbf{Probe-extension attempts dropped.} Three additional fixtures --- asymmetric demand (4:1 and 2:1 splits), low TS utilisation, and 3-way fan-out --- were each attempted as regime-coverage extensions. All three surfaced the same \texttt{SolverLN} port-specific weakness: \texttt{ln\_baseline} diverged from \texttt{lqsim} by 19--49\% while \texttt{lqns} analytical stayed within 4--6\%, F17 toggle changed the LN rel-diff by $\leq 2$\,pp on top of that 20--50\,pp baseline error. The fixtures were dropped because they contaminate the F17 ablation reading. \texttt{SolverLN}'s interlock implementation appears to have accuracy weaknesses outside the high-utilisation, narrow-fan-out, symmetric-demand regime --- a separate issue from F17, named as future work.

484	\subsubsection*{Accuracy-preserving runtime frontier}
485	
486	The fact that F17 has zero iteration-count effect and zero accuracy effect means its per-iteration cut can be stacked with the iteration-count cut of F20 to produce a combined runtime cut without accuracy loss. A combined ablation condition — disabling F17, the F20 \texttt{iter\_min} floor (Arm A; see Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20}), F21, and F24 — was measured against baseline. The result is \textbf{7.99x aggregate speedup with zero fixture accuracy degradation}: corpus iteration total 1,452 (matching the Arm A condition; F17, F21, F24 add zero iter-count change on top of Arm A), corpus wall-clock 320,472 ms, match-status distribution 50/61 \texttt{match-ln} and 11/61 \texttt{match-lqns-only} — identical to baseline on both axes.
487	
488	The closest single-cut comparison is the full F20-off condition (Arm A + B + C bundled): 8.29x aggregate speedup, with six fixtures degraded out of \texttt{match-ln} into \texttt{match-lqns-only} (A1\_chain\_d3\_N100, three A2\_multiclassA fixtures, C3\_multiclassMultiEntry\_asymmetric, C4\_lowDemand). The frontier point is a trade: the combined cut gives up approximately 0.30x of aggregate speedup in exchange for preserving all six fixtures' \texttt{match-ln} classification.
489	
490	\textbf{Why combined is not faster than F20-off alone.} Despite cutting more machinery (F17 + Arm A + F21 + F24 vs F20-off's three F20 arms only), the combined condition is slightly slower because F17, F21, and F24 are per-iteration cuts while F20-off is an iteration-count cut. F20-off drops corpus iterations by 67\% (3,801 → 1,248); per-iteration savings in the combined condition therefore apply to fewer iterations than they would at baseline scale. The iteration-count advantage of full F20-off over Arm A (1,248 vs 1,452, ~14\% fewer iterations) is large enough to outweigh combined's per-iteration cost advantage from F17/F21/F24. Per-iteration cuts compound multiplicatively with iteration-count cuts: cutting both surfaces is faster than cutting either alone, but cutting more on one surface than the other reaches diminishing returns.
491	
492	\textbf{Outlier honesty for the frontier.} Both 7.99x and 8.29x are aggregate-weighted measurements and, like the F17 per-fixture ratios above, they are dominated by the largest fan-out fixtures. The frontier \textit{trade} — −0.30x aggregate speedup in exchange for preserving six fixtures' accuracy — is robust against outlier-discounting because both sides of the trade are inflated by the same fixtures; the inflation cancels in the differential. The absolute speedup multipliers (7.99x, 8.29x) are not corpus-typical and would shrink substantially on a corpus without the largest fan-out fixtures. The robust headline is the per-fixture accuracy preservation in the combined cut, not the aggregate multiplier; the accuracy-preserving frontier is a Chapter~\ref{ch:eval} finding, not a spine claim, and the spine names F17 and F24 as runtime-surface contributors without committing to a combined-cut speedup figure.

501	\subsection{Convergence floor, moving-average, and hard-reset (F20)}
502	 
503	\texttt{SolverLN.converged(it)} is the per-iteration convergence test that decides whether the layer fixed-point iteration may stop at the given iteration. It combines four pieces of machinery: an \texttt{iter\_min = max(2$\cdot$E, ceil(iter\_max/4))} floor that delays convergence until a minimum iteration count has been reached, a sliding-window weighted average over \texttt{QN}/\texttt{UN}/\texttt{RN}/\texttt{TN} that smooths per-iteration metric noise, a three-iteration confirmation checking that the smoothed metrics remain within tolerance, and a hard-reset verification pass that re-solves every layer to confirm a fixed point survives reset. \texttt{SolverLNSimple} takes the opposite approach, sacrificing potential instability mitigations for faster convergence, just checking if \texttt{max(|X\_l $-$ X\_l\_prev|) < tol} holds for a single iteration. This is the largest single contributor to the iteration-count difference the spine claim names. Disabling it results in just a small and concentrated accuracy cost.
504	
505	\textbf{Finding 1: F20-off cuts total iteration count by 67.2\%.} The corpus total drops from 3,801 baseline iterations to 1,248 (a 3.05x reduction). It is the \texttt{iter\_min} floor that accounts for the majority of the iteration-count difference, with the reduction concentrating on the floor-binding fixtures. The 55 fixtures that sat at 53 iterations in baseline land at 5–32 iterations in this ablation, exposing their true convergence point.

The other four fixtures (\texttt{A1\_chain\_d3\_N100}, three \texttt{A2\_multiclassA} variants) exceed the 300-second simulator-side limit of the LQNS REST container even at low \texttt{run\_time} budgets, so their lqsim direction is undetermined and not reported.
572	
573	\textbf{The C3 anomaly.} The F20-off run reports \texttt{C3\_multiclassMultiEntry\_asymmetric} at $\Delta_{\text{f20off}}$ = 15.8\%; the corresponding alloff run reports a noticeably larger drift and fires an \texttt{assertEquals} failure on \texttt{AS1.ResidT} while the matching f20off row did not. F24 has zero effect on \texttt{SolverLN}'s output anywhere else in the corpus, and the two rel diffs straddle whatever pass/fail threshold the assertion uses; floating-point ordering across the F24 compute path is enough to shift the metric across the boundary without altering the fixture's qualitative classification. The two drift numbers tell a consistent story even when the pass/fail bit flips. The alloff anomaly is recorded for completeness and investigated as future work rather than treated as evidence against the spine claim.
574	
575	\textbf{The three-arm decomposition.} F20-off disables three arms simultaneously (iter\_min floor, moving-average, hard-reset); the headline measurements above report the bundle as a whole. The decomposition itself — which arm carries the iter-count cut, which arm carries the accuracy cost — is reported in the subsection below, where an isolated-floor condition (\texttt{A2\_arm\_A}) makes the arms separable.
576	
577	\subsubsection*{Arm A: the \texttt{iter\_min} floor in isolation}
578	
579	A late addition to the ablation set isolates the F20 floor from the moving-average and hard-reset machinery. The \texttt{A2\_arm\_A} condition splits \texttt{SolverLN}'s single \texttt{iter\_min} parameter into two: \texttt{iter\_min\_convergence = 1} (disabling the floor on the convergence-detection path) while leaving \texttt{iter\_min\_avg = max(2$\cdot$E, iter\_max/4)} at its baseline value (keeping the moving-average window-weighted detection rule intact). Arm A is therefore the floor cut alone; Arms B (moving-average) and C (hard-reset verification) remain in place.
580	
581	\textbf{Finding (Arm A): The floor alone accounts for $\approx$92\% of F20's iteration-count effect.} The Arm A condition reduces corpus-aggregate \texttt{SolverLN} iterations from 3,801 baseline to 1,452 — a 62\% drop. The full F20-off condition (Arm A + B + C bundled) reduces to 1,248 (a 67.2\% drop). Comparing the two: \texttt{(3,801 $-$ 1,452) / (3,801 $-$ 1,248) = 2,349 / 2,553 = 91.99\%}. The iter\_min floor is the dominant arm of F20 on the iteration-count surface; the moving-average and hard-reset arms together contribute the remaining $\approx$8\% (the additional 204 iterations cut going from Arm A's 1,452 to the bundle's 1,248). The chapter's previous static-reading prediction — that the floor dominates because 55/61 baseline fixtures sit at it — is confirmed quantitatively, and the bundled F20 attribution sharpens to the floor specifically.
582	
583	\textbf{Finding (Arm A): The floor cut leaves \texttt{SolverLN}'s output essentially unchanged.} Measured directly on LN's per-cell outputs, Arm A's drift from baseline peaks at 3.5\% (\texttt{C4\_lowDemand}, \texttt{E1.respt}) and stays below 3\% on every other fixture (46 of 61 below 1\%); compare to the full F20-off condition, where six fixtures drift by 5.6\% to 32.0\% (Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses}'s $\Delta_{\text{Arm A}}$ column reports the per-fixture Arm A drift alongside the f20off drift, an order of magnitude smaller on every affected fixture). The cut that produces the larger drift on the six affected fixtures is therefore Arms B+C (moving-average + hard-reset), not Arm A. The same Arm A condition is the one whose match-status distribution is unchanged from baseline (50/61 \texttt{match-ln}, 11/61 \texttt{match-lqns-only}) — what was previously measurable only as a coarse classification holding is, in the direct LN-vs-LN measurement, a $\leq$3.5\% drift on the worst-case cell of the worst-case fixture.
584	
585	\textbf{Wall-clock diagnostic: Arm A calibrates the Simpson's-paradox inflation on F20-axis rows.} Arm A reports 4.20$\times$ corpus-aggregate wall-clock speedup, decomposing arithmetically as 2.62$\times$ iteration-count reduction times 1.60$\times$ corpus-aggregate per-iteration speedup. But Arm A removes no per-iteration work by construction --- only the convergence floor is touched, and the moving-average and hard-reset machinery still runs on every iteration. The 1.60$\times$ apparent per-iteration speedup is therefore fixture-mix Simpson's-paradox in full: cutting the floor disproportionately removes iterations from cheap A/C fixtures, so the surviving iteration pool is heavier on average. The per-fixture median ms/iter ratio under Arm A is 1.00$\times$ exactly, confirming the diagnostic. This calibrates the Per-iter $\times$ column in Table~\ref{tab:eval-aggregate-runtime-conditions}: any row that changes the iteration count carries a fixture-mix component on the order of 1.6$\times$ that is not a real per-iteration effect.
586	
587	\textbf{The decomposition resolved.} The three arms separate cleanly along the two surfaces. Arm A (the floor) drives the iteration-count effect: $\approx$92\% of F20's iter-count contribution. Arms B and C (moving-average + hard-reset) drive the accuracy effect: on the six F20-off-degraded fixtures, baseline-to-Arm-A LN drift stays under 3.5\% while baseline-to-f20off LN drift reaches 32\% — Arms B+C carry essentially all of the per-cell accuracy cost. The floor is the iter-count machinery; the moving-average + hard-reset is the accuracy-preservation machinery. The two are separable by construction, and the dataset now isolates them.
588	
589	\textbf{Asymmetric cost of Arm B across the corpus.} The moving-average arm's protective value is locally targeted rather than uniform: it earns its keep on the six oscillating fixtures (A1, three A2s, C3, C4) where small-amplitude oscillation around the fixed point produces the 5–32\% drift Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses} reports, but on B fanouts the same machinery is pure overhead. The \texttt{tasks20/40/60\_fanout} fixtures sit at baseline counts of 81/161/201 and collapse to 21/22/22 under F20-off; LN drift on those fixtures is under 0.45\% — well below Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses}'s 5.6\% inclusion floor — so the 60–180 extra iterations bought essentially nothing on the accuracy surface and inflated the runtime-dominant partition's iteration count by an order of magnitude. The design is fixture-blind, so the protective overhead is paid uniformly to insure against the minority that needs it; the corpus shows the premium is non-trivial precisely on the partition the chapter most cares about for runtime (Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime} Finding 2). This is a defensible engineering choice, not a bug, but it is the load-bearing rationale for why the Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} \texttt{combined} frontier preserves Arms B and C rather than cutting them indiscriminately.
590	
591	\textbf{Spine implication.} On the iteration-count surface, the F20 attribution sharpens to the \texttt{iter\_min} convergence floor specifically: the chapter's previous bundled F20 description retains its accuracy here as a machinery-level naming, but the iter-count share belongs to the floor arm, not to the bundle. On the accuracy surface, the moving-average + hard-reset arms are the load-bearing machinery: omitting them shifts \texttt{SolverLN}'s output by 5–32\% on the six affected fixtures, where omitting only Arm A leaves the same fixtures within $\leq$3.5\% drift. The simple solver's omission of F20 is therefore more precisely an omission of the bundle, with the accuracy cost the chapter reports being the cost of omitting Arms B and C; omitting Arm A alone would carry essentially no accuracy cost on the corpus and would account for $\approx$92\% of the iteration-count cut. The Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} accuracy-preserving frontier subsection above leans directly on this decomposition.
592

594	  \centering

615	
616	F20-off alone covers roughly three-quarters of the corpus-aggregate iteration-count difference (F24 contributes zero iteration-count change, as the interlock ablation above reports; F17 likewise). The residual quarter is genuinely algorithmic difference, taken up in the residual subsection below. The accuracy cost of F20-off is small enough to be acceptable for the simple solver's design point (avoiding the smoothing machinery in exchange for matching \texttt{SolverLN} on the partitions it claims) but is not negligible, and any decision to remove F20 from \texttt{SolverLN} in production would need to weigh it.
617	
618	F20 is dominant; F17 and F24 add per-iteration cost but no iteration-count change (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}). The residual subsection that follows isolates the genuinely algorithmic difference that remains once the floor is removed.
619	
620	
621	
622	\subsection{Residual: the genuine algorithmic difference}
623	
624	If F20 explained the whole iteration-count difference, disabling it would produce iteration counts matching the simple solver's. It does not — a residual of about a quarter of the total difference persists. Disabling F24 alongside F20 (the \texttt{alloff} condition) reaches the same 1,248-iteration corpus total as F20-off alone, because F24 contributes zero iteration-count change (established in the interlock ablation above); F17 likewise contributes zero, so adding it to the disabled set would not move the residual either. The section uses the \texttt{alloff} totals interchangeably with F20-off on the iteration-count surface and quantifies the residual that survives.
625	
626	\textbf{Finding 1: The \texttt{alloff} ablation accounts for 75.5\% of the iteration-count difference.} The corpus-aggregate computation is direct. Baseline \texttt{SolverLN} total: 3,801 iterations. Alloff \texttt{SolverLN} total: 1,248 iterations. \texttt{SolverLNSimple} total: 418 iterations. The ablation accounts for (3,801 − 1,248) / (3,801 − 418) = 2,553 / 3,383 = 75.5\% of the difference. The remaining 24.5\% (1,248 − 418 = 830 iterations corpus-wide) is what the simple solver gains beyond turning off F20 and F24 — the residual that reflects the genuinely algorithmic difference between the two solvers. This is the chapter's central decomposition number and the one the spine claim is calibrated against.
