\section{SolverLN Ablations}
\label{sec:eval-ablations}
\label{sec:eval-interlock}
\label{sec:eval-f20}
\label{sec:eval-residual}

The runtime and iteration-count gaps reported above are attributed to specific \texttt{SolverLN} machineries by ablation: each subsection disables one machinery (or arm of one) and measures the change in iteration count, runtime, and accuracy classification against baseline. Three machineries carry the decomposition. The interlock subsystem (F17 and F24) is a runtime-surface contributor with no iteration-count or accuracy effect on this corpus; the convergence-control bundle (F20) is the dominant iteration-count contributor and carries a small, concentrated accuracy cost; and a residual algorithmic difference survives once both are disabled. The three subsections take them in that order.

\subsection{Interlock machinery (F17, F24)}

\texttt{SolverLN}'s LQNS-V5-style interlock subsystem comprises two main runtime-surface contributors. The first is the per-iteration metric-propagation block in \texttt{updateMetricsDefault} that builds a discrete time Markov chain random walk over the call graph, via matrix powers \texttt{P\textasciicircum{}step}, to compute the probability that each task is transitively called by another. Although its stated purpose is to feed the interlock pipeline, the matrix \texttt{ptaskcallers} has no consumer, causing wasted compute. The second is the rest of the interlock pipeline. This includes \texttt{initInterlock} static analysis at construction, the per-iteration \texttt{updatePopulations} and \texttt{refreshJobs} calls, the \texttt{ClosedClass.setPopulation} writeback in \texttt{updateLayers}, and the \texttt{computeInterlockProb} consumer that reads those F17 static tables. 

Interlock correction only fires when two or more client tasks call into the same shared server task. The corpus's topologies do not exercise that behaviour. This causes the interlock consumer in \texttt{updatePopulations} to short-circuit before computing the adjustment, meaning the computed data structures are never read. If the interlock case did fire, it would modify residence and call-service times, changing both iteration count and converged values, however \textit{on this corpus} it cannot. The two machineries are therefore predicted to add per-iteration cost without affecting iteration count or accuracy. This section confirms both predictions while characterising the contrasting shapes of their per-iteration contributions.

\textbf{Finding 1: The interlock machinery as zero iteration-count effect and zero accuracy effect.} Disabling the \texttt{ptaskcallers} calculation leaves every fixture's iteration count identical to baseline (corpus aggregate 3,801). Disabling the interlock pipeline does the same. The metric outputs produced from each fixture are also identical. This is the simplest hypothesis confirmation in the chapter. It is not a claim that the interlock correction is useless in general, but that on a corpus that never triggers it, the supporting machinery runs every iteration and pays its full per-iteration cost despite not altering a single output.

\textbf{Finding 2: The interlock components have complementary per-iteration scaling shapes, with F24's effect concentrated on deep chains.} F24's \texttt{ptaskcallers} per-iteration cost is detectable only on the two deepest Partition B chain fixtures (\texttt{tasks40\_chain} 1.17$\times$ speedup, \texttt{tasks60\_chain} 1.45$\times$), with every other Partition B fixture and every non-B partition mean within $\pm$6\% of unity. The depth-monotone scaling on chains (1.01$\times$ at \texttt{tasks5\_chain} growing to 1.45$\times$ at \texttt{tasks60\_chain}) is consistent with the random walk's matrix powers being proportional to call-graph size; on fan-outs F24-off is indistinguishable from baseline at any breadth (0.98--1.00$\times$). The interlock pipeline (F17) exhibits topology-shape-dependent cost in the opposite direction, approximately flat on chain fixtures (1.04--1.09$\times$) whilst fan-out fixture speedups grow monotonically from 1.13$\times$ to 3.43$\times$ as task count grows --- the data-structure refresh, where each call out contributes to the overall cost, dominates on wide fan-outs. The Finding 2 values quoted here are from a separate medianed N=3 replay (one capture per condition per run, three runs back-to-back, computed against a medianed N=4 baseline); the original single-capture data had reported a tight 43--48\% F24 speedup across all nine partitions, which the medianed replay shows was substantially JIT-noise --- the per-partition mean F24-off speedup collapses to 0.89--1.06$\times$ across all nine partitions under medianing (Table~\ref{tab:eval-f24-per-partition}), with only the deep B chains showing detectable per-iteration F24 cost.

\textbf{Residual per-iteration gap to \texttt{SolverLNSimple}.} On the two widest fan-out fixtures the F17 cut alone closes essentially the whole per-iteration gap to \texttt{SolverLNSimple} (\texttt{tasks60\_fanout}: baseline LN/Sim 6.5$\times$ $\to$ 1.9$\times$; \texttt{tasks40\_fanout}: 7.4$\times$ $\to$ 3.0$\times$); on chains and narrower fan-outs the residual gap to the simple solver remains multiples wide after the cut.

\textbf{Finding 3: F17-off + F24-off jointly --- the total cost of removing the interlock subsystem on this corpus.} The joint ablation disables both pieces of interlock work simultaneously: the \texttt{ptaskcallers} compute (F24) and the entire \texttt{options.config.interlocking}-gated pipeline (F17). The corpus iteration count and \texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} match distribution are invariant (Finding 1). Under medianed N=3 captures against a medianed N=4 baseline, the corpus wall-clock under \texttt{f17\_f24off} is 921,012 ms vs baseline's 2,464,596 ms (a 2.68$\times$ aggregate speedup), and the B-partition wall-clock drops from 2,402,680 ms to 868,039 ms (a 2.77$\times$ B-aggregate speedup over the same 1,098 iterations). Table~\ref{tab:eval-f17_f24-per-iter} reports the per-fixture B per-iter values against the F17 $\times$ F24 multiplicative prediction (the per-fixture product of the F17 and F24 speedups in Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter}); under medianing, the joint cut correctly exceeds F17-alone on every B fixture and multiplicativity holds cleanly (\texttt{meas $\div$ pred} = 1.01--1.07 across all ten B fixtures).

The table's load-bearing signals remain on the two largest fan-out fixtures (where absolute baselines are multi-second and any residual run-to-run noise is a small relative perturbation): \texttt{tasks60\_fanout} drops from 8,317.1 ms/iter baseline to 2,393.2 ms/iter joint (3.48$\times$ joint speedup), and \texttt{tasks40\_fanout} from 2,476.2 to 992.4 ms/iter (2.50$\times$). On those two fixtures the joint cut closes the LN-Sim per-iteration gap to 1.9--3.0$\times$ from baseline ratios of 6.5--7.4$\times$ --- on the widest fan-out fixture, the per-iteration gap to \texttt{SolverLNSimple} is essentially eliminated.

\textbf{Multiplicativity holds cleanly under medianed measurement.} The \texttt{meas $\div$ pred} column sits at 1.01--1.07 on every B fixture, with the corpus-aggregate joint speedup (2.68$\times$) within 7\% of the multiplicative prediction (F17 $\times$ F24 = 2.45 $\times$ 1.02 = 2.50$\times$). The medianed replay resolves the ambiguity decisively in favour of reading (b): with multiplicativity holding to within 7\% under repeated-run averaging, the original sub-additivity was substantially JIT-noise rather than evidence of shared underlying cost between F17 and F24. The two cuts attack disjoint per-iteration work --- consistent with their distinct mechanisms (\texttt{ptaskcallers}'s matrix powers for F24, the \texttt{options.config.interlocking}-gated pipeline for F17) --- and removing both saves what the multiplicative prediction would suggest.

\textbf{Finding 4: Medianed N=3 captures dissolve the aggregate-ratio anomaly and re-anchor F24's contribution at the noise floor.} The original single-capture aggregate speedups (\texttt{f24off} 1.68$\times$, \texttt{f17off} 2.67$\times$, \texttt{f17\_f24off} 2.04$\times$) included an algorithmic contradiction: the joint cut's 2.04$\times$ was \textit{lower} than the F17-alone 2.67$\times$ despite the joint condition disabling strictly more machinery. Under medianed N=3 captures against a medianed N=4 baseline, the ordering becomes algorithmically consistent: \texttt{f24off} 1.02$\times$, \texttt{f17off} 2.45$\times$, \texttt{f17\_f24off} 2.68$\times$, with \texttt{f17\_f24off} correctly exceeding \texttt{f17off}. The medianed F24-off corpus speedup (1.02$\times$) confirms the Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime} noise-band framing: F24's apparent corpus-aggregate effect under single-capture measurement was substantially JIT-noise, sitting essentially at the unity line under repeated-run averaging. The B-partition per-iteration evidence (Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter}) therefore carries the load for F24: deep-chain fixtures show 1.17$\times$ (\texttt{tasks40\_chain}) and 1.45$\times$ (\texttt{tasks60\_chain}) F24-off speedup --- consistent with \texttt{ptaskcallers}'s matrix-power cost growing with call-graph depth --- while shallow chains and all fan-outs show F24-off effects within $\pm$3\% of baseline. F17-off's aggregate (2.45$\times$) sits well outside the noise floor and is preserved at qualitatively similar magnitude to the original single-capture reading (2.67$\times$); the spine claim that F17 is a runtime-surface contributor whose per-iteration cost grows with fan-out breadth (H8) remains calibrated to the per-fixture scaling shape, which the medianed replay reproduces at slightly compressed magnitudes (1.04--1.09$\times$ flat on chains, 1.13--3.43$\times$ growing on fan-outs). The honest characterisation of all three machineries' per-iteration costs is the \textit{scaling shape} visible in Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter} and the load-bearing rows of Table~\ref{tab:eval-f17_f24-per-iter} (the two largest fan-outs, where absolute times are large enough for any residual run-to-run noise to be a small relative perturbation).

\textbf{Mechanism: refuted candidate, hedged refinement.} F24's mechanism is straightforward and visible directly in \texttt{SolverLN.java}: \texttt{ptaskcallers}'s random walk loops over task-caller pairs, with cost approximately proportional to the call graph's size. F17's mechanism is less clean. The natural candidate --- that interlock probability is computed per pair of tasks calling a common server, giving O(k$^2$) growth in fan-out width $k$ --- is refuted by direct inspection of the source. The B fan-out fixtures have exactly one client task per server (the reference task T0 makes $k$ independent calls, but each callee is called by T0 alone), so the caller-pair loops inside \texttt{findInterlockForServer} short-circuit at the \texttt{clientEntryPairs.size() < 2} guard before doing real work. The caller-pair quadratic loops never execute on these fixtures, and \texttt{computeInterlockProb} is never invoked; the cost responsible for the observed scaling must lie elsewhere. A refined mechanism is consistent with the source but is \textit{not} provable from \texttt{SolverLN.java} alone: the fan-out caller's host layer (P0) carries one closed class per outgoing synchronous call, so P0's class count grows linearly with $k$; per-iteration interlock work calls \texttt{refreshJobs()} on every layer, which hard-rebuilds each layer's \texttt{NetworkStruct} through O(nclasses) inner loops, and the downstream per-layer MVA/NC solve may re-derive cached state after the refresh. The combination is consistent with the measured scaling --- extra cost rides on P0's growing class count, amplified by whatever downstream solver work the rebuild triggers --- but the amplification step is not visible in \texttt{SolverLN.java}; confirming it requires either profiling the network solver or auditing \texttt{SolverMVA} / \texttt{SolverNC}'s caching behaviour across hard refreshes. The chapter therefore states what the data shows (F17's per-iteration cost grows with fan-out breadth) without claiming the source explains it. The full source-level investigation, with the refutation and the refined mechanism developed in detail, is recorded in \texttt{report/data/f17-mechanism-findings.md}.

\subsubsection*{Targeted F17 accuracy probe on interlock-triggering models}
\label{sec:eval-interlock-accuracy-probe}

Finding 1's accuracy claim is scoped to the 61-fixture corpus, which (by inspection of the \texttt{findInterlockForServer} branch-point test, in the interlock subsection's mechanism paragraph above) never exercises the interlock correction. That scoping leaves an open question: on models that \textit{do} trigger interlock, does the F17 correction make a measurable accuracy difference? This subsection answers it with a small targeted probe, kept separate from the main corpus so the interlock subsection's corpus-aggregate statistics remain calibrated against their original scope.

\textbf{Methodology.} Four fixtures, all 3-tier (or 4-tier) diamonds where one upstream reference task \texttt{R0} fans out to two intermediates which call a shared single-server FCFS server \texttt{TS}: \texttt{P1\_directInterlock} at $n \in \{8, 16\}$, \texttt{P2\_transitiveInterlock} (extra intermediate layer between branch point and shared server), and \texttt{P4\_multiclassInterlock} (two parallel diamonds, two reference classes, shared bottleneck). The FCFS scheduling on \texttt{TS} is essential: \texttt{initInterlock} skips INF-scheduled task servers at line 4002 of \texttt{SolverLN.java}, so the corpus's INF-on-PS pattern (used throughout \texttt{sharedCalleeMC} and similar) cannot reach the correction even when topologically interlock-shaped. Each fixture is solved under three configurations: \texttt{lqsim} (LQNS discrete-event simulator, 100k samples, ground truth), \texttt{ln\_baseline} (\texttt{SolverLN} with \texttt{config.interlocking = true}), and \texttt{ln\_f17off} (\texttt{SolverLN} with \texttt{config.interlocking = false}). The F17 accuracy contribution is reported as the difference between the two LN configurations' worst-case relative difference vs \texttt{lqsim} across \{QLen, RespT, Tput\} on every matching node name. \texttt{Util} is excluded because LQNS reports total $\Sigma X{\cdot}D$ while \texttt{SolverLN} reports per-server $\Sigma X{\cdot}D / c$ on multi-server PS hosts --- the convention mismatch would dominate any rel-diff comparison. The fixtures and runner live at \texttt{jar/src/test/java/jline/solvers/ln\_simple/fixtures/InterlockProbeFixtures.java} and \texttt{SolverLNInterlockAccuracyTest.java} respectively; the captured CSV is \texttt{report/data/interlock-probe.csv}, the per-node tables (one row per model node, columns per solver) are at \texttt{report/data/interlock-probe-tables.md}. The reported \texttt{lqsim} rel-diff has a Monte Carlo standard error: re-running each fixture with a fresh \texttt{lqsim} sample (\texttt{InterlockProbeFullTableTest}) and recomputing the worst rel-diff from the resulting tables shifts each cell by $\leq 0.5$ percentage points relative to the captured CSV, well below the F17 contribution magnitude reported here.

\textbf{Probe-extension attempts dropped.} Three additional fixtures --- asymmetric demand (4:1 and 2:1 splits), low TS utilisation, and 3-way fan-out --- were each attempted as regime-coverage extensions. All three surfaced the same \texttt{SolverLN} port-specific weakness: \texttt{ln\_baseline} diverged from \texttt{lqsim} by 19--49\% while \texttt{lqns} analytical stayed within 4--6\%, F17 toggle changed the LN rel-diff by $\leq 2$\,pp on top of that 20--50\,pp baseline error. The fixtures were dropped because they contaminate the F17 ablation reading. \texttt{SolverLN}'s interlock implementation appears to have accuracy weaknesses outside the high-utilisation, narrow-fan-out, symmetric-demand regime --- a separate issue from F17, named as future work.

Queue lengths at the bottleneck $T_S$ are essentially identical with and without F17 ($\leq 0.001$ difference) --- \texttt{SolverLN}'s per-layer MVA gets the customer distribution correct on its own; F17 polishes the upstream caller's residence-time accounting.

\textbf{Implication for the interlock subsection's Finding 1.} The corpus-aggregate ``zero accuracy effect'' statement in that subsection's Finding 1 is therefore scope-bound, not a no-op claim about the F17 machinery in general. On non-interlock corpora, F17 has no work to do --- the consumer (\texttt{computeInterlockProb}) short-circuits before computing any adjustment, so disabling it changes nothing. On interlock-triggering topologies, F17 is genuine accuracy-machinery that contributes a small but non-zero adjustment to activity response times. The accuracy-preserving runtime frontier characterised in the next subsection therefore remains intact \textit{for the Chapter~\ref{ch:eval} corpus} (where the probe shows F17 does no work because interlock does not fire), but extends to interlock-triggering corpora only with the small accuracy degradation quantified above.

\subsubsection*{Accuracy-preserving runtime frontier}

The fact that F17 has zero iteration-count effect and zero accuracy effect means its per-iteration cut can be stacked with the iteration-count cut of F20 to produce a combined runtime cut without accuracy loss. A combined ablation condition — disabling F17, the F20 \texttt{iter\_min} floor (Arm A; see Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20}), F21, and F24 — was measured against baseline. The result is \textbf{7.99x aggregate speedup with zero fixture accuracy degradation}: corpus iteration total 1,452 (matching the Arm A condition; F17, F21, F24 add zero iter-count change on top of Arm A), corpus wall-clock 320,472 ms, match-status distribution 50/61 \texttt{match-ln} and 11/61 \texttt{match-lqns-only} — identical to baseline on both axes.

The closest single-cut comparison is the full F20-off condition (Arm A + B + C bundled): 8.29x aggregate speedup, with six fixtures degraded out of \texttt{match-ln} into \texttt{match-lqns-only} (A1\_chain\_d3\_N100, three A2\_multiclassA fixtures, C3\_multiclassMultiEntry\_asymmetric, C4\_lowDemand). The frontier point is a trade: the combined cut gives up approximately 0.30x of aggregate speedup in exchange for preserving all six fixtures' \texttt{match-ln} classification.

\textbf{Why combined is not faster than F20-off alone.} Despite cutting more machinery (F17 + Arm A + F21 + F24 vs F20-off's three F20 arms only), the combined condition is slightly slower because F17, F21, and F24 are per-iteration cuts while F20-off is an iteration-count cut. F20-off drops corpus iterations by 67\% (3,801 → 1,248); per-iteration savings in the combined condition therefore apply to fewer iterations than they would at baseline scale. The iteration-count advantage of full F20-off over Arm A (1,248 vs 1,452, ~14\% fewer iterations) is large enough to outweigh combined's per-iteration cost advantage from F17/F21/F24. Per-iteration cuts compound multiplicatively with iteration-count cuts: cutting both surfaces is faster than cutting either alone, but cutting more on one surface than the other reaches diminishing returns.

\textbf{Outlier honesty for the frontier.} Both 7.99x and 8.29x are aggregate-weighted measurements and, like the F17 per-fixture ratios above, they are dominated by the largest fan-out fixtures. The frontier \textit{trade} — −0.30x aggregate speedup in exchange for preserving six fixtures' accuracy — is robust against outlier-discounting because both sides of the trade are inflated by the same fixtures; the inflation cancels in the differential. The absolute speedup multipliers (7.99x, 8.29x) are not corpus-typical and would shrink substantially on a corpus without the largest fan-out fixtures. The robust headline is the per-fixture accuracy preservation in the combined cut, not the aggregate multiplier; the accuracy-preserving frontier is a Chapter~\ref{ch:eval} finding, not a spine claim, and the spine names F17 and F24 as runtime-surface contributors without committing to a combined-cut speedup figure.








\subsection{Convergence floor, moving-average, and hard-reset (F20)}
 
\texttt{SolverLN.converged(it)} is the per-iteration convergence test that decides whether the layer fixed-point iteration may stop at the given iteration. It combines four pieces of machinery: an \texttt{iter\_min = max(2$\cdot$E, ceil(iter\_max/4))} floor that delays convergence until a minimum iteration count has been reached, a sliding-window weighted average over \texttt{QN}/\texttt{UN}/\texttt{RN}/\texttt{TN} that smooths per-iteration metric noise, a three-iteration confirmation checking that the smoothed metrics remain within tolerance, and a hard-reset verification pass that re-solves every layer to confirm a fixed point survives reset. \texttt{SolverLNSimple} takes the opposite approach, sacrificing potential instability mitigations for faster convergence, just checking if \texttt{max(|X\_l $-$ X\_l\_prev|) < tol} holds for a single iteration. This is the largest single contributor to the iteration-count difference the spine claim names. Disabling it results in just a small and concentrated accuracy cost.

\textbf{Finding 1: F20-off cuts total iteration count by 67.2\%.} The corpus total drops from 3,801 baseline iterations to 1,248 (a 3.05x reduction). It is the \texttt{iter\_min} floor that accounts for the majority of the iteration-count difference, with the reduction concentrating on the floor-binding fixtures. The 55 fixtures that sat at 53 iterations in baseline land at 5–32 iterations in this ablation, exposing their true convergence point.

The cost concentrates where the static reading of F20 predicted: on partitions where the iteration sits in small-amplitude oscillation around an already-reached fixed point and the moving-average pass was filtering the oscillation out. \texttt{SolverLN}'s convergence detection takes the windowed maximum error (via \texttt{computeMaxItErr}) rather than the current-iteration error — a robust rule when the iteration oscillates. Without the moving-average, detection fires the moment the \textit{current} iteration's error drops below threshold, which on these six fixtures can land on a momentary low during an oscillation phase rather than a converged state; the per-cell value the output table records is whatever phase the iteration happened to be in when detection fired.

On both fixtures the f20off drift is therefore not LN drifting toward a more accurate steady state; it is LN drifting away from the simulation reference's steady state, which is the directional evidence that F20's smoothing pass is doing protective work rather than masking convergence to a fixed point that lqsim would endorse. The other four fixtures (\texttt{A1\_chain\_d3\_N100}, three \texttt{A2\_multiclassA} variants) exceed the 300-second simulator-side limit of the LQNS REST container even at low \texttt{run\_time} budgets, so their lqsim direction is undetermined and not reported.

\textbf{The C3 anomaly.} The F20-off run reports \texttt{C3\_multiclassMultiEntry\_asymmetric} at $\Delta_{\text{f20off}}$ = 15.8\%; the corresponding alloff run reports a noticeably larger drift and fires an \texttt{assertEquals} failure on \texttt{AS1.ResidT} while the matching f20off row did not. F24 has zero effect on \texttt{SolverLN}'s output anywhere else in the corpus, and the two rel diffs straddle whatever pass/fail threshold the assertion uses; floating-point ordering across the F24 compute path is enough to shift the metric across the boundary without altering the fixture's qualitative classification. The two drift numbers tell a consistent story even when the pass/fail bit flips. The alloff anomaly is recorded for completeness and investigated as future work rather than treated as evidence against the spine claim.

\textbf{The three-arm decomposition.} F20-off disables three arms simultaneously (iter\_min floor, moving-average, hard-reset); the headline measurements above report the bundle as a whole. The decomposition itself — which arm carries the iter-count cut, which arm carries the accuracy cost — is reported in the subsection below, where an isolated-floor condition (\texttt{A2\_arm\_A}) makes the arms separable.

\subsubsection*{Arm A: the \texttt{iter\_min} floor in isolation}

A late addition to the ablation set isolates the F20 floor from the moving-average and hard-reset machinery. The \texttt{A2\_arm\_A} condition splits \texttt{SolverLN}'s single \texttt{iter\_min} parameter into two: \texttt{iter\_min\_convergence = 1} (disabling the floor on the convergence-detection path) while leaving \texttt{iter\_min\_avg = max(2$\cdot$E, iter\_max/4)} at its baseline value (keeping the moving-average window-weighted detection rule intact). Arm A is therefore the floor cut alone; Arms B (moving-average) and C (hard-reset verification) remain in place.

\textbf{Finding (Arm A): The floor alone accounts for $\approx$92\% of F20's iteration-count effect.} The Arm A condition reduces corpus-aggregate \texttt{SolverLN} iterations from 3,801 baseline to 1,452 — a 62\% drop. The full F20-off condition (Arm A + B + C bundled) reduces to 1,248 (a 67.2\% drop). Comparing the two: \texttt{(3,801 $-$ 1,452) / (3,801 $-$ 1,248) = 2,349 / 2,553 = 91.99\%}. The iter\_min floor is the dominant arm of F20 on the iteration-count surface; the moving-average and hard-reset arms together contribute the remaining $\approx$8\% (the additional 204 iterations cut going from Arm A's 1,452 to the bundle's 1,248). The chapter's previous static-reading prediction — that the floor dominates because 55/61 baseline fixtures sit at it — is confirmed quantitatively, and the bundled F20 attribution sharpens to the floor specifically.

\textbf{Finding (Arm A): The floor cut leaves \texttt{SolverLN}'s output essentially unchanged.} Measured directly on LN's per-cell outputs, Arm A's drift from baseline peaks at 3.5\% (\texttt{C4\_lowDemand}, \texttt{E1.respt}) and stays below 3\% on every other fixture (46 of 61 below 1\%); compare to the full F20-off condition, where six fixtures drift by 5.6\% to 32.0\% (Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses}'s $\Delta_{\text{Arm A}}$ column reports the per-fixture Arm A drift alongside the f20off drift, an order of magnitude smaller on every affected fixture). The cut that produces the larger drift on the six affected fixtures is therefore Arms B+C (moving-average + hard-reset), not Arm A. The same Arm A condition is the one whose match-status distribution is unchanged from baseline (50/61 \texttt{match-ln}, 11/61 \texttt{match-lqns-only}) — what was previously measurable only as a coarse classification holding is, in the direct LN-vs-LN measurement, a $\leq$3.5\% drift on the worst-case cell of the worst-case fixture.

\textbf{Wall-clock diagnostic: Arm A calibrates the Simpson's-paradox inflation on F20-axis rows.} Arm A reports 4.20$\times$ corpus-aggregate wall-clock speedup, decomposing arithmetically as 2.62$\times$ iteration-count reduction times 1.60$\times$ corpus-aggregate per-iteration speedup. But Arm A removes no per-iteration work by construction --- only the convergence floor is touched, and the moving-average and hard-reset machinery still runs on every iteration. The 1.60$\times$ apparent per-iteration speedup is therefore fixture-mix Simpson's-paradox in full: cutting the floor disproportionately removes iterations from cheap A/C fixtures, so the surviving iteration pool is heavier on average. The per-fixture median ms/iter ratio under Arm A is 1.00$\times$ exactly, confirming the diagnostic. This calibrates the Per-iter $\times$ column in Table~\ref{tab:eval-aggregate-runtime-conditions}: any row that changes the iteration count carries a fixture-mix component on the order of 1.6$\times$ that is not a real per-iteration effect.

\textbf{The decomposition resolved.} The three arms separate cleanly along the two surfaces. Arm A (the floor) drives the iteration-count effect: $\approx$92\% of F20's iter-count contribution. Arms B and C (moving-average + hard-reset) drive the accuracy effect: on the six F20-off-degraded fixtures, baseline-to-Arm-A LN drift stays under 3.5\% while baseline-to-f20off LN drift reaches 32\% — Arms B+C carry essentially all of the per-cell accuracy cost. The floor is the iter-count machinery; the moving-average + hard-reset is the accuracy-preservation machinery. The two are separable by construction, and the dataset now isolates them.

\textbf{Asymmetric cost of Arm B across the corpus.} The moving-average arm's protective value is locally targeted rather than uniform: it earns its keep on the six oscillating fixtures (A1, three A2s, C3, C4) where small-amplitude oscillation around the fixed point produces the 5–32\% drift Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses} reports, but on B fanouts the same machinery is pure overhead. The \texttt{tasks20/40/60\_fanout} fixtures sit at baseline counts of 81/161/201 and collapse to 21/22/22 under F20-off; LN drift on those fixtures is under 0.45\% — well below Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses}'s 5.6\% inclusion floor — so the 60–180 extra iterations bought essentially nothing on the accuracy surface and inflated the runtime-dominant partition's iteration count by an order of magnitude. The design is fixture-blind, so the protective overhead is paid uniformly to insure against the minority that needs it; the corpus shows the premium is non-trivial precisely on the partition the chapter most cares about for runtime (Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime} Finding 2). This is a defensible engineering choice, not a bug, but it is the load-bearing rationale for why the Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} \texttt{combined} frontier preserves Arms B and C rather than cutting them indiscriminately.

\textbf{Spine implication.} On the iteration-count surface, the F20 attribution sharpens to the \texttt{iter\_min} convergence floor specifically: the chapter's previous bundled F20 description retains its accuracy here as a machinery-level naming, but the iter-count share belongs to the floor arm, not to the bundle. On the accuracy surface, the moving-average + hard-reset arms are the load-bearing machinery: omitting them shifts \texttt{SolverLN}'s output by 5–32\% on the six affected fixtures, where omitting only Arm A leaves the same fixtures within $\leq$3.5\% drift. The simple solver's omission of F20 is therefore more precisely an omission of the bundle, with the accuracy cost the chapter reports being the cost of omitting Arms B and C; omitting Arm A alone would carry essentially no accuracy cost on the corpus and would account for $\approx$92\% of the iteration-count cut. The Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} accuracy-preserving frontier subsection above leans directly on this decomposition.

\begin{figure}[h!]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/eval-e71-iter-ablation.pdf}
  \caption[Per-fixture iteration counts across ablation conditions]{
    Per-fixture \texttt{ln\_iters} across the four ablation conditions,
    grouped horizontally by partition. X-axis: outer-loop iteration
    count (linear scale, so the 53 floor reads as a vertical
    cluster). Y-axis: fixture name. Bars per fixture: baseline (red),
    F24-off (orange), F20-off (blue), all-off (purple). The black dot
    overlays \texttt{SolverLNSimple}'s iteration count. The red and
    orange bars coincide for every fixture (F24 has no iteration
    effect); the blue and purple bars coincide for every fixture (F24
    contributes zero iteration change on top of F20). The 53 floor is
    visible as a vertical cluster of red/orange bars; the blue/purple
    bars cluster at 10--20 except for the three chain-B fixtures
    (\texttt{tasks20\_chain}, \texttt{tasks40\_chain},
    \texttt{tasks60\_chain}) which spill to 63, 123, and 184. The
    isolated black dot at 100 on \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} is the
    simple solver's cap-hit.
  }
  \label{fig:eval-iter-ablation}
\end{figure} 

F20-off alone covers roughly three-quarters of the corpus-aggregate iteration-count difference (F24 contributes zero iteration-count change, as the interlock ablation above reports; F17 likewise). The residual quarter is genuinely algorithmic difference, taken up in the residual subsection below. The accuracy cost of F20-off is small enough to be acceptable for the simple solver's design point (avoiding the smoothing machinery in exchange for matching \texttt{SolverLN} on the partitions it claims) but is not negligible, and any decision to remove F20 from \texttt{SolverLN} in production would need to weigh it.

F20 is dominant; F17 and F24 add per-iteration cost but no iteration-count change (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}). The residual subsection that follows isolates the genuinely algorithmic difference that remains once the floor is removed.



\subsection{Residual: the genuine algorithmic difference}

If F20 explained the whole iteration-count difference, disabling it would produce iteration counts matching the simple solver's. It does not — a residual of about a quarter of the total difference persists. Disabling F24 alongside F20 (the \texttt{alloff} condition) reaches the same 1,248-iteration corpus total as F20-off alone, because F24 contributes zero iteration-count change (established in the interlock ablation above); F17 likewise contributes zero, so adding it to the disabled set would not move the residual either. The section uses the \texttt{alloff} totals interchangeably with F20-off on the iteration-count surface and quantifies the residual that survives.

\textbf{Finding 1: The \texttt{alloff} ablation accounts for 75.5\% of the iteration-count difference.} The corpus-aggregate computation is direct. Baseline \texttt{SolverLN} total: 3,801 iterations. Alloff \texttt{SolverLN} total: 1,248 iterations. \texttt{SolverLNSimple} total: 418 iterations. The ablation accounts for (3,801 − 1,248) / (3,801 − 418) = 2,553 / 3,383 = 75.5\% of the difference. The remaining 24.5\% (1,248 − 418 = 830 iterations corpus-wide) is what the simple solver gains beyond turning off F20 and F24 — the residual that reflects the genuinely algorithmic difference between the two solvers. This is the chapter's central decomposition number and the one the spine claim is calibrated against.

No single ablation condition isolates the simple solver's structural choices that remain in \texttt{SolverLN} after F20 and F24 are turned off, so the inference is structural rather than empirical. The contribution chapter names three mechanisms the simple solver omits. First, predicate-gated fixed-α damping (\texttt{LqnGraph.callerFansOut} firing exactly where damping is needed) rather than \texttt{SolverLN}'s unconditional omega-blend on every layer every iteration: on layers where damping is unnecessary, the simple solver skips the blend, shortening the trajectory toward the fixed point. Third, single-iteration convergence detection that fires the moment the per-layer throughput change falls below \texttt{iter\_tol}, versus \texttt{SolverLN}'s three-iteration confirmation rule that adds two to three iterations per fixture beyond the first-low point. The corpus-specificity caveat: 75.5\% is the corpus-aggregate share, not a per-fixture proportion; per-partition the share moves between approximately 57\% and 87\% (excluding A4's cap-anomaly), and the spine claim's "approximately three-quarters" wording is calibrated to the aggregate.

689	The data above isolates F24 to per-iteration runtime and F20 to iteration-count machinery (with an accuracy cost). Three boundary regimes (C1/C2 design-divergent and B-fanout F24 scale-axis) are intentionally outside the simple solver's accuracy claim --- they are the next section's subject.

691	
692	
693	
694	\section{Boundary regimes (Partition B fanout, C1, C2)}
695	\label{sec:eval-boundary}
696	
697	Three of the corpus's nine partitions were designed to expose disagreement between the solvers rather than to demonstrate agreement: the C1 fan-out callers (where the simple solver's predicate-gated damping fires), the C2 INF-task fixtures (where SolverLN computes IS utilisation > 1 by design and the simple solver clamps to 1.0), and the B fan-out fixtures (the F24 scale axis, where SolverLN's M/M/inf-like reference values at moderate utilisation differ from the simple solver's closed-PFQN M/M/c values). This section reports the disagreement explicitly rather than glossing it.
698	
699	\textbf{Finding 1: C1 --- fan-out callers.} All six C1 fixtures are \texttt{match-lqns-only} in baseline --- within LQNS V5's tolerance bar (\texttt{atol = 1e-3, rtol = 1e-1}) but outside \texttt{SolverLN}'s. The maximum relative differences against \texttt{SolverLN} are 0.2939 on the two \texttt{fanOut2} fixtures, 0.3624 on the two \texttt{fanOut3} fixtures, and 0.3029 on the two \texttt{fanOut4} fixtures --- a disagreement of approximately 29--36\% across the partition; against LQNS V5 the same six fixtures sit at 4.44e-02, 4.28e-02, and 4.14e-02 respectively, comfortably inside LQNS's rtol bar. The disagreement concentrates on the caller queue length and downstream metrics (throughput at the REF task tier and residence time at the fan-out target). This is the regime where the simple solver's \texttt{LqnGraph.callerFansOut} predicate fires and fixed-$\alpha$ damping is applied; the disagreement with \texttt{SolverLN} is the structural divergence of the fan-out coupling characterised in Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step5} of the contribution chapter, and corresponds to structural disagreement between the two solvers' coupling-iteration behaviour at moderate utilisation when the caller is shared across multiple sibling callees. The simple solver's behaviour on this partition is not a claim of better accuracy than \texttt{SolverLN}; both solvers produce defensible outputs on these fixtures under different structural assumptions, and which is "correct" depends on the oracle one trusts. The two references disagree on this partition and \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falls within tolerance of one; the chapter does not adjudicate which reference is correct, it reports the disagreement and the LQNS-side coverage.
700	
701	\textbf{Finding 2: C2 — INF-task fixtures.} The three C2 fixtures were predicted "no --- measurement" in the manifest but now match \texttt{SolverLN} to approximately 8 significant figures on every metric except the IS Util column: maximum relative differences of 1.48e-08, 2.30e-08, and 4.63e-08 — within double-precision representation of identity. The disagreement on Util is definitional: \texttt{SolverLN} reports the mean number of busy IS servers (which can exceed 1.0 on an INF processor running at high load), and the simple solver clamps to 1.0. We mark the C2 fixtures with the ★ marker; the contribution chapter's late infinite-server refinement (Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step5}) is the empirical confirmation that lands the change.
702	
703	\textbf{Finding 3: B-fanout --- five fixtures.} The five \texttt{B\_scaleAxis\_tasks*\_fanout} fixtures are \texttt{match-lqns-only} across the board --- within LQNS V5's tolerance bar but outside \texttt{SolverLN}'s. The maximum relative differences against \texttt{SolverLN} grow monotonically with task count: 0.281 at tasks=5, 0.466 at tasks=10, 0.594 at tasks=20, 0.723 at tasks=40, and 0.808 at tasks=60; against LQNS V5 the same five fixtures sit at 5.14e-02, 4.93e-02, 3.08e-02, 1.20e-02, and 1.08e-02 --- all inside LQNS's rtol bar. The growth on the \texttt{SolverLN} side reflects the contribution chapter's structural argument: at moderate per-server utilisation, \texttt{SolverLN} substitutes the M/M/inf-like \texttt{R ≈ D} approximation at the host while \texttt{SolverLNSimple} computes the closed-PFQN M/M/c queueing tail via \texttt{pfqn\_mvams}. The gap against \texttt{SolverLN} grows with fan-out width because the fan-out tree forces a higher per-callee population and the M/M/inf approximation diverges further from the queueing tail. This is reported rather than litigated; which solver is "right" depends on whether the LQN model's fan-out tree is sized for queueing-tail or M/M/inf behaviour, and the chapter takes no position. The two references disagree on this partition and \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falls within tolerance of one. Discussion (Section~\ref{sec:eval-discussion}) treats the field-level implications.
704	
705	\textbf{Finding 4: A4\_chainPlusFanout --- helper absorbs an LN-vs-LQNS disagreement.} The fixture is \texttt{match-ln} in baseline because the match-either-LN-or-LQNS helper absorbs a divergence between the two references: \texttt{SolverLNSimple} lands within LQNS V5's tolerance (\texttt{sim\_vs\_lqns} rel diff 3.10e-02), while \texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} (4.76e-02) sits just below the rtol bar. The fixture is a four-tier multi-class chain with a multi-entry middle tier --- exactly the topology class the contribution chapter's late multi-class/multi-entry fix was designed to address --- and the simple solver hits its 100-iteration cap without satisfying its inner \texttt{iter\_tol}. The disagreement is between \texttt{SolverLN}'s handling of the multi-class multi-entry middle tier and the simple solver's handling on the same topology; the two references disagree on this fixture, and where they disagree \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falls within LQNS's tolerance band. We carry the result throughout the chapter with the \texttt{‡} marker and treat the fixture as a finding about LN-vs-LQNS disagreement on this class of models rather than as a clean pass or a clean failure.
706	
707	The C3 anomaly on the alloff condition (the \texttt{C3\_multiclassMultiEntry\_asymmetric} assertion failure described in Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20}) is a related boundary effect on the same topology family (multi-class with multi-entry callees): the matching f20off row passed without firing the assertion, F24 has zero accuracy effect anywhere else in the corpus, and the rel diff numbers (f20off 0.066 vs alloff 0.134) straddle the assertion's pass/fail threshold without altering the qualitative classification. The C3 fixture and A4\_chainPlusFanout together mark the multi-class × multi-entry interaction as the project's most sensitive accuracy boundary, and both are flagged for investigation as future work.
708	
709	\textbf{F15 — the load-bearing accuracy machinery for multi-entry / multi-class fixtures.} The Pass 2 ablation campaign measured \texttt{SolverLN}'s F15 (the per-iteration class-switching routing-probability update, \texttt{updateRoutingProbabilities}) by disabling its body. The result is the largest accuracy effect in the ablation set on this corpus: 13 fixtures move from \texttt{match-ln} to \texttt{match-lqns-only} --- F15 is load-bearing for tight-LN-fidelity on multi-entry / multi-class fixtures; without it, those fixtures shift to LQNS-validity rather than failing both references --- concentrated in the same multi-entry / multi-class subpartitions identified above as boundary-sensitive — five A2 fixtures (multiclassB demands\_3to1 and 5to1, multiclassC think\_4to1), four A4 fixtures, one C2 (infTaskShared), and three C3 fixtures. Iteration counts and corpus-aggregate match-status outside these 13 fixtures are bit-identical to baseline; F15's effect is concentrated rather than diffuse. The chapter does not list F15 among the spine-named runtime contributors (those are F17 and F24, both with zero accuracy effect); F15 sits with F20's moving-average machinery as accuracy-preservation work the construction could not safely omit. The two complement each other: where F20's moving-average preserves accuracy on small-amplitude-oscillation fixtures (Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Arm A finding), F15's routing updates preserve it on multi-entry / multi-class fixtures. Together they are the accuracy-preserving machinery the construction needed to retain — and the build-led account is honest rather than triumphalist about it. \textbf{Caveat on the F15 measurement:} the F15-off condition gates the entry of \texttt{updateRoutingProbabilities} with an early return, which disables both the \texttt{rtorig} writes the function performs and the downstream \texttt{relinkFromRtorig} propagation. The function also contains a call to \texttt{updateClassSwitchNodes}; that call is reportedly unreachable on the current code path, so the F15-off measurement isolates the writes-plus-propagation cost rather than the full intended class-switching machinery.
710	
711	One further fixture warrants reporting in the same symmetric register the C1 and B-fanout findings adopt. The fixture \texttt{B\_scaleAxis\_tasks60\_chain} is baseline \texttt{match-ln} (\texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} 3.26e-03, well within tolerance), while \texttt{sim\_vs\_lqns} reaches 5.87 --- a 587\% disagreement between the two references on this fixture. The classification is unaffected because the LN-check short-circuits before LQNS is consulted; the underlying LN-LQNS divergence is real and sharp, with LQNS V5 converging to a substantially different steady state on the 60-task chain. This is a property of LQNS on this topology, not of \texttt{SolverLNSimple}; the chapter takes no position on which reference describes the topology's steady state correctly.

777	\section{Identified failure modes}
778	\label{sec:eval-failure-modes}
779	
780	Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} reports the in-corpus boundary regimes --- fixtures the simple solver passes by matching one of the two references where the references themselves disagree. This section turns the lens the other way and catalogues the model classes \textit{outside} the evaluation corpus on which the simple solver visibly fails, preserved in \texttt{SolverLNSimpleFailingTest} (every fixture \texttt{@Disabled}) as standing regression placeholders for the spine claim's reach. The catalogue is backwards-looking evidence rather than forward-looking speculation: each mode is grounded in a specific fixture in the failing test suite, with a diagnosed root cause and a named \texttt{SolverLN} or LQNS feature whose absence accounts for it. The five modes together delineate the precise edge of the spine claim's accuracy reach. Four of the five are scope decisions consistent with the bottom-up methodology (machinery the corpus did not force); one is an implementation gap the section flags as a follow-up bug rather than a feature absence. The summary table at the end of the section places each mode against its corresponding entry in the feature delta (Section~\ref{sec:concl-future-parity}) and the conclusion's scope categorisation (Section~\ref{sec:concl-scope}).
781	
782	\textbf{Mode 1 --- \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} 100-iteration cap (in-corpus borderline pass).} The fixture is a 4-tier multi-class chain with multi-entry middle tier (two REF tasks \texttt{R1}, \texttt{R2} each call distinct entries \texttt{E2A}, \texttt{E2B} on the shared intermediate \texttt{T2}; \texttt{T2}'s entries both call \texttt{T3}'s entry, \texttt{T3} calls \texttt{T4}). It is the only Partition A fixture the simple solver runs to its 100-iteration cap on, and it is carried through the chapter with the \texttt{‡} marker (Section~\ref{sec:eval-hypotheses} fourth concession, Section~\ref{sec:eval-correctness} footnote, Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} Finding 4). The fixture's pass classification is helper-absorbed: \texttt{sim\_vs\_ln = 4.76$\times$10$^{-2}$} sits just below the \texttt{rtol = 5e-2} bar while \texttt{sim\_vs\_lqns = 3.10$\times$10$^{-2}$} sits cleanly inside LQNS's 0.1 bar, and the match-either helper records \texttt{match-ln} on the strength of the LN comparison. The cap-hit nonetheless represents the simple solver's iteration-count failure on this fixture: the inner \texttt{iter\_tol = 5$\times$10$^{-3}$} convergence criterion is never satisfied within 100 outer iterations, and the values the solver returns are whatever phase the iteration was in when the cap fired. \textit{Diagnosis.} Under \texttt{f20off} (LN's floor and moving-average disabled, single-iteration max-delta detection), \texttt{SolverLN} converges genuinely in 17 iterations on this fixture to a point \texttt{SolverLNSimple} agrees with to within \texttt{4.76$\times$10$^{-2}$}, so the converged state itself is reachable and the two solvers' fixed points are close; the simple solver's failure is in the trajectory toward it, not in the trajectory's destination. The damping predicates the simple solver does carry both fire on this fixture --- \texttt{isInfOnMultiServerPs} returns true on \texttt{T2/T3/T4} (each INF-scheduled on a 4-server PS host), so the \texttt{D\_RELAX\_ALPHA = 0.5} blend is applied on every D-write at those layers --- but \texttt{callerFansOut} is false on \texttt{R1}, \texttt{R2}, and the intermediate bound activities (none of them carries more than one distinct sibling callee), so Z-writes flow through undamped. The structural reading is that the trajectory enters small-amplitude oscillation in the per-class apportionment at the shared \texttt{E3} callee (the point where the two reference classes' chains converge), and the simple solver's single-iteration max-delta detection cannot see through the oscillation's amplitude band. The missing machinery is the same one the Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Arms B+C decomposition identifies as accuracy-preserving on the six F20-off-degraded fixtures: \texttt{SolverLN}'s moving-average window over \texttt{QN/UN/RN/TN} and its three-iteration confirmation rule, which together filter exactly this kind of small-amplitude oscillation around a reached fixed point. The cap-hit is mechanistically a member of the same family as the six F20-off accuracy losses, surfacing on baseline rather than under ablation because the simple solver does not carry the smoothing arm to begin with. The fixture also shares the multi-entry middle-tier topology that Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary}'s F15 paragraph identifies as the corpus's most accuracy-sensitive subpartition; both candidate mechanisms (the F20-style smoothing absence and the F15-style class-switching routing-update absence) are individually consistent with the observed behaviour, and the chapter does not separate them.
783	
784	\textbf{Mode 2 --- Deep multi-call chains with all-Exp service (\texttt{sc2\_three\_tier}, \texttt{sc10\_deep\_chain}).} Two fixtures in \texttt{SolverLNSimpleFailingTest}'s Group 2 generalise the Mode 1 pattern outside the multi-class regime: \texttt{sc2\_three\_tier} is single-class with a multi-call edge at the intermediate (3 tiers, $N=100$, all-Exp service, \texttt{synchCall(E3, 2)} mid-chain); \texttt{sc10\_deep\_chain} is single-class without multi-call but at greater depth (4 tiers, $N=80$, all-Exp service). The symptom on both is the same as Mode 1's --- the simple solver runs to its 100-iteration cap with outputs that drift outside the standard tolerance bar against \texttt{SolverLN}. Reference fixtures in the same family that do pass --- \texttt{sc1\_simple\_chain} (single-class 2-tier $N=50$ no multi-call) and \texttt{sc7\_multicore} ($N=200$ on 4/8-server processors with sufficient capacity headroom) --- locate the failure regime as ``three or more tiers of all-Exp service, intermediate-tier population large enough to keep the chain's coupling loop tight, with or without a multi-call edge amplifying the per-iteration error feedback''. As with Mode 1, the converged state itself is not far from \texttt{SolverLN}'s; the failure is convergence-rate rather than fixed-point. The missing machinery is the same as Mode 1's, with the chain-depth axis raising a second candidate the corpus's \texttt{A1\_chain\_d8\_N100} (which passes) does not exercise: whether \texttt{SolverLN}'s three-iteration confirmation, possibly together with its alternating elevator scan (F21), damps a depth-driven small-amplitude oscillation that the simple solver's single-iteration max-delta detection lets through. We raise this against the sweep evidence rather than asserting it. Configuring the simple solver with the reference solvers' own elevator sweep raises its corpus iteration count rather than lowering it (Section~\ref{sec:eval-iteration-counters}), so the bounce is not doing ``extra'' per-tier work that the elevator would avoid, and Mode 2's failure is more plausibly attributable to the absent smoothing/confirmation arm than to the sweep direction. The bounce being the simple solver's chosen single-pass propagation, not an inefficiency, the candidate is the missing detection machinery on top of it. F21 is not load-bearing on the Section~\ref{sec:eval-residual} ablation set --- under F21+F20-off, iteration counts are bit-identical to F20-off corpus-wide --- but the F21 measurement runs with the floor active and could not measure F21's convergence-acceleration potential on unfloored trajectories beyond the corpus's depth axis; the Mode 2 fixtures sit outside that depth axis, and the F21+F20-off measurement does not reach them.
785	
786	\textbf{Mode 3 --- Multi-entry intermediate task throughput scaling (\texttt{minimal\_multiEntryCaller}, implementation gap).} A single REF caller \texttt{T1} issues two synchronous calls per cycle to two distinct entries (\texttt{ES1}, \texttt{ES2}) of an intermediate task \texttt{T2}; each intermediate entry issues one call to a leaf. The simple solver's reported \texttt{T2.tput} comes out at the per-\texttt{T1}-cycle rate rather than the per-call rate at \texttt{T2}, leaving \texttt{ER1.RespT} approximately 50\% above \texttt{SolverLN}'s value. The root cause is a scope mismatch in \texttt{ResultsCollector.scaleLeafTaskThroughputs} (\texttt{jar/src/main/kotlin/jline/solvers/ln\_simple/results/ResultsCollector.java}, lines 254--268): the scaling pass multiplies leaf-task throughput by \texttt{LqnGraph.getTotalInboundCallMean}, but the guard at line 259 (\texttt{taskCalledTask.containsKey(task.getName()) continue}) skips any task with downstream callees --- so intermediates that themselves receive multi-call traffic are left at the upstream caller-cycle rate. The same per-call-vs-per-visit distinction the multi-class/multi-entry fix (Contribution Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step5}) addressed at the coupling layer is missing from the results-side aggregation for intermediates. Unlike the other four modes, this is an implementation bug in \texttt{SolverLNSimple}'s reporting path rather than a scope decision about which \texttt{SolverLN} features to absorb: the underlying coupling iteration on this fixture converges correctly (the per-class entry-side metrics that the iteration drives are right; the wrong number is the post-iteration task-throughput aggregation only). The fix is local to \texttt{ResultsCollector} and would extend the scaling pass to intermediates with inbound \texttt{callMean > 1}, mirroring the leaf path. We flag this as the one failure mode in the catalogue that should be promoted from out-of-scope to follow-up bug in Section~\ref{sec:concl-scope}; it is not material to the spine claim's accuracy decomposition (the iteration's converged state is unaffected) but it is material to the simple solver's reporting correctness on multi-entry intermediate-tier topologies.

\textbf{Finding 3: The residual is the genuinely algorithmic difference.} What does the residual 24.5\% (830 iterations corpus-wide) represent? No single ablation condition isolates the simple solver's structural choices that remain in \texttt{SolverLN} after F20 and F24 are turned off, so the inference is structural rather than empirical. The contribution chapter names three mechanisms the simple solver omits. First, predicate-gated fixed-α damping (\texttt{LqnGraph.callerFansOut} firing exactly where damping is needed) rather than \texttt{SolverLN}'s unconditional omega-blend on every layer every iteration: on layers where damping is unnecessary, the simple solver skips the blend, shortening the trajectory toward the fixed point. Second, structural service-time propagation through the \texttt{Z\_callee\_host} and \texttt{Z\_callee\_clients} coupling formulas, rather than \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{*\_prev} snap-back arrays — iteration recovery is structural rather than memoised. Third, single-iteration convergence detection that fires the moment the per-layer throughput change falls below \texttt{iter\_tol}, versus \texttt{SolverLN}'s three-iteration confirmation rule that adds two to three iterations per fixture beyond the first-low point. None of these three is F20 or F24, and none is individually measured; the chapter attributes the residual to them at the structural level.

The simple solver hits its 100-iteration cap on this fixture; alloff \texttt{SolverLN} runs to 17 iterations and converges, so the per-fixture gap closure is negative (sim\_iters = 100 > alloff.ln\_iters = 17). Restricting the A4 calculation to the five fixtures the simple solver does converge on gives a closure of approximately 82\%, consistent with the rest of the A and C partitions.

The 75.5\% / 24.5\% split is the chapter's load-bearing empirical number. F20 (mostly the \texttt{iter\_min} floor) is responsible for the lion's share of the iteration-count difference; F24 has no effect on iteration count (its data is not consumed); the residual reflects the genuinely algorithmic difference between the simple solver's predicate-gated, structurally-recovering, single-iter detection rule and \texttt{SolverLN}'s unconditional-damping, \texttt{*\_prev}-snap-back, three-iter-confirmation rule. The corpus-specificity caveat: 75.5\% is the corpus-aggregate share, not a per-fixture proportion; per-partition the share moves between approximately 57\% and 87\% (excluding A4's cap-anomaly), and the spine claim's "approximately three-quarters" wording is calibrated to the aggregate.

The data above isolates F24 to per-iteration runtime and F20 to iteration-count machinery (with an accuracy cost). Three boundary regimes (C1/C2 design-divergent and B-fanout F24 scale-axis) are intentionally outside the simple solver's accuracy claim --- they are the next section's subject.




\section{Boundary regimes (Partition B fanout, C1, C2)}
\label{sec:eval-boundary}

Three of the corpus's nine partitions were designed to expose disagreement between the solvers rather than to demonstrate agreement: the C1 fan-out callers (where the simple solver's predicate-gated damping fires), the C2 INF-task fixtures (where SolverLN computes IS utilisation > 1 by design and the simple solver clamps to 1.0), and the B fan-out fixtures (the F24 scale axis, where SolverLN's M/M/inf-like reference values at moderate utilisation differ from the simple solver's closed-PFQN M/M/c values). This section reports the disagreement explicitly rather than glossing it.

\textbf{Finding 1: C1 --- fan-out callers.} All six C1 fixtures are \texttt{match-lqns-only} in baseline --- within LQNS V5's tolerance bar (\texttt{atol = 1e-3, rtol = 1e-1}) but outside \texttt{SolverLN}'s. The maximum relative differences against \texttt{SolverLN} are 0.2939 on the two \texttt{fanOut2} fixtures, 0.3624 on the two \texttt{fanOut3} fixtures, and 0.3029 on the two \texttt{fanOut4} fixtures --- a disagreement of approximately 29--36\% across the partition; against LQNS V5 the same six fixtures sit at 4.44e-02, 4.28e-02, and 4.14e-02 respectively, comfortably inside LQNS's rtol bar. The disagreement concentrates on the caller queue length and downstream metrics (throughput at the REF task tier and residence time at the fan-out target). This is the regime where the simple solver's \texttt{LqnGraph.callerFansOut} predicate fires and fixed-$\alpha$ damping is applied; the disagreement with \texttt{SolverLN} is the structural divergence of the fan-out coupling characterised in Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step5} of the contribution chapter, and corresponds to structural disagreement between the two solvers' coupling-iteration behaviour at moderate utilisation when the caller is shared across multiple sibling callees. The simple solver's behaviour on this partition is not a claim of better accuracy than \texttt{SolverLN}; both solvers produce defensible outputs on these fixtures under different structural assumptions, and which is "correct" depends on the oracle one trusts. The two references disagree on this partition and \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falls within tolerance of one; the chapter does not adjudicate which reference is correct, it reports the disagreement and the LQNS-side coverage.

\textbf{Finding 2: C2 — INF-task fixtures.} The three C2 fixtures were predicted "no --- measurement" in the manifest but now match \texttt{SolverLN} to approximately 8 significant figures on every metric except the IS Util column: maximum relative differences of 1.48e-08, 2.30e-08, and 4.63e-08 — within double-precision representation of identity. The disagreement on Util is definitional: \texttt{SolverLN} reports the mean number of busy IS servers (which can exceed 1.0 on an INF processor running at high load), and the simple solver clamps to 1.0. We mark the C2 fixtures with the ★ marker; the contribution chapter's late infinite-server refinement (Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step5}) is the empirical confirmation that lands the change.

\textbf{Finding 3: B-fanout --- five fixtures.} The five \texttt{B\_scaleAxis\_tasks*\_fanout} fixtures are \texttt{match-lqns-only} across the board --- within LQNS V5's tolerance bar but outside \texttt{SolverLN}'s. The maximum relative differences against \texttt{SolverLN} grow monotonically with task count: 0.281 at tasks=5, 0.466 at tasks=10, 0.594 at tasks=20, 0.723 at tasks=40, and 0.808 at tasks=60; against LQNS V5 the same five fixtures sit at 5.14e-02, 4.93e-02, 3.08e-02, 1.20e-02, and 1.08e-02 --- all inside LQNS's rtol bar. The growth on the \texttt{SolverLN} side reflects the contribution chapter's structural argument: at moderate per-server utilisation, \texttt{SolverLN} substitutes the M/M/inf-like \texttt{R ≈ D} approximation at the host while \texttt{SolverLNSimple} computes the closed-PFQN M/M/c queueing tail via \texttt{pfqn\_mvams}. The gap against \texttt{SolverLN} grows with fan-out width because the fan-out tree forces a higher per-callee population and the M/M/inf approximation diverges further from the queueing tail. This is reported rather than litigated; which solver is "right" depends on whether the LQN model's fan-out tree is sized for queueing-tail or M/M/inf behaviour, and the chapter takes no position. The two references disagree on this partition and \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falls within tolerance of one. Discussion (Section~\ref{sec:eval-discussion}) treats the field-level implications.

\textbf{Finding 4: A4\_chainPlusFanout --- helper absorbs an LN-vs-LQNS disagreement.} The fixture is \texttt{match-ln} in baseline because the match-either-LN-or-LQNS helper absorbs a divergence between the two references: \texttt{SolverLNSimple} lands within LQNS V5's tolerance (\texttt{sim\_vs\_lqns} rel diff 3.10e-02), while \texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} (4.76e-02) sits just below the rtol bar. The fixture is a four-tier multi-class chain with a multi-entry middle tier --- exactly the topology class the contribution chapter's late multi-class/multi-entry fix was designed to address --- and the simple solver hits its 100-iteration cap without satisfying its inner \texttt{iter\_tol}. The disagreement is between \texttt{SolverLN}'s handling of the multi-class multi-entry middle tier and the simple solver's handling on the same topology; the two references disagree on this fixture, and where they disagree \texttt{SolverLNSimple} falls within LQNS's tolerance band. We carry the result throughout the chapter with the \texttt{‡} marker and treat the fixture as a finding about LN-vs-LQNS disagreement on this class of models rather than as a clean pass or a clean failure.

The C3 anomaly on the alloff condition (the \texttt{C3\_multiclassMultiEntry\_asymmetric} assertion failure described in Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20}) is a related boundary effect on the same topology family (multi-class with multi-entry callees): the matching f20off row passed without firing the assertion, F24 has zero accuracy effect anywhere else in the corpus, and the rel diff numbers (f20off 0.066 vs alloff 0.134) straddle the assertion's pass/fail threshold without altering the qualitative classification. The C3 fixture and A4\_chainPlusFanout together mark the multi-class × multi-entry interaction as the project's most sensitive accuracy boundary, and both are flagged for investigation as future work.

\textbf{F15 — the load-bearing accuracy machinery for multi-entry / multi-class fixtures.} The Pass 2 ablation campaign measured \texttt{SolverLN}'s F15 (the per-iteration class-switching routing-probability update, \texttt{updateRoutingProbabilities}) by disabling its body. The result is the largest accuracy effect in the ablation set on this corpus: 13 fixtures move from \texttt{match-ln} to \texttt{match-lqns-only} --- F15 is load-bearing for tight-LN-fidelity on multi-entry / multi-class fixtures; without it, those fixtures shift to LQNS-validity rather than failing both references --- concentrated in the same multi-entry / multi-class subpartitions identified above as boundary-sensitive — five A2 fixtures (multiclassB demands\_3to1 and 5to1, multiclassC think\_4to1), four A4 fixtures, one C2 (infTaskShared), and three C3 fixtures. Iteration counts and corpus-aggregate match-status outside these 13 fixtures are bit-identical to baseline; F15's effect is concentrated rather than diffuse. The chapter does not list F15 among the spine-named runtime contributors (those are F17 and F24, both with zero accuracy effect); F15 sits with F20's moving-average machinery as accuracy-preservation work the construction could not safely omit. The two complement each other: where F20's moving-average preserves accuracy on small-amplitude-oscillation fixtures (Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Arm A finding), F15's routing updates preserve it on multi-entry / multi-class fixtures. Together they are the accuracy-preserving machinery the construction needed to retain — and the build-led account is honest rather than triumphalist about it. \textbf{Caveat on the F15 measurement:} the F15-off condition gates the entry of \texttt{updateRoutingProbabilities} with an early return, which disables both the \texttt{rtorig} writes the function performs and the downstream \texttt{relinkFromRtorig} propagation. The function also contains a call to \texttt{updateClassSwitchNodes}; that call is reportedly unreachable on the current code path, so the F15-off measurement isolates the writes-plus-propagation cost rather than the full intended class-switching machinery.

One further fixture warrants reporting in the same symmetric register the C1 and B-fanout findings adopt. The fixture \texttt{B\_scaleAxis\_tasks60\_chain} is baseline \texttt{match-ln} (\texttt{sim\_vs\_ln} 3.26e-03, well within tolerance), while \texttt{sim\_vs\_lqns} reaches 5.87 --- a 587\% disagreement between the two references on this fixture. The classification is unaffected because the LN-check short-circuits before LQNS is consulted; the underlying LN-LQNS divergence is real and sharp, with LQNS V5 converging to a substantially different steady state on the 60-task chain. This is a property of LQNS on this topology, not of \texttt{SolverLNSimple}; the chapter takes no position on which reference describes the topology's steady state correctly.

\section{Identified failure modes}
\label{sec:eval-failure-modes}

Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} reports the in-corpus boundary regimes --- fixtures the simple solver passes by matching one of the two references where the references themselves disagree. This section turns the lens the other way and catalogues the model classes \textit{outside} the evaluation corpus on which the simple solver visibly fails, preserved in \texttt{SolverLNSimpleFailingTest} (every fixture \texttt{@Disabled}) as standing regression placeholders for the spine claim's reach. The catalogue is backwards-looking evidence rather than forward-looking speculation: each mode is grounded in a specific fixture in the failing test suite, with a diagnosed root cause and a named \texttt{SolverLN} or LQNS feature whose absence accounts for it. The five modes together delineate the precise edge of the spine claim's accuracy reach. Four of the five are scope decisions consistent with the bottom-up methodology (machinery the corpus did not force); one is an implementation gap the section flags as a follow-up bug rather than a feature absence. The summary table at the end of the section places each mode against its corresponding entry in the feature delta (Section~\ref{sec:concl-future-parity}) and the conclusion's scope categorisation (Section~\ref{sec:concl-scope}).

\textbf{Mode 1 --- \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} 100-iteration cap (in-corpus borderline pass).} The fixture is a 4-tier multi-class chain with multi-entry middle tier (two REF tasks \texttt{R1}, \texttt{R2} each call distinct entries \texttt{E2A}, \texttt{E2B} on the shared intermediate \texttt{T2}; \texttt{T2}'s entries both call \texttt{T3}'s entry, \texttt{T3} calls \texttt{T4}). 903	\subsection{Where the evidence stops being conclusive}
904	
905	Three limits, matching the Section~\ref{sec:eval-hypotheses} concessions. First, single-capture JIT noise on aggregate timing makes the original single-capture F24 corpus speedup unattributable in isolation (1.68x F24-off single capture, with no detectable algorithmic content); a medianed N=3 replay against a medianed N=4 baseline collapses F24-off's aggregate to 1.02x, confirming the noise reading directly, and the per-iteration B-partition deep-chain rows (tasks40\_chain 1.17x, tasks60\_chain 1.45x) are the load-bearing F24 evidence instead. Second, the F20 bundle is decomposed only on the Arm A axis (floor vs floor+moving-avg+hard-reset): the Arm A condition isolates the floor's iter-count contribution at $\approx$92\% and the moving-average + hard-reset as the accuracy-preserving residual, but Arm B and Arm C are not separated from each other within the bundled remainder. Third, the \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} pass is borderline and helper-masked --- the simple solver hits its 100-iteration cap, the rel diff against \texttt{SolverLN} (4.76e-02) is just below the rtol bar, and the match-either helper absorbs a divergence that a strict LN-only check would surface.
906	
907	\subsection{Promise 13's segmentation revisited}
908	
909	The accuracy claim is bounded as the spine claim states. AMVA-path and LD-path fixtures separately match \texttt{SolverLN} within tolerance (confirmed by Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime}'s dispatch distribution). The fixtures where the two solvers disagree (C1 fan-out callers and B-fanout) are LD-path fixtures where the disagreement is rooted in \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{R ≈ D} substitution against the simple solver's closed-PFQN M/M/c queueing tail at moderate utilisation — the moderate-ρ multi-server PS regime Promise 13's wording names. The chapter does not adjudicate which solver is "right"; the contribution chapter's Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step5} and Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step4} argue the disagreement is structural rather than implementational, and the data supports that framing.
910	
911	\subsection{What the chapter does NOT claim}
912	
913	The chapter does not claim that \texttt{SolverLN}'s machineries are unnecessary in general. F24's \texttt{ptaskcallers} matrix is unread on this corpus because F17's downstream consumer short-circuits at the \texttt{clientEntryPairs.size() < 2} guard, but other model topologies might exercise the consumer and would then read the matrix. F20's smoothing carries a real accuracy cost when disabled (Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses} is evidence that the moving-average does useful work on small-amplitude-oscillation fixtures). F15 is load-bearing for tight-LN-match on 13 multi-entry / multi-class fixtures (Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary}) and is not removable without a 21\% drop in match-ln rate on this corpus. F21, F23, and F30 have no observable effect on this corpus but may serve corpora the present one does not exercise (Table~\ref{tab:eval-aggregate-runtime-conditions}). The claim is that on this corpus, omitting the spine-named machineries (F20's floor on iteration count; F17 and F24 on per-iteration runtime) recovers most of the iteration-count difference and a large fraction of the per-iteration runtime with a small bounded accuracy cost; the accuracy-preserving \texttt{combined} cut (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}) further shows that the F20 floor plus F17 / F21 / F24 can be removed together without any fixture's classification changing.
914	
915	The chapter also does not claim correctness in an adjacent saturation regime of the fan-out shapes --- per-server $\rho \geq 0.85$ at the widest callee in B-fanout trees or C1 fan-out callers. In that regime the simple solver's closed-PFQN M/M/c queueing tail diverges from both \texttt{SolverLN}'s M/M/inf-style host substitution and LQNS V5's MoL by 8--14\% on QLen, Util, and RespT at the saturated callee. The corpus deliberately covers the moderate-load regime ($\rho \leq 0.8$); the saturation regime sits just outside the chapter's tolerance bar and is not measured here.

917	\subsection{Future Work pointers}

919	Two follow-ups. First, separate Arms B and C of F20 (moving-average vs hard-reset) on the moving-avg-degraded fixtures; the Arm A condition isolates the floor from the bundle but Arms B and C remain entangled in the residual. Second, extend the medianed N=3 replay (which currently covers \texttt{f17off}, \texttt{f24off}, and \texttt{f17\_f24off} only --- the conditions for which the original single-capture aggregate ratios disagreed across captures) to the remaining ablation conditions (\texttt{f15off}, \texttt{f20off}, \texttt{combined}, \texttt{alloff}, etc.), and confirm F17's per-iteration scaling mechanism through profiling or kernel-cache auditing of \texttt{SolverMVA} / \texttt{SolverNC} under hard refreshes (the source-level investigation in \texttt{report/data/f17-mechanism-findings.md} narrows but does not prove the amplification mechanism).
