\textbf{Mode 3 --- Multi-entry intermediate task throughput scaling (\texttt{minimal\_multiEntryCaller}, implementation gap).} A single REF caller \texttt{T1} issues two synchronous calls per cycle to two distinct entries (\texttt{ES1}, \texttt{ES2}) of an intermediate task \texttt{T2}; each intermediate entry issues one call to a leaf. The simple solver's reported \texttt{T2.tput} comes out at the per-\texttt{T1}-cycle rate rather than the per-call rate at \texttt{T2}, leaving \texttt{ER1.RespT} approximately 50\% above \texttt{SolverLN}'s value. The root cause is a scope mismatch in \texttt{ResultsCollector.scaleLeafTaskThroughputs} (\texttt{jar/src/main/kotlin/jline/solvers/ln\_simple/results/ResultsCollector.java}, lines 254--268): the scaling pass multiplies leaf-task throughput by \texttt{LqnGraph.getTotalInboundCallMean}, but the guard at line 259 (\texttt{taskCalledTask.containsKey(task.getName()) continue}) skips any task with downstream callees --- so intermediates that themselves receive multi-call traffic are left at the upstream caller-cycle rate. The same per-call-vs-per-visit distinction the multi-class/multi-entry fix (Contribution Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step5}) addressed at the coupling layer is missing from the results-side aggregation for intermediates. Unlike the other four modes, this is an implementation bug in \texttt{SolverLNSimple}'s reporting path rather than a scope decision about which \texttt{SolverLN} features to absorb: the underlying coupling iteration on this fixture converges correctly (the per-class entry-side metrics that the iteration drives are right; the wrong number is the post-iteration task-throughput aggregation only). The fix is local to \texttt{ResultsCollector} and would extend the scaling pass to intermediates with inbound \texttt{callMean > 1}, mirroring the leaf path. We flag this as the one failure mode in the catalogue that should be promoted from out-of-scope to follow-up bug in Section~\ref{sec:concl-scope}; it is not material to the spine claim's accuracy decomposition (the iteration's converged state is unaffected) but it is material to the simple solver's reporting correctness on multi-entry intermediate-tier topologies.

\textbf{Mode 4 --- Saturated regime ($\rho_{\text{per-server}} \geq 0.85$ at the widest callee).} Six fixtures in \texttt{SolverLNSimpleFailingTest}'s Group 7 (three saturated B-scaleAxis fan-out variants at $k \in \{4, 9, 19\}$ callees; three saturated C1 fan-out caller variants at width $\in \{2, 3, 4\}$ with $c=2$ caller capacity) preserve the original saturated parameters the evaluation suite was tuned away from. The evaluation suite's B-fanout and C1 partitions land at per-server $\rho \leq 0.7$ at the widest callee; the failing test suite's saturated counterparts land at $\rho \approx 0.99$ via tighter think times and population scaling. In this regime \texttt{SolverLNSimple}'s load-dependent closed-network MVA disagrees with both references by 8--14\% on \texttt{QLen}, \texttt{Util}, and \texttt{RespT} at the saturated callee. The three-way disagreement is structurally explicit: \texttt{SolverLN} substitutes its \texttt{R $\approx$ D} approximation at the saturated host (under-counting queueing), \texttt{SolverLNSimple} computes the closed-PFQN M/M/c queueing tail via \texttt{pfqn\_mvams} (over-counting queueing relative to the open-system steady state), and LQNS V5's open-system overtaking approximation lands between the two via a separate analytical path. None of the three approximations remains defensible in this regime under the conventions the other two use to compare. This is the same M/M/$\infty$-vs-M/M/c structural boundary Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} Finding 3 reports on the moderate-load B-fanout fixtures, pushed past the regime where any of the three solvers can be treated as ground truth; the chapter's Section~\ref{sec:eval-notclaim} conclusion ``the chapter does not claim correctness in an adjacent saturation regime'' is the prospective concession that this mode is the retrospective evidence for. The missing machinery is a higher-moment or open-system inner kernel along the lines of \texttt{SolverLN}'s F18 (3-moment APH propagation) or LQNS's open-system overtaking treatment; the simple solver's mean-only closed-form kernel is the structurally limiting factor, and absorbing either alternative requires switching the inner kernel rather than extending the coupling layer.

\textbf{Mode 5 --- AND-fork on a finite-server PS host (\texttt{combinedDag\_PsHost}).} The fixture is a DAG-rich callee task with AND\_FORK / AND\_JOIN inside the entry, hosted on a single-server PS processor. The simple solver's closed-form $E[\max]$ join correction (\texttt{LqnGraph.andForkMaxCorrection}, the Heidelberger--Trivedi formula from Franks's thesis eq.~2.6) assumes the two branches are independent --- exact on an INF host, where the branches run on separate notional servers, but mis-representing the join delay on a finite-server host where the branches serialise through the shared queue. The structural absence is acknowledged in source: \texttt{ResultsCollector.adjustAndForkTaskThroughputs} restricts its $E[\max]$-based throughput correction to INF processors at line 294 with the explicit comment ``Restricted to INF processors: finite-server PS adds real branch contention that the closed-form $E[\max]$ doesn't capture (Franks §5.2.1 CCD overlap compensation --- out of scope here)''. The matching passing test \texttt{D\_combinedDag} (the same DAG on an INF host) confirms the regime is purely the host-side: the AND-fork composition itself is handled correctly on every host where branches do not contend. The principled fix is Franks's §5.2.1 concurrent-customer-dependency overlap compensation, replacing the independence assumption with an overlap term derived from the branch-pair joint busy probability at the shared server. The fix is the natural extension of the Section~\ref{sec:concl-future-parity} AND\_FORK / AND\_JOIN feature parity candidate and would interact with the bottom-up methodology in the same way the existing $E[\max]$ correction already does --- bottom-up, motivated by a specific fixture, scoped to the modelling construct the fixture exercises.

The five modes do not all sit at the same epistemic register. Modes 4 and 5 are structural limits on the simple solver's analytical machinery (closed-PFQN M/M/c tail at saturation, closed-form $E[\max]$ join under branch contention) named explicitly in the contribution chapter and the Section~\ref{sec:eval-notclaim} conclusion concession; their absorption requires switching or extending the inner kernel rather than extending the coupling layer. Modes 1 and 2 are convergence-detection failures rather than fixed-point failures: the simple solver reaches a point close to \texttt{SolverLN}'s converged state in both cases, but its single-iteration max-delta detection cannot quench small-amplitude oscillation that \texttt{SolverLN}'s moving-average window filters out. They are members of the same family the Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Arms B+C decomposition identified as accuracy-preserving machinery the construction could not safely omit; their re-import would follow the same bottom-up logic as F15's. Mode 3 is the one outlier: a results-side scaling gap localised to one helper method, with no underlying iteration consequence and no \texttt{SolverLN}-feature dependency. We flag it explicitly here so the catalogue does not silently bundle it with the four scope modes; the conclusion's Section~\ref{sec:concl-scope} ``out of scope'' bucket should grow a brief addendum naming Mode 3 as a follow-up bug rather than a methodological concession. Together, the catalogue places the simple solver's accuracy reach inside an explicitly named perimeter: the spine claim's ``broad class of closed LQN models'' wording is bounded by the four scope modes on the outside (the bottom-up build has a clear shape for absorbing each when a motivating fixture forces it) and by the one implementation gap on the inside (a local results-side fix that does not require any new machinery at all).




\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:eval-discussion}
\label{sec:eval-notclaim}

This section interprets the chapter's findings — why the ablation patterns are what they are, what they imply for the spine claim, and where the evidence runs out. The chapter's findings are read against the hypotheses, and the boundary of the spine claim is named explicitly.

\subsection{Findings against the hypotheses}

\textbf{H1 (correctness on Partition A): confirmed.} All 36 Partition A fixtures classified \texttt{match-ln} (Table~\ref{tab:eval-partition-a-reldiff}). The largest residual is the helper-masked \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} at 4.76e-02 (just below rtol); the next largest (\texttt{A3\_multiserver\_c2\_loadLow} at 2.81e-02) is within AMVA's own approximation error.

\textbf{H2 (iteration-count reduction on Partition A): confirmed with exception.} On 35 of 36 Partition A fixtures, the simple solver converges in 2–8 iterations against \texttt{SolverLN}'s 53. The exception is \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout}, where the simple solver hits its 100-iteration cap; strictly, the hypothesis is falsified on that single fixture (100 > 53). We carry the result as confirmed-with-exception, with the exception characterised under H1 and Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary}.

\textbf{H3 (F24 has zero effect on iteration count): confirmed.} The per-fixture diff vector between baseline and f24off \texttt{ln\_iters} is the zero vector across 61 fixtures. The simplest hypothesis confirmation in the chapter: the static-reading prediction that \texttt{ptaskcallers}'s output is computed but not consumed is matched exactly by the empirical invariance.

\textbf{H4 (F24 contributes per-iteration cost on Partition B that scales with chain depth): confirmed, narrowed scope.} The original single-capture H4 framing claimed F24 contributed 38–61\% of per-iteration cost on Partition B (per-fixture speedups 1.57$\times$–2.58$\times$). Under the medianed N=3 replay against the medianed N=4 baseline, F24's per-iteration effect is detectable only on the two deepest chain fixtures: \texttt{tasks40\_chain} 1.17$\times$ (14\% F24-fraction) and \texttt{tasks60\_chain} 1.45$\times$ (31\%). All other B fixtures and every non-B partition mean sit within $\pm$6\% of unity, indistinguishable from the JIT-noise band (Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime}). The chain-depth-scaling \textit{shape} is preserved (1.01$\times$ at \texttt{tasks5\_chain} growing monotonically to 1.45$\times$ at \texttt{tasks60\_chain}, consistent with \texttt{ptaskcallers}'s matrix-power cost scaling with call-graph depth); the per-fan-out values that the single-capture data had reported as 1.57$\times$–1.74$\times$ flat collapse to 0.98$\times$–1.00$\times$ under medianing, indicating that band was JIT-noise. The medianed corpus-aggregate F24 speedup (1.02$\times$) is a second independent measurement of the Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime} noise band; the per-iteration B-partition deep-chain rows are the load-bearing F24 evidence.

\textbf{H5 (F20 dominates the iteration-count difference): confirmed.} F20-off drops corpus-aggregate iterations from 3,801 to 1,248 (67.2\% reduction). 58 of 61 fixtures fall below the previous 50-iteration floor; the 3 exceptions are the three chain-B fixtures with topology-driven counts above 50. The \texttt{iter\_min} floor is the dominant arm — the Arm A condition (floor only, leaving moving-average and hard-reset intact) accounts for $\approx$92\% of F20-off's iter-count effect (3,801 → 1,452 vs F20-off 3,801 → 1,248), and the floor's binding on 55/61 baseline fixtures gives the structural reading directly.

\textbf{H6 (F20-off accuracy cost): confirmed and quantified.} Six of 61 fixtures move from \texttt{match-ln} to \texttt{match-lqns-only}: one A1, three A2, one C3, one C4 (Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses}). The cost concentrates on partitions where small-amplitude oscillation was being masked by the moving-average pass; it is small (10\% of the corpus) and non-zero, and the chapter reports it at the same prominence as F20's iteration-count savings.

\textbf{H7 (residual algorithmic difference remains): confirmed at 24.5\%.} Alloff corpus total (1,248) exceeds the simple solver's (418) by 830 iterations — a 24.5\% residual after a 75.5\% gap closure. The spine claim's three-quarters / one-quarter split is calibrated against this figure.

\textbf{H8 (F17 is a runtime-surface contributor scaling with fan-out breadth): confirmed.} F17-off iteration counts are bit-identical to baseline corpus-wide; match-status distribution unchanged; per-iteration runtime ratio splits cleanly by topology shape on Partition B. Under the medianed N=3 replay against the medianed N=4 baseline, F17-off is flat at 1.04--1.09$\times$ across chain task counts and grows monotonically from 1.13$\times$ to 3.43$\times$ across fan-out task counts --- the single-capture data had reported 1.10$\times$ flat on chains and 1.18$\times$--3.81$\times$ on fan-outs, qualitatively the same scaling shape at slightly compressed magnitudes. The medianed corpus-aggregate F17 speedup (2.45$\times$) is dominated by the largest fan-out fixtures and is not the load-bearing figure; the per-fixture scaling is. F17 joins F24 as a runtime-surface contributor with zero iteration-count or accuracy effect, with F17's per-iteration scaling dominating across most B fixtures (flat on chains, growing with fan-out) while F24's per-iteration scaling shows only on the two deepest chain fixtures.

\textbf{H9 (F15 is the load-bearing accuracy machinery for multi-entry / multi-class fixtures): confirmed.} F15-off iteration counts are bit-identical to baseline; exactly 13 fixtures move from \texttt{match-ln} to \texttt{match-lqns-only}, all in the multi-entry / multi-class subpartitions named in Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} (5 A2, 4 A4, 1 C2, 3 C3); A1, A3, B, C1, C4 unaffected. The effect is concentrated rather than diffuse. F15 sits alongside F20's moving-average + hard-reset arms as accuracy-preservation machinery the construction could not safely omit; the two complement each other (F20-B/C on small-amplitude-oscillation fixtures, F15 on multi-entry / multi-class fixtures).

\subsection{What the residual is}

The residual is named structurally rather than measured: Section~\ref{sec:eval-residual} identified three mechanisms the simple solver omits that \texttt{SolverLN} retains — predicate-gated damping (skipping the omega-blend on layers where damping is unneeded), structural service-time propagation rather than \texttt{*\_prev} snap-back, and single-iteration detection rather than three-iteration confirmation. None of these is F20 or F24; none is individually measured here; the chapter attributes the residual to them at the structural level. A four-arm ablation gating each separately would settle the per-mechanism decomposition (future work below).

\subsection{Why F20 is the iteration-count contributor and F17/F24 are runtime-surface contributors}

The spine's two-surface decomposition reads from the data directly. F20's contribution is structurally direct on the iteration-count surface: on 55 of 61 baseline fixtures, the \texttt{iter\_min = 50} floor holds \texttt{SolverLN}'s reported count at 53 regardless of when convergence actually occurred, while the simple solver's count on the same fixtures lands at 2–10. F20 \textit{is} the iteration-count difference on those fixtures, by construction, and the Arm A decomposition in Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} attributes $\approx$92\% of F20's iter-count cut to the floor specifically. F17 and F24, by contrast, have no iteration-count effect at all --- the consumer of both pieces of interlock work short-circuits on this corpus before the output reaches the convergence decision, so removing either removes per-iteration cost without altering outputs or the convergence decision (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}). The 75.5\% / 24.5\% split on the iteration-count surface is therefore approximately (F20's floor) / (residual algorithmic difference). F17 and F24 contribute on the runtime surface only (quantified jointly in Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}): F17's per-iteration cost grows with fan-out breadth across the corpus, while F24's per-iteration cost is detectable only on the two deepest Partition B chain fixtures under medianed measurement and is indistinguishable from the JIT-noise band elsewhere.

The two frontier points are \texttt{combined} (Arm A + F17-off + F21-off + F24-off, 7.99x speedup, all 61 fixtures preserve their \texttt{match-ln} classification) and \texttt{f20off} (the full F20 bundle, 8.29x speedup, six fixtures move from \texttt{match-ln} to \texttt{match-lqns-only}). The combined cut captures approximately 96\% of \texttt{f20off}'s aggregate speedup at zero observable accuracy cost on this corpus; the additional 0.30x speedup \texttt{f20off} delivers is the price the six fixtures pay in classification (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} frontier subsection; Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Finding 4). The \texttt{alloff} composite (F20 + F24 off, 9.33x) is faster still but inherits \texttt{f20off}'s six-fixture accuracy cost --- F24 contributes zero algorithmic change on top --- so its higher speedup is on the same point of the accuracy frontier as \texttt{f20off}, not beyond it.

The decomposition principle is that runtime factorises arithmetically across the two surfaces: wall-clock = iter-count $\times$ per-iter. The factorisation is clean on iter-count-invariant rows (F17, F24, F23, F30, F15, F17+F24); on F20-axis rows (those that reduce \texttt{ln\_iters}) the per-iter factor is additionally inflated by fixture-mix Simpson's-paradox, calibrated at $\approx$1.6$\times$ by the Arm A control (third caveat below). With that caveat: \texttt{f20off}'s 8.29x factors as $3.05\times$ iteration-count reduction (the F20 bundle's effect on \texttt{ln\_iters}, with the floor accounting for $\approx$92\% and the moving-average plus hard-reset arms the remaining $\approx$8\%) times $\approx 2.72\times$ corpus-aggregate per-iteration reduction (per-fixture median $\approx$1.58$\times$ from the moving-average window-mutation block; the gap is Simpson's). \texttt{combined}'s 7.99x factors as $2.62\times$ iteration-count reduction (Arm A floor only) times $\approx 3.06\times$ corpus-aggregate per-iteration reduction (per-fixture median 1.03$\times$ but reaching 2.59$\times$ on the heaviest fan-out fixture where F17/F24 work concentrates; the aggregate is again Simpson's-inflated). The per-iteration cuts compound multiplicatively with the iteration-count cut, but their absolute time savings shrink as iteration count drops --- the Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} frontier subsection's "diminishing returns" finding. Per-iteration cuts (F17, F24) are most valuable in absolute terms when iteration count is high; the runtime headline depends on which surface the cut targets and which surface the rest of the cut-set has already attacked.

For reference, the LQNS V5 corpus-aggregate wall-clock is 20,837 ms (≈21 seconds) and is invariant across all twelve conditions in Table~\ref{tab:eval-aggregate-runtime-conditions} because the ablations modify \texttt{SolverLN}'s source only; LQNS is invoked the same way on every fixture and condition. None of the twelve \texttt{SolverLN} conditions reaches the LQNS V5 wall-clock figure: the fastest condition (\texttt{alloff} at 275 s) remains 13.2x slower than LQNS V5, the combined frontier (\texttt{combined} at 320 s) is 15.4x slower, and baseline is 123x slower. The aggregate-runtime gap to LQNS V5 is therefore not closeable by the ablation set the chapter measures, even when every named machinery is disabled at once; closing it would require addressing per-layer MVA kernel cost rather than the outer-loop machineries the spine claim names. The simple solver's 19,259 ms medianed aggregate (Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime} Finding 1) is the only \texttt{SolverLN}-family figure in the chapter that aggregates within an order of magnitude of LQNS V5; under the fair bracket it matches LQNS V5 within 9\% rather than sitting below the reference line.

Three cautions on the runtime numbers. First, the aggregate-corpus ratios are dominated by the largest fan-out fixtures (\texttt{B\_scaleAxis\_tasks60\_fanout} alone is 1,757,244 ms of baseline's 2,561,103 ms, Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime} Finding 4), so the 7.99x and 8.29x multipliers would shrink substantially on a corpus without those fixtures; the per-fixture scaling visible in Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} Table~\ref{tab:eval-interlock-per-iter} (F24 medianed: 1.01x--1.45x on chains with monotone depth-growth, 0.98x--1.00x flat on fan-outs; F17 medianed: 1.04x--1.09x flat on chains, 1.13x--3.43x on fan-outs) is the corpus-portable evidence. Second, the JIT-noise band the chapter identifies is directly measured by the medianed F24-off comparison: F24-off's apparent 1.68x single-capture aggregate collapses to 1.02x under medianed N=3 captures against a medianed N=4 baseline (Table~\ref{tab:eval-aggregate-runtime-conditions}'s $\dagger$-marked row), confirming that the original single-capture F24 aggregate ratio was substantially JIT-noise and cannot be attributed to F24 in isolation --- Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} Finding 2's per-partition table (with the per-partition F24-off speedup means now 0.89--1.06x medianed) and the deep-chain rows of Figure~\ref{fig:eval-interlock-speedup}'s update (tasks40\_chain 1.17x, tasks60\_chain 1.45x) are the load-bearing F24 evidence, not the corpus aggregate. Third, on the five F20-axis rows (\texttt{A2\_arm\_A}, \texttt{f21+f20off}, \texttt{combined}, \texttt{f20off}, \texttt{alloff}) the Per-iter $\times$ column carries an additional fixture-mix Simpson's-paradox component: F20-axis cuts disproportionately remove iterations from cheap A/C floor-bound fixtures, concentrating the surviving iteration pool on the expensive B fixtures and inflating the corpus-aggregate ms/iter ratio even where no per-iteration work has been removed. The \texttt{A2\_arm\_A} control (Arm A floor cut only, no per-iteration changes by construction; Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Arm A wall-clock diagnostic) calibrates this inflation at $\approx$1.60$\times$. The per-fixture median ms/iter speedups on the F20-axis rows are 1.00$\times$ (\texttt{A2\_arm\_A}), 1.00$\times$ (\texttt{f21+f20off}), 1.58$\times$ (\texttt{f20off}), 1.03$\times$ (\texttt{combined}), and 1.59$\times$ (\texttt{alloff}) --- substantially smaller than the Per-iter $\times$ column reports. The per-fixture median itself is a robust but blunt summary: on rows where per-iteration savings are topology-specific (notably \texttt{combined}, where F17/F24 bite hardest on the heaviest fan-outs), the median understates the runtime-dominant fixtures' actual speedup --- \texttt{combined}'s per-iteration ratio on \texttt{B\_scaleAxis\_tasks60\_fanout} alone is 2.59$\times$. All three qualifications are absorbed into Table~\ref{tab:eval-aggregate-runtime-conditions}'s "ordering and shape, not two-decimal precision" framing.

\subsection{Where the evidence stops being conclusive}

Three limits, matching the Section~\ref{sec:eval-hypotheses} concessions. First, single-capture JIT noise on aggregate timing makes the original single-capture F24 corpus speedup unattributable in isolation (1.68x F24-off single capture, with no detectable algorithmic content); a medianed N=3 replay against a medianed N=4 baseline collapses F24-off's aggregate to 1.02x, confirming the noise reading directly, and the per-iteration B-partition deep-chain rows (tasks40\_chain 1.17x, tasks60\_chain 1.45x) are the load-bearing F24 evidence instead. Second, the F20 bundle is decomposed only on the Arm A axis (floor vs floor+moving-avg+hard-reset): the Arm A condition isolates the floor's iter-count contribution at $\approx$92\% and the moving-average + hard-reset as the accuracy-preserving residual, but Arm B and Arm C are not separated from each other within the bundled remainder. Third, the \texttt{A4\_chainPlusFanout} pass is borderline and helper-masked --- the simple solver hits its 100-iteration cap, the rel diff against \texttt{SolverLN} (4.76e-02) is just below the rtol bar, and the match-either helper absorbs a divergence that a strict LN-only check would surface.

\subsection{Promise 13's segmentation revisited}

The accuracy claim is bounded as the spine claim states. AMVA-path and LD-path fixtures separately match \texttt{SolverLN} within tolerance (confirmed by Section~\ref{sec:eval-runtime}'s dispatch distribution). The fixtures where the two solvers disagree (C1 fan-out callers and B-fanout) are LD-path fixtures where the disagreement is rooted in \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{R ≈ D} substitution against the simple solver's closed-PFQN M/M/c queueing tail at moderate utilisation — the moderate-ρ multi-server PS regime Promise 13's wording names. The chapter does not adjudicate which solver is "right"; the contribution chapter's Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step5} and Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step4} argue the disagreement is structural rather than implementational, and the data supports that framing.

\subsection{What the chapter does NOT claim}

The chapter does not claim that \texttt{SolverLN}'s machineries are unnecessary in general. F24's \texttt{ptaskcallers} matrix is unread on this corpus because F17's downstream consumer short-circuits at the \texttt{clientEntryPairs.size() < 2} guard, but other model topologies might exercise the consumer and would then read the matrix. F20's smoothing carries a real accuracy cost when disabled (Table~\ref{tab:eval-f20-accuracy-losses} is evidence that the moving-average does useful work on small-amplitude-oscillation fixtures). F15 is load-bearing for tight-LN-match on 13 multi-entry / multi-class fixtures (Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary}) and is not removable without a 21\% drop in match-ln rate on this corpus. F21, F23, and F30 have no observable effect on this corpus but may serve corpora the present one does not exercise (Table~\ref{tab:eval-aggregate-runtime-conditions}). The claim is that on this corpus, omitting the spine-named machineries (F20's floor on iteration count; F17 and F24 on per-iteration runtime) recovers most of the iteration-count difference and a large fraction of the per-iteration runtime with a small bounded accuracy cost; the accuracy-preserving \texttt{combined} cut (Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock}) further shows that the F20 floor plus F17 / F21 / F24 can be removed together without any fixture's classification changing.

The chapter also does not claim correctness in an adjacent saturation regime of the fan-out shapes --- per-server $\rho \geq 0.85$ at the widest callee in B-fanout trees or C1 fan-out callers. In that regime the simple solver's closed-PFQN M/M/c queueing tail diverges from both \texttt{SolverLN}'s M/M/inf-style host substitution and LQNS V5's MoL by 8--14\% on QLen, Util, and RespT at the saturated callee. The corpus deliberately covers the moderate-load regime ($\rho \leq 0.8$); the saturation regime sits just outside the chapter's tolerance bar and is not measured here.

\subsection{Future Work pointers}

Two follow-ups. First, separate Arms B and C of F20 (moving-average vs hard-reset) on the moving-avg-degraded fixtures; the Arm A condition isolates the floor from the bundle but Arms B and C remain entangled in the residual. Second, extend the medianed N=3 replay (which currently covers \texttt{f17off}, \texttt{f24off}, and \texttt{f17\_f24off} only --- the conditions for which the original single-capture aggregate ratios disagreed across captures) to the remaining ablation conditions (\texttt{f15off}, \texttt{f20off}, \texttt{combined}, \texttt{alloff}, etc.), and confirm F17's per-iteration scaling mechanism through profiling or kernel-cache auditing of \texttt{SolverMVA} / \texttt{SolverNC} under hard refreshes (the source-level investigation in \texttt{report/data/f17-mechanism-findings.md} narrows but does not prove the amplification mechanism).

\subsection{Closing}

The chapter has characterised the spine claim's three-quarters / one-quarter split with the corpus the build surfaced. The Discussion chapter takes this further, asking what the residual algorithmic difference means at the field level — whether a solver that omits the convergence-smoothing machinery and per-iteration random walks is a defensible architecture for closed LQN solvers in general, or a localised result valid only on the corpus this chapter measured.

7:Modern software systems have become increasingly more complex due to the widespread adoption of distributed, multi-tier architectures. Client-server and microservice-based systems \cite{lewis2014microservices} are commonly used to achieve scalability and flexibility; however, they also introduce significant performance analysis challenges \cite{heinrich2017}. Synchronous request-reply interactions, limited server concurrency and shared hardware resources can lead to blocking, contention and non-linear behaviour \cite{urgaonkar2005}, making it difficult to predict system performance.
9:A well-established approach to understanding such systems is an analytical performance modelling technique known as queueing network models. A queueing network models a system as a collection of interconnected service stations, each with an associated queue of jobs awaiting service. By analysing these models, it is possible to derive important performance metrics such as average response time, throughput, queue length and resource utilisation \cite{lazowska84}. These can be used to guide architectural decisions and identify bottlenecks early in the design process of computer systems.
11:Queueing network models have been widely applied within computer systems research, including the analysis of processors and I/O devices, transaction processing systems and distributed applications \cite{lazowska84}. Their importance has increased as modern systems demand high throughput and low latency, allowing performance considerations to be addressed before implementation. Compared to techniques such as measurement or simulation, analytical models allow rapid exploration of system designs at a relatively low cost, making them particularly valuable during the initial stages of development \cite{franks99}.
14:Whilst analytical techniques on classical queueing network models allow for efficient solutions, they rely on the assumption of product-form behaviour and a lack of blocking \cite{lazowska84}, which are frequently violated in client-server systems. For example, synchronous remote procedure calls introduce simultaneous resource possession, where both client and server resources are held during a call, invalidating the product-form independence assumptions \cite{franks99}.
16:To address these limitations, Layered Queueing Networks (LQNs) were introduced as a natural extension: able to represent software entities, such as tasks and entries, with their limited concurrency and synchronous interactions, while also modelling hardware resources, such as processors. By structuring the model into layers and representing synchronous calls as rendezvous interactions, LQNs are able to capture blocking, nested service demands and contention effects that arise naturally in multi-tier systems \cite{franks99, franks2009}.
18:However, the increased modelling power of LQNs comes at the cost of increased computational and implementation complexity. LQN solvers rely on decomposition techniques, surrogate delays and approximate mean-value analysis (MVA) variants, combined with fixed-point iteration \cite{lazowska84,franks99}. These techniques have been used in LQNS and other advanced solver tools, which support a wide range of modelling constructs such as interlocking, multiservers and complex activity graphs \cite{franks99}. While this generality enables the analysis of realistic systems, it also results in large, complex codebases that are difficult to understand, modify, or extend and overall lead to less efficient solvers.
35:\item \textbf{\texttt{SolverLNSimple}, a simplified LQN solver built bottom-up} Construction of this solver began from a minimal LQN solver, adding one capability at a time, each driven by a specific class of LQN model a design without it could not handle. Initially delegating the inner MVA kernel to the same closed-form routine the established comparators use, we focused on writing the outer coupling iteration from scratch. The solver handles single-class chains, fan-out caller topologies, multi-class shared-callee topologies, multi-entry and reference-task models, multi-server processors, deep infinite-server topologies, and a limited activity-graph feature set spanning sequence past the bound activity, OR-fork probabilistic branching, POST\_LOOP wrapping cross-task calls, AND-fork / AND-join with the expected-maximum join correction on INF-hosted callees, and the reply phase-1 / phase-2 split. The activity-graph feature set is demonstrated on targeted fixtures outside the headline evaluation corpus, which exercises the rest of the feature set.
40:\item \textbf{An evaluation of \texttt{SolverLNSimple} against \texttt{SolverLN} and \texttt{LQNS}} On a 61-fixture evaluation corpus developed to consider a wide range of model classes, the simple solver matches either \texttt{SolverLN}'s or \texttt{LQNS}'s outputs within standard tolerance on all fixtures. Whilst outperforming both on iteration count and execution time.
41:An ablation study of \texttt{SolverLN}, isolating F20 (the \texttt{iter\_min} floor and moving-average convergence detection), F24 (the unconditional \texttt{ptaskcallers} traversal), and F19 (adaptive under-relaxation), quantified each machinery's contribution to the gap in iteration count from \texttt{SolverLNSimple}. The combined decomposition accounts for 75.5\% of the corpus-aggregate iteration-count difference, leaving a 24.5\% residual identified structurally as genuine algorithmic difference.

98:The \textbf{out of scope} category covers features the bottom-up build had a clear shape for absorbing but that the corpus did not force into it. 138:The first direction is extending \texttt{SolverLNSimple} toward feature parity with \texttt{SolverLN} and LQNS V5, with each modelling construct added when a specific model class forces its addition.
140:The feature delta against \texttt{SolverLN} records a set of modelling constructs the simple solver presently does not handle. 142:The first candidate is \textit{finite-server PS host AND\_FORK / AND\_JOIN, and corpus-scale evaluation of the activity-graph features}. ###### ABSTRACT ######
12:An evaluation of the solver, on a 61-fixture corpus (which exercises every feature except activity-graph awareness), against \texttt{SolverLN} and LQNS verifies its correctness and characterises its performance.
13:75.5\% of the iteration count difference is attributable to \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{iter\_min} convergence floor, with the rest reflecting genuine algorithmic difference, however the omission of a moving-average convergence detection carries a small, quantified accuracy cost. The activity-graph machinery is demonstrated separately and does not enter this decomposition.

###### INTRODUCTION ######
40:\item \textbf{An evaluation of \texttt{SolverLNSimple} against \texttt{SolverLN} and \texttt{LQNS}} On a 61-fixture evaluation corpus developed to consider a wide range of model classes, the simple solver matches either \texttt{SolverLN}'s or \texttt{LQNS}'s outputs within standard tolerance on all fixtures. Whilst outperforming both on iteration count and execution time.
41:An ablation study of \texttt{SolverLN}, isolating F20 (the \texttt{iter\_min} floor and moving-average convergence detection), F24 (the unconditional \texttt{ptaskcallers} traversal), and F19 (adaptive under-relaxation), quantified each machinery's contribution to the gap in iteration count from \texttt{SolverLNSimple}. The combined decomposition accounts for 75.5\% of the corpus-aggregate iteration-count difference, leaving a 24.5\% residual identified structurally as genuine algorithmic difference.

###### CONCLUSION ######
25:The difference between \texttt{SolverLN} and \texttt{SolverLNSimple} on closed LQN models, measured against the 61-fixture evaluation corpus (which exercises every feature except activity-graph awareness), is measurable on two surfaces. On iteration count, approximately three-quarters (75.5\% on the evaluation corpus) is attributable to the \texttt{iter\_min} convergence floor within F20, the remaining quarter reflecting genuine algorithmic difference. On runtime, two machineries the construction omits impose per-iteration cost without iteration-count or accuracy effect: the interlock correction (F17), whose cost grows with fan-out breadth, and the unconditional task-caller traversal computed but not consumed (F24), whose cost is roughly uniform across the corpus. The simple solver's omission of F20's moving-average machinery has a small accuracy cost --- loss of tight-LN-match on a minority of fixtures, which retain match within tolerance of LQNS V5 --- which the evaluation quantifies. The activity-graph features sit outside this corpus and are demonstrated separately (Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step6}); they do not enter the per-machinery decomposition reported here.

Each of the three machineries the ablation isolates — F19 (adaptive under-relaxation), F20 (the \texttt{iter\_min} floor combined with moving-average convergence detection and hard-reset verification), and F24 (the unconditional \texttt{ptaskcallers} traversal) — is gated by a separate ablation condition, and the union of all three off (\texttt{alloff}) is compared against the simple solver's converged iteration counts. The corpus-aggregate decomposition that emerges is the central numerical claim of the report.
62:\textbf{F20's \texttt{iter\_min} floor is the largest single contributor to the iteration-count difference.} Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Finding 1 reports that disabling the full F20 bundle reduces corpus-aggregate \texttt{SolverLN} iterations from 3,801 to 1,248 — a 67.2\% reduction. The pattern is structural: on 55 of 61 baseline fixtures, the \texttt{iter\_min = 50} floor holds \texttt{SolverLN}'s reported count at 53 regardless of when convergence actually occurred, while the simple solver's count on the same fixtures lands at between 2 and 10. F20 \textit{is} the iteration-count difference on those fixtures, by construction. The chapter's Arm A subsection isolates the floor from the moving-average and hard-reset arms: the floor alone (\texttt{A2\_arm\_A} condition) reduces the corpus iteration total from 3,801 to 1,452, accounting for $\approx$92\% of F20's iter-count effect; the moving-average and hard-reset arms contribute the remaining $\approx$8\% on iteration count and carry the accuracy-preservation role separately (the six fixtures degraded by full F20-off all retain their \texttt{match-ln} classification under Arm A).
64:\textbf{F24 contributes per-iteration runtime but not iteration count.} Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} Finding 1 reports that disabling F24 leaves every fixture's iteration count bit-identical to baseline; the per-fixture diff vector across 61 fixtures is exactly zero. This is the simplest hypothesis confirmation in the chapter and the most direct empirical evidence that F24's output is computed but not consumed on \texttt{SolverLN}'s default profile, exactly as the static reading of the source predicted. Section~\ref{sec:eval-interlock} Finding 2 then quantifies the per-iteration runtime cost on Partition B: F24's \texttt{ptaskcallers} random walk accounts for 38\% to 61\% of per-iteration time across the ten B fixtures, growing monotonically with task count on chain topologies (1.65x at tasks=5 to 2.58x at tasks=60) and remaining flatter on fan-out topologies (1.57x to 1.74x) where the per-layer MVA solve dominates per-iteration cost. The per-iteration ratio is JIT-noise insensitive because every B fixture runs the same iteration count across baseline and f24off; the chapter's aggregate F24 wall-clock speedup of 1.68x is reported with a caveat (the F19-off control with no algorithm change ran 1.74x faster on aggregate) and is not the load-bearing F24 evidence.
66:\textbf{F19 is essentially inert on the default profile.} Section~\ref{sec:eval-residual} reports two findings. The default \texttt{LNOptions.relax = "fixed"} means the adaptive branch is not running on baseline, so the f19off control reproduces baseline iteration counts and accuracy bit-identically. When adaptive damping is forced on Partition C1 (designed to be its stress case), auto mode's oscillation detection ramps omega to 0.5 within the first few iterations — the same value fixed mode uses from iteration 1 — and the two modes converge with iteration counts bit-identical and rel diffs agreeing to 8 or 9 decimal places. F19's adaptive branch is functionally equivalent to its fixed branch on the partition where its behaviour was most likely to differ. The claim is scoped to the measured partition.
68:\textbf{The combined ablation accounts for 75.5\% of the difference.} Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} reports the all-three-off condition's corpus aggregate: \texttt{alloff.ln\_total = 1,248} against \texttt{sim\_total = 418}, accounting for \texttt{(3,801 $-$ 1,248) / (3,801 $-$ 418) = 75.5\%} of the iteration-count difference. The remaining 24.5\% — 830 iterations corpus-wide — is the residual that survives turning off all three ablated machineries. Per-partition gap closure ranges from 56.9\% on Partition B (topology-driven convergence above the floor on the three chain fixtures, where \texttt{SolverLN}'s convergence is genuinely slower than the simple solver's even with F20 disabled) to 86.8\% on Partition C1, with the A4\_chainPlusFanout cap-hit anomaly treated explicitly in Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} Finding 3 footnote and excluded from the A4 partition average. The 75.5\% / 24.5\% split is the chapter's load-bearing empirical number and the figure to which the spine claim's "approximately three-quarters" wording is calibrated.
70:\textbf{The residual is named structurally rather than measured.} Section~\ref{sec:eval-boundary} Finding 3 names three mechanisms the simple solver omits that \texttt{SolverLN} retains after F20 and F24 are turned off: predicate-gated damping (skipping the omega-blend on layers where damping is unneeded), structural service-time propagation through the \texttt{Z\_callee\_host} and \texttt{Z\_callee\_clients} formulas rather than \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{*\_prev} snap-back arrays, and single-iteration convergence detection rather than three-iteration confirmation. None of these three is F19, F20, or F24; none is individually measured here; the chapter attributes the residual to them at the structural level. A four-arm ablation gating each separately would settle the per-mechanism decomposition, and is named as future work in Section~\ref{sec:eval-discussion} and again in Section~\ref{sec:concl-scope} below.
72:\textbf{Accuracy cost of F20-off.} Section~\ref{sec:eval-f20} Finding 2 quantifies the accuracy cost of omitting F20: six of 61 fixtures move from \texttt{match-ln} to \texttt{match-lqns-only} (one A1, three A2, one C3, one C4). The moving-average machinery is doing real work on small-amplitude oscillation fixtures, and disabling it carries a measurable accuracy penalty on a minority of the corpus. The simple solver's design point is to avoid F20 in exchange for matching \texttt{SolverLN} on the partitions it claims; the cost is small (10\% of the corpus) and non-zero, and the chapter reports it at the same prominence as F20's iteration-count savings.
74:The combined picture is the report's central field-level point. The two-surface difference is \textit{not} the simple solver being algorithmically superior to \texttt{SolverLN}. It is specific identifiable machinery in \texttt{SolverLN} that the corpus does not require — on the iteration-count surface, predominantly an iteration floor (F20's \texttt{iter\_min}) that holds the reported count above the actual convergence point; on the runtime surface, two per-iteration machineries (interlock correction F17 and the task-caller traversal F24) whose outputs are absorbed into per-iteration state or never consumed at all — combined with a residual quarter of genuine algorithmic difference on the iteration-count surface attributable to three structural choices in the simple solver's design. The framing matters because it sharpens what the project contributes. The build is not faster in the sense of having invented a better algorithm; the build's deliberate omissions made it possible to characterise where the two-surface difference lives — on iteration count, predominantly in F20's \texttt{iter\_min} floor; on runtime, in two omitted per-iteration machineries (F17 and F24) — structurally rather than algorithmically. The simple solver's design point accepts a small accuracy cost on a minority of fixtures when F20's moving-average machinery is omitted, in exchange for faster convergence on the corpus the build surfaced. The contribution is the construction with its empirical characterisation, not algorithmic superiority.
98:The \textbf{out of scope} category covers features the bottom-up build had a clear shape for absorbing but that the corpus did not force into it. Section~\ref{ch:lqn} catalogues the LQN modelling vocabulary in full, and the feature delta in the Contribution chapter's Chapter~\ref{ch:contrib} records which constructs \texttt{SolverLN} implements that the simple solver does not. The constructs in this category include open-class arrivals on entries and interlock correction. For each, the natural extension under the bottom-up methodology is identified — the contribution chapter sketches the form in passing and Section~\ref{sec:concl-future-parity} below enumerates them explicitly — and the absence is attributable to no motivating fixture having forced the addition within the project's scope. A complementary set of activity-graph constructs is built into the construction by activity-graph awareness (Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step6}) but is not exercised by the evaluation corpus: OR\_FORK / OR\_JOIN probabilistic routing, full DAG activity precedence beyond the sequential and POST\_LOOP cases, and AND\_FORK / AND\_JOIN with the expected-maximum join correction on INF-hosted callees. These sit in the contribution but not in the corpus-side grading; the AND-fork construction's finite-server PS host case (requiring Franks §5.2.1 CCD overlap compensation) remains an acknowledged scope limit on the construction itself. Interlock correction in particular is the feature whose deliberate omission the spine claim's construction depends on: the contribution chapter's Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step2} argues that on this corpus the interlock machinery is \texttt{LQNS V5-style} accreted overhead (the comment in \texttt{SolverLN.java:3963} is the source-level evidence) rather than load-bearing for the closed-LQN behaviour the simple solver targets. These absences are scope decisions: the bottom-up build has a clear shape for absorbing them, and Section~\ref{sec:concl-future-parity} below expects them to come in when motivating models force the additions.
100:The \textbf{out of reach} category covers features that the bottom-up methodology does not absorb cleanly without modification to the inner kernel, the coupling channel, or the per-iteration solver dispatch. Three constructs in the feature delta sit here, and Section~\ref{sec:concl-future-research} below treats them as research-frontier rather than feature-parity work. \textit{Cache modelling nodes} (F7) require new node types in the representation and per-iteration routing probability re-derivation; the natural form under the bottom-up methodology extends the per-layer routing machinery rather than importing the full LQNS-V5 class-switching path, and a motivating fixture with a CDN tier or in-memory cache in front of a database would force the addition. \textit{3-moment APH propagation} (F18) requires a kernel that accepts an SCV parameter or a moment-matching distribution; the closed-form MVA kernel the simple solver currently uses works on mean values only, and absorbing the higher-moment propagation requires switching the inner kernel rather than extending it. \textit{Class-switching at iteration time} interacts with the coupling structure in a way the simple solver's per-layer client/host coupling does not currently express, and absorption would require revisiting the coupling channel rather than adding a fixture and forcing a step.
114:\textbf{The absence of published audits.} The related work survey's Q4 finding is that no published paper systematically separates necessary machinery from accreted complexity in LQNS V5 or \texttt{SolverLN}. Franks and Li (2012) come closest with their self-critique of wasted inner-loop work; the Islam-Petriu-Woodside (2022) paper \cite{islam2022} recognises that surrogate-delay iteration and FESC evaluation are expensive; neither does the per-machinery decomposition the present project does on the outer-loop scaffolding. The project's evaluation is one small contribution toward filling that gap. The methodological observation that emerges is that the established literature has focused on extending solver capability — new modelling constructs, new paradigms, model-level simplification — rather than on decomposing solver implementation. The gap is a real one, and we suggest (as Section~\ref{ch:lqn}'s related-work survey already does) that it has been left to implementations rather than to papers because publication incentives have rewarded the extension surfaces more than the per-machinery decomposition ones.
116:\textbf{The historical flow of machinery.} Section~\ref{ch:lqn}'s discussion of historical flow narrates how LQNS V5 was the ancestor that \texttt{SolverLN} was ported from, and the feature delta documents the textual evidence: the \texttt{LQNS V5-style} comment at \texttt{SolverLN.java:159}, the \texttt{LQNS V5 Interlock: Static Analysis} comment at line 3963. Accreted machinery propagates across the LQN tool family because porting is faster than re-derivation. The pattern is not a fault of the tools' authors — porting is the right thing to do under time pressure and prevailing publication norms — but it does mean that machinery once added for a specific hard case tends to persist across generations of solvers and tools without revisiting whether it is still necessary on the easier cases the tools spend most of their time on. The project's bottom-up methodology is a deliberate response to that pattern: build from a base case and add only what specific models force, rather than inheriting machinery wholesale and relying on it being uniformly necessary.
120:\textbf{The honest scope of the field-level reflection.} The project is one MEng's worth of work on one corpus of closed LQN models. The field-level reflection is offered as suggestion, not as a general principle the project has established. The gap in the published record is a real finding from the Related Work survey that is supported by the systematic post-2024 follow-up searches; the historical-flow observation is supported by direct source-level evidence in \texttt{SolverLN.java}; the methodological-pattern suggestion is supported by the present project's demonstration on LQN solvers. None of the three rises to the level of a general principle for solver research, and the chapter does not present them as such. The framing is consistent with the report's overall hedging discipline: confident on positioning, carefully hedged on novelty, and explicit about what would be required to escalate any of these from suggestion to claim.
142:The first candidate is \textit{finite-server PS host AND\_FORK / AND\_JOIN, and corpus-scale evaluation of the activity-graph features}. Activity-graph awareness (Section~\ref{sec:contrib-step6}) builds AND-fork / AND-join at the construction level on INF-hosted callees via the closed-form inclusion-exclusion $E[\max]$ correction (Heidelberger and Trivedi's identity, Franks thesis eq.~2.6); the finite-server PS host case --- where parallel branches serialise through a shared queue rather than running on independent notional servers --- was acknowledged at construction as out of reach, with the \texttt{@Disabled} \texttt{D\_andForkPsHost} and \texttt{combinedDag\_PsHost} fixtures pointing at the gap. The bottom-up extension is the Franks §5.2.1 CCD overlap compensation: per-branch closed chains in every layer, sibling tracking, and $\delta_{kj} / d_{kj} / p_{kj}$ overlap factors modifying the MVA waiting-time term, replacing the branch-independence assumption that the closed-form $E[\max]$ relies on. The other half of this candidate is methodological: the activity-graph features (sequence past the bound activity, OR-fork probabilistic branching, POST\_LOOP wrapping cross-task calls, AND-fork / AND-join on INF hosts, and the reply phase-1 / phase-2 split) are currently demonstrated by the targeted DAG fixtures in \texttt{SolverLNSimpleDagTest} and the phase-walker unit tests in \texttt{LqnGraphPhase1Test} rather than by the 61-fixture evaluation corpus, so the spine claim's iteration-count and runtime characterisation is calibrated to the feature set the corpus exercises. Extending the corpus along the activity-graph axis --- and re-running the per-machinery decomposition against the extended corpus --- would let the spine claim's two-surface characterisation cover the activity-graph feature set as well.
148:The fourth candidate is \textit{open-class arrivals on entries}. \texttt{SolverLN} supports per-entry arrival distributions via \texttt{Source} / \texttt{Sink} plus an \texttt{OpenClass} (F12); the simple solver presently handles closed LQN models only, and the narrative chat record states explicitly that the open-class branch in the inner MVA kernel was deleted as the LQN ensemble in scope never produced open classes. A motivating fixture would be an external-traffic-driven system with HTTP requests arriving at a public-facing entry. The methodological cost is higher than the previous three because it relaxes the closed-PFQN assumption the simple solver's MVA path is built around; the natural shape is mixed open-plus-closed layers, with the inner kernel dispatched accordingly.
157:Three constructs in the feature delta carry this character. The first is \textit{Cache modelling}. \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{Cache} node integration (F7) constructs a cache node with \texttt{ReplacementStrategy} selected from RR, FIFO, SFIFO, and LRU, plus a per-level capacity matrix, with routing using cache hit/miss classes whose probabilities are re-derived each iteration from host-layer throughput ratios. The construct traces to Gao, Casale and Singhal's 2024 ACM TOMPECS paper \textit{Performance Modeling of Distributed Data Processing in Microservice Applications}, which introduces Layered Caching-Queueing (LCQ) models that integrate a hierarchical cache formalism into the LQN framework with a novel fixed-point iteration; the cache-analysis primitives the construct rests on are from Casale and Gast's 2021 IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking paper on list-based cache analysis and Gao and Casale's 2022 IWQoS paper on joint caching and service placement. Absorbing cache support under the bottom-up methodology is solver-side work, not modelling-side: a motivating fixture with a CDN tier or in-memory cache in front of a database would force the addition, and the natural form is to extend the per-iteration routing-probability machinery rather than to import the full LQNS-V5 class-switching path.
159:The second is \textit{FunctionTask, setupTime, and delayOff} for serverless workloads. \texttt{SolverLN}'s FunctionTask support (F8) forces the per-layer inner solver to \texttt{SolverMAM} with method \texttt{"dec.poisson"} whenever a \texttt{FunctionTask} has a Queue with \texttt{delayOffEnabled}. The construct traces to Gias and Casale's 2020 IEEE MASCOTS paper \textit{COCOA: Cold Start Aware Capacity Planning for Function-as-a-Service Platforms}, which combines an LQN model with an M/M/k-with-setup model and differentiates warm versus cold service; the literal \texttt{FunctionTask}, \texttt{setupTime} and \texttt{delayOff} class names in LINE are the API realisation of this pattern, and Wang, Casale and Filieri's 2022 ICSOC paper \textit{Enhancing Performance Modeling of Serverless Functions via Static Analysis} formalises the LQN extension capturing serverless workflows. Absorption is harder than for cache nodes because the construct requires a non-MVA inner solver (MAM) and an open-arrivals coupling channel, so a motivating FaaS fixture would force both the open-class extension described in Section~\ref{sec:concl-future-parity} and a per-layer dispatch hook of the kind \texttt{SolverLN}'s F2 provides. The bottom-up shape is preserved: each piece of machinery is added because a specific model forces it.
161:The third is \textit{3-moment APH propagation}. \texttt{SolverLN}'s \texttt{moment3} mode (F18) propagates phase-type response-time distributions recursively through LQN submodels with moment-matching refitting at each layer to keep the order bounded; the simple solver propagates only the mean via exponential-fit. The construct traces to Niu and Casale's 2021 MASCOTS paper and 2024 IEEE TSE paper on neural-density estimation of response times in layered software systems, with the underlying APH construction from Bobbio, Horváth and Telek's 2005 \textit{Stochastic Models} paper. The methodological cost of absorption is higher still, because the closed-form MVA kernel the simple solver uses works on mean values only --- adding higher-moment propagation requires switching to a kernel that accepts an SCV parameter or a moment-matching distribution. A motivating fixture would be a latency-sensitive service whose SLA is expressed in percentiles rather than means.
178:The project has shown, against the success criterion stated at the opening of this chapter and graded by this chapter, that \texttt{SolverLNSimple} matches \texttt{SolverLN} to standard tolerance on a broad class of closed LQN models with one fixture's exception characterised as an LN-vs-LQNS oracle disagreement; that on the iteration-count surface approximately three-quarters of the difference between the two solvers is attributable to F20's \texttt{iter\_min} convergence floor and the remaining quarter to a structurally identified residual algorithmic difference; that on the per-iteration runtime surface, two omitted machineries (F17 interlock correction, whose cost grows with fan-out breadth, and F24's unconditional task-caller traversal, whose cost is roughly uniform) carry the construction's runtime advantage without iteration-count or accuracy effect; and that the resulting correct solver is then optimised --- through limit-cycle detection, over-relaxation, a warm-start, and memoisation of its topological queries --- to reduce its outer-iteration count and runtime further without sacrificing that accuracy.
180:On every ablation condition the evaluation measures, \texttt{SolverLNSimple} lands within tolerance of at least one of the two references on every fixture; this corpus-wide match-either coverage is reported in Section~\ref{sec:eval-apparatus} and characterised in Section~\ref{sec:eval-failure-modes} as a supporting observation, not as a load-bearing accuracy verdict --- that role belongs to the Partition A 36/36 against \texttt{SolverLN} graded in Section~\ref{sec:concl-sub-a}.

input.content:
# Overnight refresh plan — regenerate every report number against the final solver

**Companion to** [REFRESH-INVENTORY.md](REFRESH-INVENTORY.md) (what each number is and where it lives).
This document specifies the **overnight script** that re-derives all of them. The solver is still
changing, so the script cannot be validated yet; it is written defensively and the genuinely
ambiguous parts (ablation toggling) are specified as a build-it-yourself plan rather than guessed.

A starter scaffold is provided at the end (`report/scripts/refresh-overnight.sh`, created alongside
this doc) — it implements every **unambiguous** stage and leaves clearly-marked `TODO(ablation)`
hooks for the parts that depend on decisions only you can make.

---

## 0. Pre-flight decisions (must be settled before the script runs — see INVENTORY Part 5)

1. **Corpus membership (S1).** Decide whether the 4 new A4 fixtures + any C5/C6/C7 belong in the
   canonical corpus. Recommended: keep the corpus at the **same 61** the report is calibrated to by
   *not* registering the 4 activity-graph A4 fixtures in `SolverLNSimpleEvaluationTest` (move them to
   a separate non-corpus test), OR accept 65 and re-state every count in the report. The script
   asserts the captured row count equals an expected `EXPECTED_CORPUS_N` and aborts on mismatch.
2. **Operating point (S6).** The eval-chapter baseline must be captured with optimisations **off**
   (master α=0.5, tol=5e-3, warm-start/limit-cycle as they were at the 418-iter point) — i.e. the
   `SolverLNSimple` state the spine claim was measured against. If the "final solver" *is* the
   optimised one, then either (a) re-baseline the whole eval chapter at the new operating point and
   restate 418→new everywhere, or (b) keep a flag to disable the optimisations for the eval capture.
   **This is a content decision, not a scripting one — settle it first.**
3. **Ablation mechanism (S4).** The per-condition `SolverLN.java` patches are line-based and will not
   apply after the migration. Choose one:
   - **(Recommended) Convert ablations to runtime flags.** Add permanent `-Dablation.f24=off` style
     gates inside `SolverLN.java` (a single `AblationFlags` reader). Then the overnight script just
     sets a system property per condition — no patch/recompile churn, robust across refactors.
   - **(Fallback) Re-derive the diffs.** Re-express each `.modification.diff` against the current
     `SolverLN.java`, store them, and have the script `patch`/revert per condition (revert via
     `git show HEAD:…/SolverLN.java > …/SolverLN.java` because the file has the **skip-worktree** bit
     set — `git checkout` will NOT revert it; verify with `git hash-object`).

---

## 1. The full study matrix (what to capture)

### 1.1 Three-solver corpus captures (`SolverLNSimpleEvaluationTest`, `DataCollector`)

Each row below = one `mvn test` invocation producing `report/data/<dataset>.csv` (+ `.json`,
optionally `.tables.csv`). All feed the eval chapter.

| `baseline` | baseline | none | Single-capture baseline used by e3.1, e7.1, e9.1, e10.1, and all per-fixture rel-diff numbers (§2.3, §2.4, §2.9). |
| `f24off` | F24off | skip `ptaskcallers` compute | §2.6, Fig e7.1, master table |

| `alloff` | allOff | F20off + F24off | §2.8, Fig e7.1, e9.1, master table |
| `f17off` | F17off | `options.config.interlocking = false` (constructor) | §2.6, Fig e6.1, master table |
| `f17_f24off` | F17+F24off | both | §2.6, master table |
| `f15off` | F15off | early-return `updateRoutingProbabilities` | §2.6/§2.9, master table |

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# refresh-overnight.sh — regenerate every measured number in the FYP report.
#
# STATUS: SCAFFOLD. The solver is still changing, so this has NOT been run.
# It implements the unambiguous stages (baseline N=4, single baseline, replay,
# probes, figure regen, validation) and leaves the ablation toggling as clearly
# marked TODO hooks (see REFRESH-OVERNIGHT-PLAN.md §0.3 / §3).
#
# Read REFRESH-OVERNIGHT-PLAN.md and REFRESH-INVENTORY.md before running.
#
# Usage:
#   report/scripts/refresh-overnight.sh [--force] [--stages B,C,D,...] [--dry-run]
#
# Design rules (from CLAUDE.md / repo conventions):
#   * NO git commit / stash / reset. Reverting SolverLN.java via `git show HEAD:`
#     + file write is the only git write performed (skip-worktree-safe).
#   * tsp (task-spooler) serialises mvn runs for clean timing.
#   * Every capture is row-count-asserted against EXPECTED_CORPUS_N.
#   * Idempotent: existing non-empty outputs are skipped unless --force.
# =============================================================================
set -euo pipefail

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- config
ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"   # repo root
JAR_DIR="$ROOT/jar"
DATA_DIR="$ROOT/report/data"
LOG_DIR="$DATA_DIR/refresh-logs"
FIG_SCRIPTS="$ROOT/report/source/figures/scripts"
SLN="$JAR_DIR/src/main/kotlin/jline/solvers/ln/SolverLN.java"
DIFF_DIR="$DATA_DIR/diffs"                 # re-derived <condition>.modification.diff files (fallback mech)
DRIVER_LOG="$DATA_DIR/refresh-driver.log"

# ⚠️ SET THIS once the S1 corpus decision is made (61 today; 65 if the 4 new A4 fixtures stay).
EXPECTED_CORPUS_N="${EXPECTED_CORPUS_N:-61}"

MVN="/usr/bin/mvn"
USE_TSP="${USE_TSP:-1}"                    # 0 to run mvn directly (no task-spooler)
BASELINE_REPEATS="${BASELINE_REPEATS:-4}"  # N for medianed baseline
REPLAY_REPEATS="${REPLAY_REPEATS:-3}"      # N for medianed replay
FORCE=0; DRY=0; ONLY_STAGES=""

# Ablation toggling mechanism: "flag" (recommended, requires AblationFlags in SolverLN.java)
# or "patch" (fallback, requires re-derived diffs in $DIFF_DIR). See plan §0.3.
ABLATION_MECH="${ABLATION_MECH:-patch}"

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- args
while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
  case "$1" in
    --force) FORCE=1;;
    --dry-run) DRY=1;;
    --stages) ONLY_STAGES="$2"; shift;;
    *) echo "unknown arg: $1"; exit 2;;
  esac; shift
done

mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"
exec > >(tee -a "$DRIVER_LOG") 2>&1

log(){ echo "[refresh $(date -Is)] $*"; }
have_stage(){ [[ -z "$ONLY_STAGES" || ",$ONLY_STAGES," == *",$1,"* ]]; }
csv_rows(){ [[ -f "$1" ]] && echo $(( $(wc -l < "$1") - 1 )) || echo 0; }

assert_rows(){ # <csv> — warn+return1 on mismatch, do not kill the night
  local csv="$1" n; n="$(csv_rows "$csv")"
  if [[ "$n" -ne "$EXPECTED_CORPUS_N" ]]; then
    log "WARN row-count mismatch in $(basename "$csv"): got $n expected $EXPECTED_CORPUS_N"; return 1
  fi
  log "OK $(basename "$csv"): $n rows"; return 0
}

skip_if_done(){ # <output-file> — true if we should skip
  [[ $FORCE -eq 0 && -s "$1" ]] && { log "skip (exists): $(basename "$1")"; return 0; }
  return 1
}

run_mvn(){ # <logfile> <mvn args...>
  local lf="$1"; shift
  if [[ $DRY -eq 1 ]]; then log "DRY: mvn $*"; return 0; fi
  if [[ "$USE_TSP" == "1" ]] && command -v tsp >/dev/null; then
    ( cd "$JAR_DIR" && tsp -f "$MVN" -Dtmp=false "$@" ) 2>&1 | tee "$lf"
  else
    ( cd "$JAR_DIR" && "$MVN" -Dtmp=false "$@" ) 2>&1 | tee "$lf"
  fi
}

# --- solver-state guard --------------------------------------------------------
HEAD_BLOB="$(cd "$ROOT" && git rev-parse "HEAD:jar/src/main/kotlin/jline/solvers/ln/SolverLN.java")"
sln_is_clean(){ [[ "$(git -C "$ROOT" hash-object "$SLN")" == "$HEAD_BLOB" ]]; }
revert_sln(){ ( cd "$ROOT" && git show HEAD:jar/src/main/kotlin/jline/solvers/ln/SolverLN.java > "$SLN" ); }

# --- ablation apply/revert (THE hand-off — see plan §0.3) ----------------------
apply_ablation(){  # <condition>
  local cond="$1"
  case "$ABLATION_MECH" in
    flag)  log "ablation=$cond via runtime flag (no source change)";;          # handled in run_capture via -Dablation
    patch)
      local d="$DIFF_DIR/$cond.modification.diff"
      [[ -f "$d" ]] || { log "ERROR no diff for $cond at $d — TODO: re-derive against current SolverLN.java"; return 1; }
      revert_sln; ( cd "$ROOT" && patch -p1 < "$d" )
      run_mvn "$LOG_DIR/$cond.compile.log" compile    # recompile patched solver
      ;;
    *) log "ERROR unknown ABLATION_MECH=$ABLATION_MECH"; return 1;;
  esac
}
revert_ablation(){
  [[ "$ABLATION_MECH" == "patch" ]] || return 0
  revert_sln
  sln_is_clean && log "reverted SolverLN.java OK" || { log "FATAL revert failed"; exit 1; }
  run_mvn "$LOG_DIR/revert.compile.log" compile
}

run_capture(){ # <dataset> <condition>  (3-solver corpus capture via DataCollector)
  local ds="$1" cond="$2" out="$DATA_DIR/$ds.csv"
  skip_if_done "$out" && return 0
  local flag=(); [[ "$ABLATION_MECH" == "flag" && "$cond" != "baseline" ]] && flag=(-Dablation="$cond")
  run_mvn "$LOG_DIR/$ds.log" test -DskipTests=false \
    -Dtest=SolverLNSimpleEvaluationTest \
    -Dbaseline.outdir="$DATA_DIR" -Dbaseline.dataset="$ds" -Dbaseline.condition="$cond" \
    "${flag[@]}" || log "WARN $ds exited non-zero (rows may still be captured)"
  assert_rows "$out" || true
}

# =============================================================================
# Stage A — health checks
# =============================================================================
if have_stage A; then
  log "Stage A: health checks"
  sln_is_clean || { log "FATAL SolverLN.java has un-reverted edits — fix before baselining"; exit 1; }
  command -v "$MVN" >/dev/null || { log "FATAL no mvn"; exit 1; }
  [[ "$USE_TSP" == "1" ]] && ! command -v tsp >/dev/null && log "WARN tsp not found; timing may be noisier"
  # TODO: ping lqns-rest container — a dead container fails every LQNS column.
  run_mvn "$LOG_DIR/compile.log" compile
fi

# =============================================================================
# Stage B — medianed baseline (N=4)  → baseline-medianed.csv
# =============================================================================
if have_stage B; then
  log "Stage B: medianed baseline N=$BASELINE_REPEATS"
  for r in $(seq 1 "$BASELINE_REPEATS"); do run_capture "baseline-r$r" baseline; done
  if [[ $DRY -eq 0 ]]; then python3 "$FIG_SCRIPTS/e5_4_median.py" || log "WARN e5_4_median failed"; fi
fi

# =============================================================================
# Stage C — single-capture baseline (feeds e3.1/e7.1/e9.1/e10.1 + per-fixture rel diffs)
# =============================================================================
have_stage C && { log "Stage C: single baseline"; run_capture baseline baseline; }

# =============================================================================
# Stage D — ablation conditions (3-solver corpus)
# =============================================================================
if have_stage D; then
  log "Stage D: ablations (mech=$ABLATION_MECH)"
  # dataset:condition pairs. condition feeds apply_ablation/run_capture.
  for pair in \
      f24off:F24off f20off:F20off alloff:allOff \
      f17off:F17off f17_f24off:F17_F24off f15off:F15off \
      A2_arm_A:A2_arm_A f21+f20off:f21_f20off f23off:f23off f30off:f30off \
      f19off:F19off f19true:F19true ; do
    ds="${pair%%:*}"; cond="${pair##*:}"
    [[ -s "$DATA_DIR/$ds.csv" && $FORCE -eq 0 ]] && { log "skip ablation $ds"; continue; }
    apply_ablation "$cond" || { log "WARN skipping $ds (apply failed)"; continue; }
    run_capture "$ds" "$cond"
    revert_ablation
  done
fi

# =============================================================================
# Stage E — medianed replay (N=3) for the per-iteration F17/F24 evidence
#   Plan recommends extending to f15off,f20off,combined,alloff too.
# =============================================================================
if have_stage E; then
  ts="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"; rep="$DATA_DIR/replay-$ts"; mkdir -p "$rep"
  log "Stage E: replay N=$REPLAY_REPEATS -> $rep"
  for cond in f17off f24off f17_f24off; do            # TODO: + f15off f20off combined alloff
    apply_ablation "$cond" || { log "WARN replay skip $cond"; continue; }
    for r in $(seq 1 "$REPLAY_REPEATS"); do
      run_mvn "$rep/$cond-r$r.log" test -DskipTests=false -Dtest=SolverLNSimpleEvaluationTest \
        -Dbaseline.outdir="$rep" -Dbaseline.dataset="$cond-r$r" -Dbaseline.condition="$cond" \
        || log "WARN $cond-r$r non-zero"
    done
    revert_ablation
  done
  log "replay dir: $rep (point e6_1 + per-iter analysis at it; also re-median baseline-r* alongside)"
fi

# =============================================================================
# Stage F — F20-axis bundle (.tables.csv) + lqsim, then drift analysis
# =============================================================================
if have_stage F; then
  ts="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"; ax="$DATA_DIR/f20axis-$ts"; mkdir -p "$ax"
  log "Stage F: f20-axis tables bundle -> $ax"
  # TODO: these need .tables.csv capture (per-node dump). The corpus harness must
  # be invoked with the tables-dump enabled (see DataCollector / util tables path,
  # and FastEval -Dfasteval.dumpTable). Capture baseline, f20off, A2_arm_A, lqsim.
  log "TODO(F): capture baseline/f20off/A2_arm_A/lqsim .tables.csv into $ax, then:"
  log "  python3 $FIG_SCRIPTS/ln_drift_analysis.py $ax"
fi

# =============================================================================
# Stage G — probes
# =============================================================================
if have_stage G; then
  log "Stage G: probes"
  run_mvn "$LOG_DIR/interlock-probe.log" test -DskipTests=false \
    -Dtest=SolverLNInterlockAccuracyTest || log "WARN interlock probe"
  run_mvn "$LOG_DIR/lqns-overhead.log" test -DskipTests=false \
    -Dtest=SolverLqnsRestOverheadTest || log "WARN lqns overhead"
fi

# =============================================================================
# Stage H — FastEval contribution-optimisation studies (LNSimple-only, quiet HW)
# =============================================================================
if have_stage H; then
  log "Stage H: FastEval optimisation studies"
  log "TODO(H): run FastEval per study in plan §1.4 (iters 418/192, alpha-tol grid,"
  log "  sweep order, cache ablation, warm-start, rejected accel). Mean of >=3 runs."
  # Example single run:
  # run_mvn "$LOG_DIR/fasteval.log" test -Dtest=FastEval#runFastEval \
  #   -Dfasteval.ref=... -Dfasteval.out=jar/overnight-exploration/data/fasteval-final.csv -Dfasteval.repeats=5
fi

# =============================================================================
# Stage I — regenerate figures (skip silently if inputs missing)
# =============================================================================
if have_stage I; then
  log "Stage I: figure regen"
  for s in e3_1_partition_a_reldiff e4_1_iters_by_solver e5_2_bracket_compare \
           e5_5_lqns_no_rest e6_1_interlock_speedup e7_1_iter_ablation \
           e9_1_gap_closure e10_1_bfanout_reldiff; do
    if [[ $DRY -eq 0 ]]; then python3 "$FIG_SCRIPTS/$s.py" || log "WARN $s skipped (missing input?)"; fi
  done
fi

# =============================================================================
# Stage J — validation summary (recompute headline numbers from fresh CSVs)
# =============================================================================
if have_stage J; then
  log "Stage J: validation summary"
  log "TODO(J): emit report/data/refresh-summary.md — see plan §6. Recompute:"
  log "  iteration split (base-alloff)/(base-sim); F20 base->f20off; ArmA share;"
  log "  per-partition means; medianed f24/f17/f17_f24 speedups; corpus N per condition;"
  log "  and print a STALE-TEXT list keyed to REFRESH-INVENTORY.md line refs."
fi

log "refresh-overnight.sh complete."
